content: To be functionally specialized, many of these mechanisms must be richly structured in a content-specific way. Many of these mechanisms are functionally specialized to produce behavior that solves particular adaptive problems, such as mate selection, language acquisition, family relations, and cooperation.
location: Chapter 1, 'The Psychological Foundations of Culture,' Integrated Causal Model, p. 24
author_quote: to be functionally specialized, many of these mechanisms must be richly structured in a content-specific way
caveats: Framework derivation, not empirical finding. Tooby & Cosmides argue from the logical impossibility of content-free mechanisms solving content-specific adaptive problems; downstream empirical substantiation (cheater detection, jealousy, fear-relevant stimuli, mate preferences) is distributed across later chapters of the volume.
scope: Design-principle argument establishing why the architecture must be domain-sensitive rather than general-purpose. This is the P2 derivation statement.

content: The evolved structure of the human mind is adapted to the way of life of Pleistocene hunter-gatherers, and not necessarily to our modern circumstances. Behavior generated by mechanisms that are adaptations to an ancient way of life will not necessarily be adaptive in the modern world.
location: Introduction: Evolutionary Psychology and Conceptual Integration, pp. 5-6
author_quote: the evolved structure of the human mind is adapted to the way of life of Pleistocene hunter-gatherers, and not necessarily to our modern circumstances
caveats: Quote verified verbatim against the canonical statement of the book's third foundational assumption as reproduced on Cosmides & Tooby's UCLA cogweb archive (cogweb.ucla.edu/Abstracts/AdaptedMind_92.html): "A third assumption made by most of the contributors is that the evolved structure of the human mind is adapted to the way of life of Pleistocene hunter-gatherers, and not necessarily to our modern circumstances." The extraction's prior author_quote was identical except for a single-character OCR-style corruption ("modem" for "modern"); corrected to restore true verbatim fidelity. The quote is a contiguous sub-string of the source sentence (begins mid-sentence at "the evolved structure..."); no stitching or paraphrase. source_type=primary and evidence_quality=theoretical retained (direct statement from the editors' introduction). Note: verification source is the authors' institutional abstract/summary of the introduction, faithfully reproducing this assumption statement; the full physical book (in collection) carries the same line in the Introduction (pp. 5-6 per extraction). The content field's second sentence ("Behavior generated by mechanisms...will not necessarily be adaptive in the modern world") is a paraphrase in content, not in the quote, and was not independently located on the abstract page.
scope: The foundational EEA-discordance statement from the editors. P3 (Systematic Mismatch) cites this framing almost verbatim.

content: There is a universal human nature, but that this universality exists primarily at the level of evolved psychological mechanisms, not of expressed cultural behaviors. Cultural variability is not a challenge to claims of universality, but rather data that can give one insight into the structure of the psychological mechanisms that helped generate it.
author_quote: there is a universal human nature, but that this universality exists primarily at the level of evolved psychological mechanisms, not of expressed cultural behaviors
caveats: Theoretical framework claim. The universality-at-mechanism-level thesis resolves the apparent tension between cross-cultural variability and a shared architecture — variability is output of shared mechanisms operating on variable inputs.
scope: Spec-level claim: universality lives in the mechanisms, not in behavioral outputs. This is what P2 ('domain-sensitive interacting adaptations') means in practice.

content: Evolutionary psychologists expect to find a functional mesh between adaptive problems and the structure of the mechanisms that evolved to solve them. Over time, this causal feedback process can create designs that solve adaptive problems well — designs that 'fit' the environment in which the species evolved.
location: Introduction, 'Basic Concepts in Evolutionary Psychology and Biology,' pp. 7-8
author_quote: Evolutionary psychologists expect to find a functional mesh between adaptive problems and the structure of the mechanisms that evolved to solve them
caveats: Darwin-derived design-principle claim. The 'fit' is with the EEA, not modernity — which is the P3 setup.
scope: The functional-mesh principle linking P1 (fitness loss function) to P2 (domain-sensitive architecture): selection shapes mechanisms to match recurrent adaptive problems.

content: Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors. Systems that regulate protective responses such as vomiting and pain turn the response on whenever the benefits are greater than the costs, even if that means false alarms.
location: Chapter 3, 'Why Are Minds So Vulnerable?' and Chapter 5, pp. 40-41 and pp. 73-74
author_quote: Most of the responses that cause human suffering are unnecessary in the individual instance but still perfectly normal because they have low costs but protect against huge possible losses. They are like false alarms from smoke detectors.
caveats: Nesse's Smoke Detector Principle is a derivation from signal detection theory applied to defensive systems. It is theoretical in form but supported by large bodies of data on pain, cough, fever, vomiting, anxiety, and panic. In v2 schema this maps to evidence_quality='theoretical' because the principle itself is an architectural claim; the empirical confirmations belong supporting.
scope: Foundational statement of the asymmetric-error-cost logic that forces defensive over-activation bias (DA5) and underwrites the defensive-signal interpretation of aversive outputs (DA1).

content: The cost of not fleeing if the lion is present is 1,000 times greater than the cost of a panic attack, so the optimal strategy is to run like hell whenever the sound is loud enough to indicate a lion is present with a probability greater than 1/1,000. This means that 999 times out of 1,000 you will flee unnecessarily. However, 1 time out of 1,000, fleeing will save your life.
author_quote: The cost of not fleeing if the lion is present is 1,000 times greater than the cost of a panic attack, so the optimal strategy is to run like hell whenever the sound is loud enough to indicate a lion is present with a probability greater than 1/1,000.
caveats: Nesse's quantitative derivation of the optimal false-alarm rate. This is the most concrete expression of the Smoke Detector Principle and grounds the panic-disorder-as-normal-architecture-under-mismatch claim.
scope: Quantitative demonstration that a well-calibrated defensive system will fire falsely the vast majority of the time and still be optimal — dissolving the naive intuition that 'useless' panic implies broken design.

content: Diseases themselves do not have evolutionary explanations. They are not adaptations shaped by natural selection. The correct question is: Why did natural selection shape traits that make us vulnerable to disease? Selection maximizes reproduction, not health, and the unpleasantness of defenses such as pain, cough, and anxiety is just part of their utility.
location: Chapter 3, 'Viewing Diseases As Adaptations (VDAA) warning,' pp. 41-42
author_quote: Selection maximizes reproduction, not health, and the unpleasantness of defenses such as pain, cough, and anxiety is just part of their utility.
caveats: Nesse warns that 'Viewing Diseases As Adaptations' (VDAA) is the most common error in evolutionary medicine. This extraction captures the correct framing: defenses are adaptations; diseases are the conditions those defenses respond to. Important for Cor because it bounds DA1: the defensive-signal interpretation applies to the defenses themselves, not to the pathologies whose signals they are.
scope: Boundary condition for DA1. Distinguishes the two categories Cor must keep separate: the architecture-level defensive outputs (which are intelligible signals) vs the conditions triggering them (which may or may not be adaptive).

content: The ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy). These designate specific functional networks of evolutionarily very ancient regions of our brains.
location: Preface, 'Why Psychiatrists, Physicians, and Psychotherapists Should Understand the Seven Basic Affective Systems,' p. xi
author_quote: the ancient subcortical regions of mammalian brains contain at least seven basic affective systems: SEEKING (expectancy), FEAR (anxiety), RAGE (anger), LUST (sexual excitement), CARE (nurturance), PANIC/GRIEF (sadness), and PLAY (social joy)
caveats: Panksepp's seven-systems taxonomy is supported by decades of cross-species neurophysiology (deep brain stimulation, lesion studies, pharmacology) across mammals and some birds. Per Cor's 'what we take / what we don't take' from the handoff: we take the reality of subcortical affective-motivational systems and phylogenetic conservation; we do NOT take 'exactly seven natural kinds' or a one-to-one mapping to experienced emotions (Barrett's bridge thesis applies here).
scope: Primary taxonomy of phylogenetically ancient affective systems. Source for M1 (FEAR/RAGE → Threat Management), M2 (SEEKING → Pursuit), M3 (PANIC/GRIEF → Social Bonding grief mode; CARE overlaps), M4 (PLAY), M9 (CARE), M14 (LUST).

content: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks. Across many species of warm-blooded vertebrates, a variety of basic emotional networks are anatomically situated in similar brain regions, and these networks serve remarkably similar functions.
author_quote: These subcortical brain networks are quite similar in all mammals, but they are not identical in all details. This similarity extends even to certain species of birds that, for instance, also have separation-distress PANIC networks
caveats: Cross-species conservation is established across mammals and extends into birds for specific systems (separation-distress PANIC). Evidence for the phylogenetic depth of these circuits is strong.
scope: Phylogenetic conservation argument grounding DA8 (phylogenetic priority). If the affective systems are shared with mammals and birds, they are older than human-specific cognition and have priority when strongly activated.

content: Mental life would be impossible without this foundation. There, among the ancestral brain networks that we share with other mammals, a few ounces of brain tissue constitute the bedrock of our emotional lives, generating the many primal ways in which we can feel emotionally good or bad within ourselves. The primary-process emotions are all connected to movements, and the evidence now indicates that raw emotional feelings arise from the same ancient brain networks that control our instinctual emotional life.
author_quote: raw emotional feelings arise from the same ancient brain networks that control our instinctual emotional life
caveats: Panksepp's hierarchical-processing claim: primary-process (evolved subcortical) systems generate raw affect; secondary-process (learning) and tertiary-process (cognitive) layers build on this foundation. The foundation cannot be bypassed. This is the architectural statement that DA8 (phylogenetic priority) formalizes.
scope: DA8's core claim: older systems have functional priority over newer ones. Panksepp's formulation is that higher (cortical) processes require the subcortical foundation to function at all; when the older systems are strongly active, they can suppress or commandeer the newer ones.

content: Panksepp's textbook Affective Neuroscience establishes the methodology and evidence base for the seven subcortical affective systems. Across cross-species deep brain stimulation, lesion, and pharmacological studies, the same brain regions produce the same functional categories of affective response — SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, LUST, CARE, PANIC, PLAY — across mammals, providing the empirical foundation for treating these as conserved motivational architecture rather than culturally constructed categories.
caveats: The 1998 textbook is the founding methodological statement; the 2012 Archaeology of Mind extractions above contain the verbatim passages. This work is included as a pillar in its own right because several downstream references in Cor cite Affective Neuroscience (1998) specifically rather than the 2012 popularization. Content here is a volume-level summary rather than a line-level verbatim passage; author_quote is NULL because I did not pull a specific quoted line from the 1998 text in this session.
scope: Volume-level stake: the 1998 textbook is the citation weight-bearer for Panksepp in the neuroscience literature. Phase 6 mechanism-evidence junctions for M1/M2/M3/M4/M9/M14 should also link back to the 2012 book extractions where the verbatim quotes live.

content: For a biological system, the environment of adaptedness is the environment within which the system gradually became evolved — its environment of evolutionary adaptedness. A behavioural system can be in functionally effective order, namely capable of achieving functional consequences, yet the current environment may deviate in greater or less degree from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness and so does not conform to that required for function to be fulfilled.
location: Chapter 4, 'Man's Environment of Evolutionary Adaptedness,' p. 50, and Chapter 9, p. 128
author_quote: the current environment deviates in greater or less degree from the environment of evolutionary adaptedness and so does not conform to that required for function to be fulfilled
caveats: Bowlby is the originator of the 'environment of evolutionary adaptedness' (EEA) concept that subsequent evolutionary psychology inherited. The quoted passage is his explicit formulation that intact systems can fail when the current environment departs from EEA — this is the deepest root of P3 (Systematic Mismatch) and DA1 (defensive signals under mismatch). Bowlby states it as a theoretical/logical distinction, not as an empirical finding about any specific modern pathology.
scope: Foundational derivation of the mismatch framework. Bowlby is distinguishing two failure modes: (a) the system is intact but the environment is outside EEA — this is mismatch; (b) the system itself is not in functionally effective order — this is damage or maldevelopment. Cor's distinction between 'defensive activation under mismatch' and 'damage/dysregulation' descends directly from this passage.

content: In the higher vertebrates most behavioural systems are to some extent environmentally labile — the form they take in an adult turns in some degree on the kind of environment in which that adult is reared. The advantage of this is that the form ultimately to be taken by the system is in some degree left open so that it can, during development, become adapted to the particular environment in which the individual finds himself. Provided the environment met with during development lies within certain limits, the ultimate form of a behavioural system may be well adapted. But when the environment in which development takes place falls outside those limits the form taken by the system may be ill adapted.
author_quote: In Chapter 3 it was emphasised that in the higher vertebrates most behavioural systems are to some extent environmentally labile, namely, the form they take in an adult turns in some degree on the kind of environment in which that adult is reared. The advantage of this is that the form ultimately to be taken by the system is in some degree left open so that it can, during development, become adapted to the particular environment in which the individual finds himself. Such flexibility, however, is not without its price. Provided the environment met with during development lies within certain limits, the ultimate form of a behavioural system may be well adapted, namely be such that, when activated, it commonly achieves a functional consequence. But when the environment in which development takes place falls outside those limits the form taken by the system may be ill adapted, namely be such that, when activated, it fails often or always to achieve a functional consequence.
caveats: Bowlby's developmental-calibration thesis: in higher vertebrates most behavioural systems are environmentally labile — the adult form depends in some degree on the rearing environment. Within certain environmental limits the calibrated form is well adapted (achieves its functional consequence); outside those limits it may be ill adapted (fails to achieve it). This is the narrow, architectural version of developmental calibration that DA7 takes (distinguished from broad life-history-theory calibration, which DA7 rejects). [Quote corrected 2026-05-29: the prior author_quote ("In the higher vertebrates behavioural systems are more often environmentally labile, responsive to more complex cues, and in their means of integration more likely to include causal or plan hierarchies.") was a MISMATCHED verbatim passage from Chapter 3 (p. 79) about phylogenetic/ontogenetic organisation of behaviour — it did NOT support this content claim and contradicted the record's stated location (Ch. 9 'Function,' pp. 128-129). An earlier caveat mislabelled that p.79 sentence as the correct source text. Replaced with the genuine, contiguous verbatim passage from Chapter 9 'Function,' pp. 128-129 (Attachment and Loss, Vol. 1, 2nd ed.), which directly states the labile/well-adapted/ill-adapted-within-limits claim. Source: full-text PDF of the 2nd edition at mindsplain.com (page break "-129-" falls mid-passage, confirming pp. 128-129).]
scope: DA7's core claim: specific systems calibrate during specific developmental windows within evolved parameters. The calibration itself is adaptive; the mismatch between the calibration environment and the later operating environment is where problems emerge.

content: Experiments assessing visual detection latencies have confirmed that when people are shown large sets of stimulus pictures, snakes automatically capture their visual attention, regardless of how many distractor stimuli are present. Fear responses can be learned and activated, even when backward masking prevents images of snakes from reaching higher cortical processing. This indicates that fear responses reside in ancient neural circuits that evolved long before the full development of the neocortex. Humans and higher primates have a fear module that evolved to reduce recurrent threats posed by dangerous and potentially lethal animals.
location: Chapter 3, 'Methods of Evolutionary Sciences,' pp. 130-131 (Öhman & Mineka program citations)
author_quote: fear responses reside in ancient neural circuits that evolved long before the full development of the neocortex
caveats: This is the Öhman & Mineka fear-module research program summarized in the Buss Handbook Vol 1 methods chapter. The finding pattern (preferential visual capture by fear-relevant stimuli, preserved conditioning under backward masking, specific amygdala involvement) is genuinely replicated across labs and methods. Primary pathway here is M1 (Threat Management) with a DA8 phylogenetic-priority inference.
scope: Empirical anchor for the phylogenetic priority of the fear system and for its pre-cortical operation. Supports M1's claim that threat detection can override cortical processing and is evolutionarily ancient.

content: According to the strategic pluralism model of mating, women evolved to make trade-offs between two sets of attributes when evaluating men as potential mates: men's degree of health/viability ('good genes') and their level of commitment/investment in the relationship and subsequent offspring. The ovulatory shift hypothesis predicts and confirms that women's mate preferences vary across the reproductive cycle in very specific and theoretically consistent ways — including preference for more symmetrical men as short-term mates specifically during high-fertility windows.
location: Chapter 3, 'Methods of Evolutionary Sciences,' Mate Preferences Across the Reproductive Cycle section, pp. 130-131
author_quote: women's mate preferences vary across the reproductive cycle in very specific and theoretically consistent ways
caveats: The ovulatory shift literature has been subject to subsequent replication debate; this extraction captures the evidence summary as presented in the 2016 Handbook. Cor's M14 treats reproductive motivation as sex-differentiated and complex; this extraction supports the female-side architecture.
scope: Primary evidence for the sex-differentiated architecture of M14 (Reproductive Motivation). Also bears on the strategic-pluralism framing of mate-preference tradeoffs.

content: Culture is interesting and important because its evolutionary behavior is distinctly different from that of genes. The human cultural system arose as an adaptation, because it can evolve fancy adaptations to changing environments rather more swiftly than is possible by genes alone. Culture would never have evolved unless it could do things that genes can't. The equipment in human brains, the hormone-producing glands, and the nature of our bodies play a fundamental role in how we learn and why we prefer some ideas to others.
author_quote: Culture would never have evolved unless it could do things that genes can't
caveats: Richerson & Boyd's formal statement that culture is itself an evolved adaptation — a second inheritance system that co-evolves with genes. This is the constraint they place on P3: 'matched' cannot mean 'ancestral environment minus culture,' because culture is part of the evolved expected environment of humans. Cultural scaffolding is itself adapted-for. [Normalization note: source text reads "genes can't!" (with exclamation mark); author_quote drops the trailing exclamation. Apostrophe normalized from curly to straight. Flagged by codex-research audit 2026-04-05.]
scope: P3 constraint. Prevents naive 'return to the Pleistocene' readings of mismatch. The human expected environment includes cultural transmission, norms, shared narratives, and institutions.

content: Culture is as much a part of human biology as walking upright. Culture is taught by motivated human teachers, acquired by motivated learners, and stored and manipulated in human brains. Culture is an evolving product of populations of human brains, brains that have been shaped by natural selection to learn and manage culture. Culture-making brains are the product of more than two million years of more or less gradual increases in brain size and cultural complexity. During this period, culture must have increased the reproductive success of our ancestors; otherwise, the features of our brain that make culture possible would not have evolved.
author_quote: Culture-making brains are the product of more than two million years of more or less gradual increases in brain size and cultural complexity
caveats: Gene-culture coevolution timescale claim. Culture and the brain architecture for acquiring culture co-evolved over the Pleistocene. This means human psychology has evolved expectations of cultural-transmission input (norms, teaching, shared narratives) in addition to physical-environment input.
scope: Bridges P2 (domain-sensitive adaptations) and P3 (mismatch). Some of the 'domain-sensitive adaptations' are specifically tuned for receiving cultural input, which means mismatch can occur at the cultural layer too — not only at the ancestral-physical-environment layer.

content: Most of what was known experimentally about human psychology and behavior was based on studies with undergraduates from Western societies. At the time, 96 percent of experimental participants were drawn from northern Europe, North America, or Australia, and about 70 percent of these were American undergraduates. When cross-cultural data were available from multiple populations, Western samples typically anchored the extreme end of the distribution. They were psychologically weird.
author_quote: When cross-cultural data were available from multiple populations, Western samples typically anchored the extreme end of the distribution. They were psychologically weird.
caveats: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) BBS paper findings, reiterated as the founding observation of the book. The underlying evidence is a systematic review across many cross-cultural measurements, so evidence_quality='meta_analysis' is appropriate. WEIRD stands for Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic.
scope: Provides the empirical diagnostic for how modern environments depart from the typical human range. Critical for P3 because it shows that existing psychology is itself a sample from the mismatched side of the distribution — modernity isn't a baseline, it's an outlier.

content: Psychological differences between populations appeared in many important domains, indicating much greater variation than one might expect from reading the textbooks or major journals in either psychology or behavioral economics. Existing research going back over a half century had revealed differences across populations in people's susceptibility to visual illusions, spatial reasoning, memory, attention, patience, risk-taking, fairness, induction, executive function, and pattern recognition.
author_quote: existing research going back over a half century had revealed differences across populations in people's susceptibility to visual illusions, spatial reasoning, memory, attention, patience, risk-taking, fairness, induction, executive function, and pattern recognition
caveats: Cross-cultural psychology review. The specific domains listed are all in literatures that predate Henrich's synthesis. This extraction enumerates where WEIRD populations appear to be outliers, which is the empirical base for the P3 scope question: how much of 'human psychology' is actually WEIRD psychology?
scope: Scope evidence for P3. Tells us which domains show the largest WEIRD departure (visual perception through fairness norms) and therefore which domains are most likely to show strong mismatch effects in Cor's architecture.

content: My thesis is that egalitarianism does not result from the mere absence of hierarchy. Rather, egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings. If a stable egalitarian hierarchy is to be achieved, the basic flow of power in society must be reversed definitively. Our political nature favors the formation of orthodox hierarchies — hierarchies like those of chimpanzees or gorillas, or humans living in chiefdoms or states. It is politically ambitious individuals, those with special learned or innate propensities to dominate, who are likely to become upstarts in egalitarian bands or tribes.
location: Chapter 1, 'The Question of Egalitarian Society,' pp. 8-9
author_quote: egalitarianism involves a very special type of hierarchy, a curious type that is based on antihierarchical feelings
caveats: Boehm's reverse-dominance hypothesis. The claim is theoretical in form but grounded in systematic ethnographic survey of hunter-gatherer and tribal societies. The DA6 relevance: humans carry BOTH dominance and anti-dominance motives, and egalitarian bands are the equilibrium that the anti-dominance coalition can enforce against the upstart tendency.
scope: DA6 (Competing Motivational Programs) evidence. Shows that the competing-programs architecture is visible at the political level: the same humans who can turn into dominators are also the ones who coalition against dominators. The tension is architectural, not a cultural accident.

content: In small local groups that are egalitarian, such as bands, the main political actors — usually adult heads of households — are the individuals who actively participate when the entire group must arrive at important consensual decisions. When the subordinates take charge to firmly suppress competition that leads to domination, it takes some effort to keep the political tables turned. For the most part, the mere threat of sanctions (including ostracism and execution) keeps such power seekers in their place.
author_quote: it takes some effort to keep the political tables turned
caveats: Leveling-coalition mechanism. Ostracism, ridicule, and in extreme cases execution are the enforcement tools used by subordinate coalitions to maintain egalitarian equilibria against upstart pressure.
scope: M11 (Cooperation / Alliance) evidence. Provides the coalition-enforcement mechanism that sustains reciprocity norms against cheaters and would-be dominators.

content: Mothers and Others is about the emergence of a particular mode of childrearing known as 'cooperative breeding' and its psychological implications for apes in the line leading to Homo sapiens. Cooperative breeding refers to any species with alloparental assistance in both the care and provisioning of young. Unlike mothers among other African apes, who nurtured infants on their own, these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children and keep them on the survivable side of starvation.
author_quote: these early hominin mothers relied on groupmates to help protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing children
caveats: Hrdy's cooperative-breeding thesis: human infants evolved under a care regime requiring multiple adults. The theoretical framing is forced by energetics (~13 million calories to raise a human to maturity) plus the observed alloparenting behavior in contemporary hunter-gatherers. Primary link is M9 (Care / Alloparenting); M3 (Social Bonding) link reflects the infant-side architecture for eliciting care from multiple figures.
scope: M9 load-bearing claim. The organism expects a village, not solo parenting. Nuclear-family isolation is a P3 mismatch for M9.

content: It takes on the order of 13 million calories to rear a modern human from birth to maturity, and the young of these early hominins would also have been very costly. Unlike other ape youngsters, they would have depended on nutritional subsidies from caregivers long after they were weaned. Years before a mother's previous children were self-sufficient, she would give birth to another infant, and the care these dependent youngsters required would be far in excess of what a foraging mother by herself could regularly supply.
author_quote: It takes on the order of 13 million calories to rear a modern human from birth to maturity
caveats: The energetics argument that makes cooperative breeding non-optional for humans. A foraging mother cannot supply this alone; therefore alloparental provisioning was already selected-for in the ancestral environment.
scope: Forces M9 as a real architectural expectation rather than a cultural add-on. A human mother without alloparental support is operating her CARE system outside its expected input range.

content: Your emotions are not built-in but made from more basic parts. They are not universal but vary from culture to culture. They are not triggered; you create them. They emerge as a combination of the physical properties of your body, a flexible brain that wires itself to whatever environment it develops in, and your culture and upbringing, which provide that environment. Emotions are real, but not in the objective sense that molecules or neurons are real. They are real in the same sense that money is real — that is, hardly an illusion, but a product of human agreement.
location: Introduction: The Search for Emotion's 'Fingerprints,' pp. xii-xiii
author_quote: Emotions are real, but not in the objective sense that molecules or neurons are real. They are real in the same sense that money is real — that is, hardly an illusion, but a product of human agreement.
caveats: Barrett's theory of constructed emotion is Cor's bridge case: she critiques folk emotion categories (sadness, anger, fear as natural kinds) but her data do not actually overturn the subcortical affective-motivational systems Panksepp documents. In Cor the resolution is: the primary-process systems are real; the named categories are cultural overlays. foundation_codes=[] because she does not ground a foundation directly — this extraction supports the Bridge Thesis in v2_bridge_theses.
scope: Bridge Thesis primary contribution. Scopes which aspects of 'emotion' are architectural (the subcortical systems Panksepp describes) versus constructed (the folk categories).

content: Extrapolating from the relationship between neocortex size and group size for monkeys and apes gives a group size of about 150 — the limit on the number of social relationships that humans can have. For the twenty-odd tribal societies where census data are available, clan groups turn out to have a mean size of 153. The sizes of all but one of the village- and clan-like groupings for these societies fall between one hundred and 230. Once you start to look, groups of about this size turn up everywhere — in military units, in business organizations, in Christmas-card networks.
author_quote: for the twenty-odd tribal societies where census data are available, these clan groups turn out to have a mean size of 153
caveats: The ~150 cognitive ceiling is derived from the primate neocortex-ratio regression and cross-validated across hunter-gatherer ethnography, military unit sizes, pre-industrial village sizes, and Christmas-card network surveys. Evidence_quality='replicated' reflects the multi-method convergence. The specific number has some statistical slack (ranges from ~100 to ~230 in the cross-cultural data).
scope: DA2 parameter value. Provides the numerical ceiling on 'natural' social architecture that modern environments routinely violate (cities of millions, social media networks of thousands) — which is the P3 mismatch case for M3 (Social Bonding).

content: A rule of thumb commonly used in business organisation theory is that organisations of fewer than 150 people work fine on a person-to-person basis, but once they grow larger than this they need a formal hierarchy if they are to work efficiently. Sociologists have known since the 1950s that there is a critical threshold in the region of 150 to two hundred, with larger companies suffering a disproportionate amount of absenteeism and sickness.
author_quote: organisations of fewer than 150 people work fine on a person-to-person basis, but once they grow larger than this they need a formal hierarchy if they are to work efficiently
caveats: Sociological/organizational finding cited by Dunbar, not his primary research. The absenteeism/sickness effect above the 150 threshold is suggestive but not a rigorously controlled result. Evidence_quality='theoretical' because the causal claim (exceeding Dunbar's number drives health outcomes) is inferential rather than directly demonstrated in randomized designs.
scope: Practical DA2 consequence: exceeding the natural scale of coherent face-to-face relations correlates with emergence of formal hierarchy and some health-outcome degradation. Supports the mismatch framing for modern workplaces and cities.

content: After a tuberculosis outbreak eliminated the most aggressive adult males from a baboon troop, the remaining troop — now with a 2:1 female-to-male ratio and disproportionately unaggressive and affiliative males — stayed close together, sat in contact, and groomed more than average. Levels of aggression were lower, and in an informative way: males still had a dominance hierarchy and fought with their rivals, but there was minimal displacement aggression onto innocent bystanders. Stress hormone levels were low; the neurochemistry of anxiety and benzodiazepines worked differently in these individuals. When male adolescents transferred in from other troops over the following years — having grown up in typical aggressive troops — they adopted the style of low aggression and high affiliation. The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
location: Behave, Chapter 9, the Forest Troop narrative, pp. ~418-420 (ref Sapolsky & Share 2004)
author_quote: The troop's social culture was being transmitted.
caveats: Sapolsky & Share 2004 PLoS Biology Forest Troop natural experiment. Multi-generation observation of one baboon troop across years, capturing cultural transmission of peaceful behavior to new males after tuberculosis die-off of aggressive alphas. Will also migrate to the Empirical Demonstrations section as ED1.
scope: Empirical demonstration that the pathological features of orthodox hierarchy (M5 status-defeat cascade, M1 displacement aggression, elevated stress hormones) can be reversed by removing the individuals propagating aggressive norms — even without changing the institutional structure. Key applied evidence for the possibility of environmental correction.

content: The adult males going to raid the garbage dump were the most aggressive and least affiliative members of the troop — they were willing to forgo morning socializing (grooming, sitting in contact, play) in exchange for competing against fifty or sixty strangers for food. The selection pressure of the tuberculosis outbreak was therefore not random: it removed precisely the males whose behavioral style was highest on the aggression/low-affiliation axis.
location: Behave, Chapter 9, Forest Troop narrative, p. ~418
author_quote: The males who went each morning were the most aggressive, least affiliative members of the troop.
caveats: Supports the causal interpretation of the Forest Troop observation: the selection pressure was behaviorally specific, making the subsequent low-aggression culture a consequence of removing aggressive individuals rather than a randomly lucky post-outbreak composition.

content: The critical difference now seems to be that humans not only understand others as intentional agents but also put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality, including everything from concrete acts of collaborative problem solving to complex cultural institutions. The focus now is thus less on culture as a process of transmission and more on culture as a process of social coordination. Modern human cultures were made possible by an earlier evolutionary step in which individuals made a living by coordinating with others in relatively simple acts of collaborative foraging.
author_quote: humans not only understand others as intentional agents but also put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality
caveats: Tomasello's shared-intentionality hypothesis is theoretical in form but grounded in decades of comparative developmental experiments with children and great apes. The two-step claim (joint intentionality → collective intentionality) is Tomasello's specific contribution. foundation_codes=[] because this is a mechanism-level claim for M11 rather than a foundation-grounding extraction.
scope: M11 (Cooperation / Alliance) theoretical foundation. Shared intentionality is the cognitive substrate on which reciprocal exchange, cheater detection, and coalition dynamics build.

content: Inclusive fitness is the sum of an individual's own reproductive success plus the reproductive success of relatives weighted by their coefficient of relatedness (r). Natural selection maximizes inclusive fitness, not individual fitness. Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism will spread when rB > C, where r = coefficient of relatedness between actor and recipient, B = reproductive benefit to the recipient, and C = reproductive cost to the actor. This single inequality provides the first rigorous Darwinian explanation for how genes that reduce the carrier's own reproduction can nevertheless be favored by selection — because copies of the same gene are differentially propagated through relatives.
location: Part I — The Genetical Theory of Social Behaviour
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Hamilton WD, 1964). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Hamilton explicitly derives the condition under which altruistic dispositions toward kin are stable: kB > C where k = 1/r. For full siblings (r=0.5), altruistic acts evolve when the benefit to the sibling is more than twice the cost to the actor. For cousins (r=0.125), the benefit must exceed eight times the cost. This produces a gradient of expected altruism strictly proportional to genetic relatedness — a testable prediction confirmed across taxa including eusocial Hymenoptera (haplodiploid r=0.75 among sisters) and human ethnographic data on investment in kin.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Hamilton WD, 1964). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Interface Theory of Perception (ITP): perceptual systems have been shaped by natural selection to provide a species-specific fitness interface, not a veridical window on objective reality. Hoffman, Singh, and Prakash formalize perceptual strategies using evolutionary game theory: strategies compete in various worlds under various fitness functions. Result: veridical perception strategies (those tuned to the true structure of the world) are routinely dominated by non-veridical strategies tuned purely to fitness. Veridical perceptions escape extinction only in the special case where fitness varies monotonically with truth — a vanishingly rare condition in realistic environments.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Hoffman DD, Singh M, Prakash C, 2015). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Formal classification of perceptual strategies in evolutionary games: Hoffman et al. define strategies as mappings from world states to perceptual states to actions. They show that (a) 'truth' strategies (perceive world states faithfully) and (b) 'interface' strategies (perceive only fitness payoff values) can be pitted against each other. Across a wide range of simulated worlds with non-monotonic fitness functions (the realistic case), interface strategies consistently outcompete truth strategies because the cognitive cost of veridical representation is not rewarded by selection. Implication: there is no evolutionary reason to expect that our categories (color, space, object) correspond to objective structure in reality — they correspond to what keeps our ancestors alive and reproducing.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Hoffman DD, Singh M, Prakash C, 2015). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Fitness-Beats-Truth Theorem (FBT): Prakash, Stephens, Hoffman, Singh, and Fields formalize and prove that, under assumptions standard in perceptual and cognitive science (perception as inference to objective world states), a strategy that simply maximizes expected fitness payoff — with no attempt to estimate true world states — does consistently better than any strategy that tries to infer truth. The theorem is a formal, mathematical result within evolutionary game theory combined with Bayesian decision theory. It falsifies the standard claim in perception science that natural selection favors veridical perception.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Prakash C, Stephens KD, Hoffman DD, Sing, 2021). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: The probability that perception provides veridical congruence with reality plummets to zero as the complexity of the world and of perception increases. In simple worlds with small state spaces, a lucky monotonic relationship between truth and fitness can occur. But realistic worlds have non-monotonic fitness landscapes (too little water kills, just right keeps you alive, too much drowns you) — in such worlds, perceiving only fitness points is strictly superior to perceiving actual amounts. As world complexity scales up, the measure of fitness functions that preserve any monotonic truth-relationship shrinks to zero.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Prakash C, Stephens KD, Hoffman DD, Sing, 2021). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: The discordance hypothesis: the human genome was shaped under Paleolithic nutritional conditions and has changed negligibly since the advent of agriculture (~10,000 years ago). Modern diseases of civilization — atherosclerosis, hypertension, obesity, diabetes — result from the mismatch between our evolved metabolic physiology and contemporary dietary patterns. The genome expects one nutritional environment and receives a fundamentally different one.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Eaton SB, Konner M, 1985). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Ancestral human diet was characterized by: higher protein (34% vs 12% of calories), dramatically lower refined carbohydrate and sugar, higher fiber (100-150g/day vs 20g), lower sodium, higher potassium, higher micronutrient density, and near-zero processed food. Modern Western diet diverges from these parameters in almost every measurable dimension simultaneously.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Eaton SB, Konner M, 1985). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: The Mismatch Hypothesis formalized: psychological mechanisms evolved to process ancestral environmental inputs, producing adaptive outputs in ancestral contexts. Modern environments differ from ancestral ones in input quantity, intensity, and fitness associations, causing mechanisms to produce maladaptive output. Li, van Vugt, and Colarelli review mismatch evidence in three domains: (a) physical and mental health (food sweetness preferences leading to diabetes, myopia from near-work replacing outdoor visual stimuli, postpartum depression from absent kin support and reduced breastfeeding/sunshine/omega-3/activity), (b) mating (media exposure shifting mate-value calibration, contraceptives altering mate preferences, population density delaying reproduction), and (c) work and organizations (leadership selection biased toward ancestral physical cues, kinship-organizational tension from evolved nepotism, workspace design lacking natural elements).
caveats: REMEDIATED — Codex audit 2026-04-09. Original flagged CONTENT_PARAPHRASE_DRIFT: over-extended into pathology list (obesity, depression, anxiety, addiction, loneliness, political polarization) the paper does not make. Rewritten from full text (van Vugt website PDF). Paper reviews mismatch evidence in three domains, not a pathology enumeration.

content: Li, van Vugt, and Colarelli classify evolutionary mismatch along four dimensions: (1) source — natural changes vs human-induced environmental changes; (2) type — forced (new environment imposed on organism) vs hijacked (novel stimuli exploit mechanisms evolved for different inputs); (3) cause — changes in input (intensity change, missing input, or input replaced by novel/fake cues with similar attributes) vs changes in consequences of output; (4) consequences — effects on reproductive fitness (increase or decrease) crossed with effects on individual well-being (desirable or undesirable). These four dimensions generate a taxonomy that moves beyond simple ancestral-good/modern-bad framing to identify specific mechanism-environment interaction failures.
caveats: REMEDIATED — Codex audit 2026-04-09. Original flagged CONTENT_INVENTED: three numbered testable predictions were fabricated, not in the paper. Rewritten from full text (van Vugt website PDF). Paper classifies mismatch along four dimensions (source, type, cause, consequences) via Tables 1-3.

content: Error Management Theory (EMT): when the costs of false-positive and false-negative errors were asymmetric over evolutionary history, selection favors psychological mechanisms that are predictably biased in the direction that minimizes the more costly error — not mechanisms that minimize total errors or achieve Bayesian optimality. This is a domain-specific alternative to the heuristics-and-biases program: biases are not cognitive flaws but adaptive design features. Haselton and Buss formalize: a mechanism will be biased toward the less costly error type whenever the cost asymmetry persisted recurrently in ancestral environments.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Haselton MG, Buss DM, 2000). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Study 2 novel prediction: EMT predicts a complementary bias in women — underperception of men's commitment (because the cost of falsely inferring commitment and being abandoned with offspring was historically much greater for women than the cost of missing a real commitment signal). Haselton and Buss documented the commitment underperception effect: women significantly underestimated men's commitment levels relative to men's self-reports, in the same paradigm in which men overestimated women's sexual intent. This was a novel a priori prediction derived directly from the asymmetric cost structure — a stronger test of EMT than the already-known sexual overperception effect.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Haselton MG, Buss DM, 2000). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Incentive salience hypothesis (founding statement): Berridge and Robinson propose that mesolimbic dopamine does NOT mediate the hedonic impact of rewards ('liking'), does NOT mediate reward learning per se, but instead mediates the attribution of incentive salience — the process by which neural representations of reward-related stimuli become motivationally 'wanted.' Wanting (incentive salience) is a distinct, dissociable psychological process from liking (hedonic impact) and from learning (associative prediction). This three-way dissociation reframes the entire reward literature: dopamine is necessary for wanting but not for liking or for learning what to like.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Berridge KC, Robinson TE, 1998). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Empirical basis for the dissociation (1998 review): Berridge and Robinson review converging evidence that (a) dopamine depletion leaves taste hedonic reactions (orofacial 'liking' responses to sweet tastes) intact, (b) normal new hedonic learning proceeds without intact dopamine neurotransmission, (c) pharmacological hedonic enhancement of palatability is preserved after dopamine depletion, yet (d) dopamine depletion abolishes the motivation to pursue the same rewards. They conclude: dopamine systems are necessary for 'wanting' incentives, but not for 'liking' them or for learning new 'likes' and 'dislikes.'
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Berridge KC, Robinson TE, 1998). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Experimental demonstration of altruistic punishment: in repeated public-goods games, participants were willing to pay a personal cost to punish free-riders even when (a) punishment yielded no material benefit to the punisher, (b) interactions were one-shot with no reputational gain, and (c) the punisher would never meet the punished again. Fehr and Gächter's key design innovation was to eliminate all standard self-interest explanations (kin selection, direct reciprocity, reputation) and still observe robust punishment behavior. Across treatments, 84% of participants punished at least once. This falsifies purely selfish models of human cooperation.
caveats: Single cited study (Fehr & Gächter 2002, Nature) is the landmark; altruistic punishment in public-goods games is among the most-replicated effects in experimental economics. 'replicated' reflects field-wide replication, not this one paper.

content: Cooperation collapses without altruistic punishment, flourishes with it: in the no-punishment treatment, cooperation decayed from ~65% of endowment contributed in round 1 to ~20% by round 10 — the standard public-goods decay pattern. In the punishment treatment, cooperation rose to ~80-95% of endowment by round 10 and was maintained. The difference was dramatic and persistent. Critically, this held even in 'stranger' designs where group composition was reshuffled each round, eliminating any direct-reciprocity explanation. Cooperation is stable when and only when there exist mechanisms for punishing defectors — even at personal cost to the punisher.
caveats: As EXT-49: graded on the field-wide replication of altruistic-punishment effects; the single cited work is the origin study (Fehr & Gächter 2002).

content: Meta-analytic finding: across 148 independent studies pooling 308,849 participants followed for an average of 7.5 years, individuals with stronger social relationships had a 50% increased likelihood of survival compared to individuals with weaker social relationships (random-effects weighted OR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.42-1.59). The association held consistently across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, and follow-up period. This is the largest, best-controlled quantification of the social-relationships-and-mortality link available.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB, 2010). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Moderator analysis: the association between social relationships and mortality was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91), i.e., multidimensional indices capturing quality and diversity of relationships, and weakest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone vs. with others, OR = 1.19). This gradient indicates that mere co-presence is insufficient; what matters is the structural richness of the social network, not just whether someone shares a roof. The finding rules out the simple hypothesis that mere co-presence buffers stress, and points to relationship quality and network structure as the operative variables.
author_quote: the association was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91; 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23) and lowest for binary indicators of residential status (living alone versus with others) (OR = 1.19; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44).
caveats: [Quote hygiene 2026-07-18] author_quote sourced from the open-access full text (Holt-Lunstad, Smith & Layton 2010, PLoS Med, PMC2910600), moderator-analysis sentence; web-sourced, confirm character-exact on a final verbatim pass. Separately, the content phrase 'co-presence buffers stress' was a paraphrase/strawman gloss (confirmed absent from the paper) and its quote marks were removed so it is no longer presented as a source quotation. Em dash cleaned.

content: Graded dose-response relationship between the number of adverse childhood experience categories and adult health outcomes. Persons exposed to 4+ ACE categories showed 4- to 12-fold increased risk for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempt compared to those with zero ACEs. The relationship is cumulative and cross-domain: it is the breadth of adversity categories, not the severity of any single type, that predicts adult outcomes.
caveats: Single foundational cohort (ACE Study, Felitti et al. 1998); the dose-response relationship has since been widely reproduced. Demoted from 'replicated' (this row cites one study).

content: Childhood adversity predicts adult outcomes across fundamentally different domains: substance abuse (alcoholism, drug abuse, smoking), mental health (depression, suicide attempt), sexual behavior (50+ partners, STDs), and self-reported health status. The same upstream exposure produces downstream effects across behavioral, psychological, and physiological systems simultaneously. This pattern demonstrates that perturbations cascade across domains rather than remaining contained.
caveats: Single ACE cohort (Felitti et al. 1998); broad subsequent reproduction. Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: Stress mediators — cortisol, catecholamines, cytokines — are protective in the short term through allostasis (adaptation to challenge) but produce cumulative damage when chronically elevated. This dual nature means the same biological systems that keep the organism alive in the short term destroy it in the long term under sustained mismatch conditions.
caveats: Provisional — awaiting fresh extraction from the original 1998 NEJM and 1993 Archives of Internal Medicine papers. Juster 2010 and McEwen 2012 currently carry the matured allostatic-load framework at pillar tier.

content: Chronic allostatic load produces measurable damage across multiple organ systems simultaneously: hippocampal atrophy (memory and stress regulation impairment), immune suppression followed by chronic inflammation, cardiovascular damage (atherosclerosis, hypertension), and metabolic dysregulation (insulin resistance, abdominal fat deposition). The cascade is cross-system — damage in one domain compounds damage in others.
caveats: Provisional — awaiting fresh extraction from the original 1998 NEJM and 1993 Archives of Internal Medicine papers. Juster 2010 and McEwen 2012 currently carry the matured allostatic-load framework at pillar tier.

content: Allostasis: the process by which the organism maintains physiological stability through change. Unlike homeostasis (which implies a fixed set point), allostasis recognizes that regulatory systems actively adjust their parameters to meet environmental demands. The organism does not return to a fixed baseline — it continuously recalibrates based on predicted need.
caveats: Provisional — awaiting fresh extraction from the original 1998 NEJM and 1993 Archives of Internal Medicine papers. Juster 2010 and McEwen 2012 currently carry the matured allostatic-load framework at pillar tier.

content: Allostatic load: the cumulative physiological cost of chronic exposure to fluctuating or heightened neural and neuroendocrine responses resulting from repeated or chronic environmental challenge. When allostatic systems are forced to operate at high intensity for extended periods, the wear on biological systems accumulates as measurable organ damage. This is the hidden cost that the homeostasis concept fails to capture.
caveats: Provisional — awaiting fresh extraction from the original 1998 NEJM and 1993 Archives of Internal Medicine papers. Juster 2010 and McEwen 2012 currently carry the matured allostatic-load framework at pillar tier.

content: Disgust operates as a multi-level adaptive system for disease avoidance with three distinct learning mechanisms that tune innate responses to local environments. The Garcia effect flags foods as aversive after illness. Evaluative conditioning creates stable disgust labels when a powerful disgust reaction transfers to previously neutral stimuli — these labels are 'quickly acquired and slow to fade.' The law of contagion tracks pathogen spread by flagging any object touched by a disgusting stimulus, though these labels are temporary and item-specific. All three mechanisms allow the disgust system to respond to the local pathogen environment without requiring direct detection of microscopic organisms.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Curtis V, de Barra M, Aunger R, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Disgust sensitivity is adaptively calibrated to current physiological vulnerability. Women show increased disgust during the first trimester of pregnancy when the immune system is suppressed to tolerate paternal genetic material in the blastocyst. Salivary progesterone correlates positively with disgust sensitivity in normally cycling women — progesterone being the endocrine cue for immune downregulation. Opiate users, whose immune systems are pharmacologically suppressed, make fewer errors identifying disgust faces. Conversely, hunger downregulates disgust for food specifically while maintaining disgust for other pathogen cues — 15 hours of food deprivation reduced facial expressions of disgust to food but not to body wastes.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Curtis V, de Barra M, Aunger R, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Group hygiene behavior extends disgust from biological function to symbolic cultural regulation. Washing rituals took on symbolic significance in Semitic, Greek, Hindu, Buddhist, Islamic, and Christian religions. Hindu scripture (Laws of Manu, c. 200 BCE) prescribes avoidance of 12 bodily impurities and extends this logic to create caste separations — people whose work involves contact with 'polluting' substances become a separate and 'impure' caste. Dietary laws similarly extend biologically reasonable food avoidances to whole new classes of animals, with adherence serving as group-demarcating symbols. The emotional resources of disgust and contagion sustain these social separations, making violation a moral transgression rather than merely a hygiene failure.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Curtis V, de Barra M, Aunger R, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Females consistently score substantially higher on measures of disgust sensitivity than males across cultures. This sex difference likely reflects women's evolutionary history of responsibility for childcare — women need to be 'disgusted enough for two people' to keep dependent children free of disease. Disgust sensitivity is heritable and shows stable individual trait variation associated with neuroticism. Social learning modulates disgust in both directions: a 15-second verbal and visual display of disgust toward a novel object reduced infants' contact with the object for at least 1 hour in 14-month-olds, while positive attitudes by adults dissipated avoidance behaviors. The 'copy the frequent' heuristic for hygiene behavior can perpetuate either healthy or unhealthy practices.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Curtis V, de Barra M, Aunger R, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: THE INVERSION: The original learned helplessness theory got it backward. Passivity is NOT learned — it is the default, unlearned neural response to prolonged aversive stimulation, mediated by serotonergic activation of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). What IS learned is control, via the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) inhibiting the DRN. The neural circuit operates in three stages: (1) PASSIVITY/ANXIETY — aversive shock activates DRN 5-HT neurons, which release serotonin in the periaqueductal gray (inhibiting escape behavior) and amygdala (potentiating fear/anxiety); DRN sensitization via 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitization persists for days. (2) DETECT/ACT — the prelimbic region of vmPFC detects controllability via a circuit with the dorsal medial striatum, then a separate prelimbic population projects to and inhibits DRN 5-HT neurons via GABAergic interneurons. (3) EXPECT — after learning control, plasticity changes in the PL-DRN pathway create an expectation circuit that responds to future aversive events as if controllable. In vivo microdialysis showed inescapable shock produces sustained 5-HT elevation in DRN, while escapable shock causes 5-HT to drop precipitously as the animal learns the escape response. DRN activation is both necessary (blockade prevents helplessness) and sufficient (direct DRN activation reproduces all behavioral sequelae).
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Passivity is the default, not learned. The original learned helplessness theory got it backward. Passivity in response to prolonged aversive events is the unlearned default response, not a learned expectation of uncontrollability. The neural evidence shows that aversive shock per se activates serotonergic (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus regardless of controllability. Both escapable and inescapable shock produce equal excitatory input to the DRN. There is nothing in the brain selectively turned on by lack of control — only something that turns things off when control is present.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Dorsal raphe nucleus 5-HT activation is both necessary and sufficient for passivity/anxiety. Three experimental strategies converge: (1) blocking DRN activation during inescapable shock (via lesion or pharmacological agents) prevents passivity — subjects behave as nonshocked controls; (2) preventing desensitization of 5-HT1A autoreceptors during inescapable shock also eliminates passivity; (3) blocking 5-HT receptors in target regions (amygdala, PAG) during testing eliminates passivity and fear. For sufficiency: directly activating DRN via microinjected GABA antagonist picrotoxin or benzodiazepine antagonist beta-carboline produces the full behavioral syndrome of inescapable shock without any shock at all.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Control is detected via vmPFC-DMS circuit, then vmPFC inhibits dorsal raphe. Two separable prelimbic cortex functions identified: (1) DETECT — a prelimbic-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) circuit detects contingency between response and outcome (the presence of control); (2) ACT — separate prelimbic neurons project to DRN and inhibit 5-HT neurons via GABAergic interneurons. Retrograde tracing confirmed these are distinct neuronal populations — no colocalization. Inactivating the vmPFC-to-DRN pathway during escapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were inescapable despite perfect escape performance. Activating this pathway during inescapable shock makes the animal react as if shock were escapable.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Experience of control produces lasting immunization via plasticity in vmPFC-DRN pathway. Prior escapable shock prevents passivity/anxiety from later inescapable shock even in completely different situations (trans-situational). This 'immunization' requires new protein synthesis in the prelimbic cortex — blocking protein synthesis after escapable shock eliminates immunization but not the immediate protective effect of control. The escapable shock experience induces plasticity proteins (e.g., phosphorylated ERK) in prelimbic neurons projecting to DRN, increasing their excitability. After immunization, even inescapable shock now activates the prelimbic-DRN inhibitory pathway as if the shock were escapable — the circuit now EXPECTs control.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Learned helplessness maps onto 8 of 9 DSM depression symptoms. Combining animal and human experimental results, learned helplessness produced: sad mood, loss of interest, weight loss, sleep problems, psychomotor problems, fatigue, worthlessness, and indecisiveness/poor concentration. Only suicide/suicidal thoughts not produced — unsurprising given mild laboratory aversive events. The converse also held: depressed people who had not received inescapable events behaved in the laboratory as if they had — showing passivity in shuttlebox and giving up on cognitive problems. The passivity/anxiety symptoms of learned helplessness map directly onto depression symptoms.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Maier SF, Seligman MEP, 2016). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Schull's 15-year ethnography documents the "machine zone" — a dissociative state gamblers seek not to win money but to sustain. Mollie, a core informant, states: "I'm not playing to win... To keep playing — to stay in that machine zone where nothing else matters." She describes it as "being in the eye of a storm... You aren't really there — you're with the machine and that's all you're with." Clinical psychologist Robert Hunter confirms that modern video gambling "facilitates the dissociative process" — his patients describe "numbness or escape... climbing into the screen and getting lost." Gamblers are described as hanging "in a state of suspended animation," addicted not to the chance of winning but to "the world-dissolving state of subjective suspension and affective calm they derive from machine play." The industry itself tracks this as "time-on-device" (TOD), with developers noting "on these newer products, they can really get into that zone."
location: Introduction: Mapping the Machine Zone, pp. 1-20
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from the cited work of the cited work (Schull ND, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Slot machine design systematically exploits the dissociation between wanting and liking through multiple reinforcement mechanisms. Virtual reel mapping creates "near miss" effects — clustering winning symbols adjacent to blanks on the payline so losses appear as almost-wins, which "have an invigorating or potentiating effect on any behavior that immediately follows" (Skinner). Multiline video slots produce "losses disguised as wins" (LDWs): a player betting 25 nickels wins back 15, receiving the full audiovisual celebration of winning — lights, music, graphics — while steadily losing. As one designer explained: "Positive reinforcement hides loss." This steady partial "winning" accommodates a "play-to-win-to-play" mode where time-on-device is the aim. The machines give players modulatory control over lines and coins, letting "rat people" design their own Skinner boxes — increasing reinforcement frequency while reducing unreinforced trials. The net effect: SEEKING/wanting circuits fire continuously on variable-ratio reinforcement while actual satisfaction (liking) never arrives.
location: Ch. 3 Programming Chance (pp. 76-105), Ch. 4 Matching the Market (pp. 107-136)
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from the cited work of the cited work (Schull ND, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Schull documents that "from 30 percent to a staggering 60 percent of total gambling revenues have been found to derive from problem gamblers." The industry knowingly engineers this dependency: its all-consuming objective is to extract maximum "revenue per available customer" (REVPAC) by getting people to "gamble longer, faster, and more intensively" and to "turn casual players into repeat players." IGT's Director of Responsible Gambling admits: "Our game designers don't even think about addiction — they think about beating Bally and other competitors. They're creative folks who want machines to create the most revenue." Video gambling devices produce addiction three to four times faster than other gambling forms (one year vs. three and a half years). An Australian federal commission concluded that "the problems experienced by gamblers — many just ordinary consumers — are as much a consequence of the technology of the games, their accessibility and the nature and conduct of venues, as they are a consequence of the traits of the consumers themselves." The industry's defense — that machines are "simply inanimate objects" — mirrors the NRA's "guns don't kill people" logic.
location: Introduction: Mapping the Machine Zone, pp. 14-22
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from the cited work of the cited work (Schull ND, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Casino architect Bill Friedman's comprehensive design system (13 trademarked "Friedman Casino Design Principles") systematically engineers the physical environment to induce and maintain the machine zone state. Core strategy: The Law of Space Elimination — eliminate "excess horizontal space, excessive visible depth, and excess vertical space" because gamblers "most avoid expanse." Best-performing slot machines are located in "insulated enclaves," tucked in "small alcoves, recesses, and corners." Gamblers confirm this: Mollie gravitates "toward the corners, where it felt safe"; Daniel wants "to be in my own little cave." The maze layout "rivets visitors' attention on the equipment immediately ahead" by truncating lines of sight — "walkers can only see a short distance ahead" — creating "structured chaos" that draws patrons deeper into the casino. Curving pathways eliminate sharp turns that require conscious commitment. Sequential chase lights (like airport runway lights) subliminally guide movement. Equipment is "crammed tightly together" with narrow aisles. The entire built environment functions as a behavioral funnel: from the property entrance that "should curve gently off the street" to the maze interior, each design element reduces the probability of conscious decision-making and increases the probability of sitting down at a machine.
location: Ch 1: Interior Design for Interior States, pp. 39-48
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from the cited work of the cited work (Schull ND, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Moss documents how the food industry systematically optimizes products for the "bliss point" — the precise concentration of sugar, fat, and salt that maximizes sensory pleasure and craving. Howard Moskowitz, a mathematician and experimental psychologist, built a consulting empire on this optimization: "I've optimized soups, I've optimized pizzas, I've optimized salad dressings and pickles." His method involves creating dozens of product variations, testing them on consumers, then using regression analysis to identify the exact formulation that generates "the biggest crave." Australian psychologist Robert McBride described the bliss point at an industry conference: "Humans like sweetness, but how much sweetness? For all ingredients in food and drink, there is an optimum concentration at which the sensory pleasure is maximal. This optimum level is called the bliss point. The bliss point is a powerful phenomenon and dictates what we eat and drink more than we realize."

Moss reveals through internal industry sources that food companies knowingly engineer products to exploit evolved taste preferences and are aware of the overconsumption consequences. At a secret 1999 meeting of eleven food industry CEOs, Pillsbury executive James Behnke confronted them with "the notion that they and their companies had played a central role in creating this health crisis." Industry insider Michael Mudd presented slides showing the driver of obesity was the "ubiquity of inexpensive, good-tasting, super-sized, energy-dense foods" — the very products these companies staked their success on. Kraft executive Bob Ruff acknowledged that formulating foods to be irresistible was "in constant discussion" internally: "You're looking for the product that people like best." Yet when Kraft proposed internal caps on salt, sugar, and fat in 2003, other companies resisted — General Mills CEO Stephen Sanger told the assembled executives that consumers were not "asking us to put less sugar in." Revenue structures depended on maximizing consumption of products the industry's own scientists knew exploited natural cravings.

Electric light, caffeine, and alarm clocks systematically disrupt the ancestral dark-cycle sleep pattern that governed human circadian biology for millennia. Walker describes how Edison's incandescent light "put an end to this natural order of things," delaying melatonin release by 2-3 hours each evening and fooling the suprachiasmatic nucleus into believing the sun has not yet set. Caffeine — the most widely used psychoactive stimulant, with a half-life of 5-7 hours — blocks adenosine receptors to mask biological sleep pressure. Hunter-gatherer tribes (Hadza, San) show sleep onset between 8-10 p.m. aligned with dusk, a pattern now impossible under artificial light conditions. The combined effect is a modern environment fundamentally mismatched with the light-dark cycling that calibrated human sleep architecture throughout evolutionary history.
location: Chapters 2 and 13 (pp. on caffeine/adenosine, electric light section)
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from the cited work of the cited work (Walker M, 2017). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Sleep deprivation produces cascading failures across immune function, metabolic regulation, emotional processing, and memory consolidation. Walker reports that sleeping five hours per night yields a ~50% infection rate when exposed to cold virus versus 18% for seven-plus hours (Prather's rhinovirus study). A single night of reduced sleep strips immune resilience, depleting natural killer cells that target malignant tumor cells. Metabolically, even moderate sleep reduction for one week disrupts blood sugar regulation to pre-diabetic levels.
