Emotionally, REM sleep recalibrates emotional brain circuits daily — without it, amygdala reactivity spikes. Memory consolidation during NREM sleep shows 20-40% retention advantage over equivalent waking time, replicated since Jenkins and Dallenbach (1924).
location: Chapters 3, 7, 8 (immune system section, memory consolidation, emotional processing)
caveats: Trade book (Walker, Why We Sleep 2017) = ONE input; several magnitude claims are contested (Guzey 2019 critique). Demoted from 'replicated' to theoretical synthesis.

content: During puberty, the suprachiasmatic nucleus shifts the adolescent circadian rhythm progressively forward, pushing sleep onset several hours later than both younger children and adult parents. Walker describes how a nine-year-old's melatonin-driven sleep onset around 9 p.m. shifts so dramatically by age sixteen that the teenager remains at peak wakefulness at that hour, with biological sleep readiness not arriving until hours after parental bedtime. Asking a teenager to sleep at 10 p.m. is the circadian equivalent of asking a parent to sleep at 7-8 p.m.; waking them at 7 a.m. equals a parent rising at 4-5 a.m. Early school start times force adolescents to truncate sleep during their biological night, cutting into spindle-rich late-morning sleep phases critical for learning consolidation. Walker notes this is "non-volitional, non-negotiable, and strongly biological."
location: Chapter 4 (adolescent circadian shift section) and Chapter 9 (school start times)
caveats: Trade book (Walker 2017), one input; circadian-phase-delay claim is mainstream but cited from a popular work, not multi-study here. Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: Roenneberg identifies "social jet lag" — the chronic discrepancy between an individual's biological clock and socially imposed schedules — as a pervasive mismatch condition in industrialized societies. Over 40% of the Central European population suffers from social jet lag of two or more hours, and over 15% experience three or more hours of misalignment between internal and external time. The main symptom is chronic sleep deprivation, which cascades into health and mood problems. Roenneberg's data show that social jet lag severity is strongly linked to smoking: among those with less than one hour of social jet lag, 15-20% are smokers, rising systematically to over 60% when internal and external time are more than five hours out of synch. Social jet lag is worst during adolescence, when body clocks are biologically delayed but school start times remain early, coinciding with the age most individuals start smoking. Roenneberg notes that "while real jet lag is acute and transient, social jet lag is chronic," representing a persistent mismatch between evolved circadian biology and modern social time structures.
location: Chapters 16-17 (The Scissors of Sleep; Early Socialists, Late Capitalists)
caveats: Trade book (Roenneberg, Internal Time 2012) = one input. Demoted from 'replicated' to theoretical synthesis; see EXT-92/93/94 for the primary social-jetlag data.

content: In a randomized crossover study (N=12), reading a light-emitting eReader (LE-eBook) for 4 hours before bedtime for 5 consecutive evenings produced multiple measurable disruptions compared to reading a printed book in identical dim light conditions. Melatonin was suppressed by 55.12% (±20.12%) in the LE-eBook condition versus no suppression in the print condition (P<0.001). Dim light melatonin onset was delayed by >1.5 hours (22:31 vs 21:01, P<0.001). Sleep latency increased by ~10 minutes (25.65 vs 15.75 min, P=0.009). REM sleep was significantly reduced (109.04 vs 120.86 min, P=0.03). Next-morning sleepiness was significantly greater after LE-eBook reading (P<0.001), and it took participants hours longer to fully "wake up." The specific mechanism is short-wavelength (blue) light enrichment, with LE-eBook spectral peak at 452nm versus 612nm for reflected light from print books.
caveats: Single randomized crossover lab study (Chang et al. 2015, PNAS; N=12). Demoted from 'replicated' (one study).

content: The circadian disruption from evening LE-eReader use persisted beyond the reading session. Next-morning sleepiness was significantly greater after LE-eBook reading (P<0.001) and participants took hours longer to fully wake up. The circadian phase shift (dim light melatonin onset delayed by >1.5 hours) means that the biological night was pushed later by the light exposure, creating a form of acute social jetlag when participants had to wake at a fixed time. The specific mechanism is short-wavelength enrichment: LE-eBook spectral peak at 452nm (blue light) versus 612nm for reflected light from print books. This wavelength-specific suppression targets melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells that serve as the primary input to the circadian pacemaker.
caveats: Same single crossover study (Chang et al. 2015, N=12). Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: The crossover design (N=12, each participant served as own control across 5 consecutive evenings per condition) demonstrated dose-dependent effects: melatonin suppression accumulated over the 5 evenings of LE-eBook reading. The 55% melatonin suppression, combined with 10-minute increase in sleep latency and significant REM sleep reduction (109 vs 121 min), represents disruption of multiple sleep parameters simultaneously from a single environmental exposure. The study used a realistic exposure level (4 hours of evening reading with a commercially available iPad) rather than laboratory light boxes, increasing ecological validity.
caveats: Same single crossover study (Chang et al. 2015, N=12). Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: Precise estimation using forced desynchrony protocol in 24 healthy subjects (11 young men, mean age 23.7; 13 older subjects, mean age 67.4) revealed the intrinsic period of the human circadian pacemaker averages 24.18 hours (PCV 0.54% in young, 0.58% in older), with nearly 90% of estimates between 24.00 and 24.35 hours. Temperature, melatonin, and cortisol rhythm periods were highly correlated within individuals (r=0.951 to 0.984, all P<0.0001). The tight distribution (coefficient of variation ~0.55%) is consistent with circadian period variability in other species (kangaroo rat 0.08%, hamsters 0.3%, gila monster 0.54%, mice 0.7%).
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Charles A. Czeisler, Jeanne F. Duffy, Th, 1999). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Previous estimates of human circadian period (~25 hours, range 13-65 hours) were artifacts of self-selected light exposure in free-running protocols. When two subjects participated in both forced desynchrony and classical free-running protocols, their temperature period was 24.28-24.29 hours under forced desynchrony but 25.0-25.1 hours under free-running conditions with self-selected ~150 lux room light. Mathematical modeling confirmed that feedback effects of ordinary room light alone can lengthen apparent circadian period by more than 0.7 hours. Free-running subjects preferentially select room light exposure before the circadian temperature minimum and darkness after, systematically eliciting light-induced phase delays and minimizing phase advances.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Charles A. Czeisler, Jeanne F. Duffy, Th, 1999). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: No significant age-related difference in intrinsic circadian period was found between young (24.18 +/- 0.04 hours) and older (24.18 +/- 0.04 hours) subjects, challenging the hypothesis that circadian period shortens with age and thereby causes early-morning awakening in the elderly. Despite comparable circadian periods, older subjects exhibited characteristic changes in circadian amplitude and sleep consolidation. The intrinsic period was independent of the imposed sleep-wake cycle length (equivalent on 20-hour, 28-hour, and 42.85-hour protocols), confirming it reflects the endogenous pacemaker, not behavioral entrainment.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Charles A. Czeisler, Jeanne F. Duffy, Th, 1999). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Oxytocin (OT) operates through three distinct but neurobiologically consistent mechanisms to support human affiliative bonds. (a) Parent-infant bonding: maternal OT levels measured in the first trimester predicted postpartum behavior (gaze, positive affect, motherese, affectionate touch); OT was stable within individuals across pregnancy; fathers showed comparable baseline OT to mothers and active paternal care activated the OT system. OT administration to fathers increased their touch behavior AND independently increased infant salivary OT, RSA, social gaze, and toy exploration — demonstrating cross-dyadic transmission. (b) Pair bonding: new romantic partners showed significantly higher plasma OT than singles, even higher than new parents; OT correlated with interactive synchrony (social focus, positive affect, affectionate touch) and was stable over six months. (c) Group affiliation: OT was linked to children's best-friend relationship quality and broader social engagement. Across all bond types, OT levels showed "biological synchrony" between partners — mother-father OT was inter-correlated, parent-infant OT was inter-related, and romantic partners' OT levels were concordant.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Ruth Feldman, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: In a study of 112 parents and their 4-6 month olds, active parental touch triggered measurable OT responses. Mothers providing high levels of affectionate touch (>66% of interaction time) showed increased salivary OT from pre- to post-interaction, while mothers providing minimal touch (<33%) showed no such increase. Fathers who provided high levels of stimulatory contact (moving child's limbs, throwing infant in air) similarly increased their OT levels, but those engaging in minimal stimulatory touch did not. Risk alleles on the OXTR rs2254298 and CD38 rs3796863 SNPs were associated with both lower plasma OT and reduced parental affectionate touch, paralleling findings of high vs. low licking-and-grooming rat dams.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Ruth Feldman, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Cross-generational transmission of the oxytocin system operates through parenting behavior rather than genetics alone. In a study of parents and 6-month-old infants, parent-infant OT levels were inter-related at both baseline and following contact, and the degree of OT increase was correlated between parent and child. Critically, parent-infant behavioral synchrony moderated the intergenerational effect: when synchrony was high, parent-child OT concordance was strong; when synchrony was low, no association emerged. Adults' retrospective accounts of warm parental care in childhood predicted higher current plasma OT. Risk alleles on OXTR and CD38 predicted lower OT, less affectionate touch, and shorter episodes of gaze synchrony. Mothers and fathers who reported more positive care in their own childhood provided more affectionate touch to their infants.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Ruth Feldman, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Bio-behavioral synchrony is the mechanism by which organisms become members of a social group. Among mammalian species, dyad-specific maternal-infant bonds are built on repeatedly experienced patterns of sensory, motor, and behavioral cues. Human mothers provide approximately 70% of their social behaviors during the 7% of the time newborns spend in alert-scanning state, creating temporal contingencies between infant state and maternal social behavior from the first post-birth hours. These social contingencies are supported by physiological periodicities maturing in the fetus during the third trimester: the biological clock and cardiac pacemaker. As soon as the human infant is born, it can experience a temporal match between its own state and the response of the social environment. This early temporal concordance is a critical human addition to the physiological provisions embedded in maternal proximity in other mammals.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Ruth Feldman, 2012). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: In a large epidemiological database (n>65,000, primarily Central European), social jetlag — the discrepancy between biological circadian clock and socially imposed sleep timing — is associated with increased BMI independently of sleep duration. 69% of the population experiences at least 1 hour of social jetlag, and one-third suffers 2+ hours. Logistic regression showed social jetlag significantly increased probability of being overweight (OR=3.30, 95% CI 2.51-4.33) after controlling for age, sex, chronotype, and sleep duration. Hierarchical multiple regression revealed social jetlag positively predicts BMI in the overweight group (BMI>=25, n=20,731) with an effect size more than half that of sleep duration, but does not predict BMI in the normal weight group (BMI<25, n=43,308). Over the study period (2003-2010), chronotype progressively delayed in the population (r=0.07, p<0.001) while workday sleep duration shortened (r=-0.14, p<0.001), driven by ~80% of workers using alarm clocks. Social jetlag peaks in late adolescence due to the collision of late biological chronotype with early school start times.
caveats: Single large chronotype database (Roenneberg et al. 2012, Current Biology, n>65,000). Demoted from 'replicated' — one dataset, not multi-study convergence.

content: Social jetlag — the discrepancy between biological and social clocks — is chronic throughout working careers. 69% of the population (N>65,000, central European) experiences at least 1 hour of social jetlag; one-third suffers 2+ hours. Social jetlag peaks in late adolescence due to collision of late biological chronotype with early school start times. Chronotype progressively delayed across the study period 2003-2010 (r=0.07, p<0.001) while workday sleep duration shortened (r=-0.14, p<0.001), driven by ~80% of workers using alarm clocks. Unlike travel jetlag (transient until re-entrainment), social jetlag is chronic and unresolvable without schedule change, producing persistent misalignment between the endogenous circadian system and socially imposed timing.
caveats: Same single Roenneberg 2012 database (n>65,000). Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: Hierarchical multiple regression revealed social jetlag positively predicts BMI specifically in the overweight group (BMI>=25, n=20,731), with an effect size more than half that of sleep duration, but does NOT predict BMI in the normal weight group (BMI<25, n=43,308). Logistic regression with BMI group as outcome showed social jetlag as a significant predictor (OR=3.30, 95% CI: 2.51-4.33) of being overweight after controlling for age, sex, chronotype, and sleep duration. The differential effect by weight group suggests social jetlag may interact with metabolic vulnerability — once the system is pushed past a threshold, circadian misalignment accelerates weight gain through disrupted energy homeostasis.
caveats: Same single Roenneberg 2012 database; BMI association in the overweight subgroup (n=20,731). Demoted from 'replicated'.

content: The behavioral immune system comprises evolved psychological mechanisms that detect cues of infectious pathogens and trigger disgust-mediated avoidance responses. Operating on the 'smoke detector principle,' it minimizes costly false-negative errors (missing real pathogens) at the cost of many false-positive errors -- generating aversive responses to people with physical disabilities, obesity, elderly appearance, or foreign ethnicity who pose no actual infection risk. The system exhibits functional flexibility: responses intensify when perceivers feel more vulnerable to infection (e.g., women in first trimester of pregnancy show heightened ethnocentrism and xenophobia; Navarrete et al., 2007). At a population level, cross-national data show that higher historical pathogen prevalence predicts lower extraversion, lower openness to experience, and higher collectivism (r = 0.73 for collectivism-pathogen correlation; Fincher et al., 2008), with correlations surviving controls for confounds. Mere visual perception of diseased-looking people triggers perceivers' white blood cells to mount more vigorous antibacterial responses, suggesting behavioral and physiological immune systems interact.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Mark Schaller, Justin H. Park, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: The behavioral immune system's functional flexibility operates at both individual and societal levels. At the individual level, people with chronically higher 'germ aversion' report chronically lower extraversion, and pathogen salience causes reduced extraversion and avoidant motor movements toward pictures of people. At the societal level, countries with higher historical pathogen prevalence show lower population-level extraversion, lower openness to experience, and higher collectivism. The culinary spice usage pattern illustrates this: spices are natural antibiotics, and their use in food preparation is more common under ecological circumstances of high pathogen prevalence, reflecting the cost-benefit calculus of pathogen defense across populations.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Mark Schaller, Justin H. Park, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: The behavioral immune system operates on the smoke detector principle: it minimizes costly false-negative errors (missing real pathogens) at the cost of many false-positive errors — generating aversive responses to people with physical disabilities, obesity, elderly appearance, or foreign ethnicity who pose no actual infection risk. The system exhibits functional flexibility: responses intensify when perceivers feel more vulnerable to infection. Mere visual perception of diseased-looking people triggers perceivers white blood cells to mount more vigorous antibacterial responses (interleukin-6 upregulation), demonstrating that behavioral and physiological immune systems interact bidirectionally. This cross-talk means that simply SEEING signs of disease activates actual immune defenses.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Mark Schaller, Justin H. Park, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: At a population level, cross-national data show higher historical pathogen prevalence predicts lower extraversion, lower openness to experience, and higher collectivism (r=0.73 for collectivism-pathogen correlation, Fincher et al. 2008), with correlations surviving controls for latitude, climate, and socioeconomic status. Culinary spice usage illustrates the population-level cost-benefit calculus: spices are natural antibiotics, and their use in food preparation is more common under ecological circumstances of high pathogen prevalence. Women in first trimester of pregnancy show heightened ethnocentrism and xenophobia (Navarrete et al. 2007), consistent with upregulated behavioral immune responses during adaptive immunosuppression.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (Mark Schaller, Justin H. Park, 2011). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.

content: Cross-fostering pups of low-licking/grooming (low-LG) rat mothers to high-LG mothers REVERSED the epigenetic programming at the glucocorticoid receptor gene promoter in hippocampus. Offspring of low-LG mothers who were cross-fostered to high-LG mothers showed: (1) reversed DNA methylation patterns matching biological high-LG offspring, (2) normalized histone acetylation, (3) restored NGFI-A transcription factor binding, (4) increased GR expression, and (5) attenuated HPA stress responses. These changes emerged over the first week of life and persisted into adulthood. Additionally, central infusion of a histone deacetylase inhibitor in adult offspring of low-LG mothers removed all group differences, demonstrating that the epigenomic state is causally responsible for the phenotypic differences.
caveats: Single landmark rodent study (Weaver et al. 2004, Nat Neurosci); maternal-care epigenetic programming subsequently reproduced. Demoted from 'replicated' (cross-species single study).

content: 10-year longitudinal RCT (N=146): Kangaroo Care (14 days skin-to-skin) vs incubator care in preterm infants. KC increased autonomic functioning (RSA), maternal attachment, reduced maternal anxiety. Enhanced child cognitive development and executive functions from 6 months to 10 years. By age 10: better sleep organization, more mature EEG patterns, better cognitive control. 14 days of contact correction produced a decade of measurable developmental advantage.
caveats: Single 10-year cohort/RCT (Feldman et al. 2014, N=146). Demoted from 'replicated'; also remove implied multi-study 'RCT' framing — it is one trial.

content: The EAAT paradox: if cognitive faculties are unreliable products of selection, the EAAT itself cannot be trusted (self-defeating). But dismissing EAAT requires assuming fitness-truth correlation (veridical perceptual congruence) which contemporary evolutionary biology cannot establish. Evolution is not progressive: gnats may be fitter than mammals yet perceive less veridically. Result: EAAT is both tenable and untenable simultaneously.
caveats: Philosophical challenge to the Evaluativist-Analogical-Axiomatic Theory frame. Presents a self-defeating paradox in the specific EAAT formulation; does not invalidate the broader mismatch thesis.

content: Three nationally representative time-use-diary studies (N=17,247; Ireland, US, UK) found little evidence for substantial negative associations between digital-screen engagement and adolescent well-being, including screen time before bedtime. Time-use diaries are more accurate than self-report, and the effect sizes were negligible. This challenges the dominant narrative that screen time per se is harmful.
caveats: Time-use diary data from Orben & Przybylski and adjacent meta-analyses show small effects for social-media-use / wellbeing correlations, on the order of r ≈ 0.05. Challenges the largest versions of the social-media-harm thesis without invalidating mechanism-level claims.

content: Meta-analysis of social media use and depressive symptoms among adolescents (11-18 years) found a small but significant positive correlation (k=12, r=0.11, p<.01) with high heterogeneity (I2=95.22%). The small overall effect size and extreme heterogeneity suggest that overall use measures mask highly variable effects depending on type of use, platform, and individual vulnerability.
caveats: Meta-analytic finding of a small (r ≈ 0.11) positive correlation between adolescent social-media use and depressive symptoms, with extreme heterogeneity. The small overall effect and high variance indicate that aggregate-use measures hide substantial differences by platform, type of use, and individual vulnerability.

content: Largest meta-analysis to date on social media and adolescent internalizing symptoms (143 studies, N=1,094,890, 886 effect sizes). Found small but significant meta-correlations: time spent on social media and internalizing symptoms r=0.08 (clinical samples) and similar in community samples. User engagement showed r=0.12 in clinical samples. Only 11% of studies examined clinical populations, revealing a critical gap: research focuses on general population while public concern is about clinical-level symptoms.
caveats: Large meta-analysis (approx. N = 1 million) finds small effects with high heterogeneity for the social-media-to-internalizing-symptoms link. Reports the effect-size reality check that mechanism-level claims must respect, and highlights the gap between general-population research and clinical-sample concerns.

content: Meta-analysis of 50 studies (published and unpublished) testing whether incidental disgust amplifies moral judgment. Raw effect: d=0.11 (small), strongest for gustatory/olfactory induction. After correcting for publication bias, the effect disappears entirely (d=-0.01). Prevalent confounds mean d=0.11 is an upper bound. The finding that the incidental disgust amplification effect may be artifactual challenges strong claims about emotion causally driving moral judgment and suggests the Haidt and Wheatley 2005 disgust-priming finding may not generalize robustly.
caveats: Publication-bias-corrected meta-analysis of the disgust-moral-judgment effect yields effect size ≈ 0. Challenges the strong version of the disgust-amplifies-moral-judgment literature, including the generalizability of the Haidt & Wheatley 2005 disgust-priming finding.

content: Cross-sectional analysis of 1,237,194 US adults: exercisers had 43.2% fewer days of poor mental health per month (1.49 fewer days) than matched non-exercisers. All exercise types associated with reduced mental health burden. Optimal dose: 3-5 sessions/week, 45 minutes each. Exercise effect on mental health LARGER than effects of education or income.

Owing to this struggle for life, any variation, however slight and from whatever cause proceeding, if it be in any degree profitable to an individual of any species, in its infinitely complex relations to other organic beings and to external nature, will tend to the preservation of that individual, and will generally be inherited by its offspring.
location: Chapter III, 'Struggle for Existence,' opening, p. 61
author_quote: Owing to this struggle for life, any variation, however slight and from whatever cause proceeding, if it be in any degree profitable to an individual of any species, in its infinitely complex relations to other organic beings and to external nature, will tend to the preservation of that individual, and will generally be inherited by its offspring.
caveats: Darwin's first statement of the selection principle in Origin, appearing before he formally names it Natural Selection on the next page. This is the most compact Darwinian statement of P1 (inclusive fitness as loss function): variations that are profitable to an individual in its struggle for life tend to be preserved and inherited. [OCR corrected in author_quote: 'strugele' → 'struggle'; 'beigs' → 'beings'. Source file lines 3324 and 3327 contain these Internet Archive OCR artifacts; the author_quote above restores Darwin's canonical 1859 wording.]
scope: Founding statement of the selection principle in its full Darwinian form: variation + differential survival under struggle for life + inheritance → preservation. P1 (the loss function) is derived directly from this in Cor.

content: I should premise that I use the term Struggle for Existence in a large and metaphorical sense, including dependence of one being on another, and including (which is more important) not only the life of the individual, but success in leaving progeny.
location: Chapter III, 'Struggle for Existence,' definition section, p. 62
author_quote: I should premise that I use the term Struggle for Existence in a large and metaphorical sense, including dependence of one being on another, and including (which is more important) not only the life of the individual, but success in leaving progeny.
caveats: Darwin's own explicit definition: 'struggle for existence' means survival AND reproductive success, not bare survival alone. This is the Darwinian origin of the 'both halves of P1' rule that Cor enforces (survival AND reproduction). [Source-location note: the body text at lines 3373-3378 of the .txt file (Chapter III p. 62) is severely OCR-garbled ('aie term' for 'the term'; 'one wean on sais and mac lneiaS' for 'one being on another, and including (which is more important)'; 'ae but success ag cre anaes io canine' for 'not only the life of the individual, but success in leaving progeny'). The author_quote above is the canonical Darwin wording AND appears verbatim in the Ernst Mayr introduction to this edition at lines 449-453 of the same .txt file. The quote is correct Darwin; only the body-text OCR at the cited Ch III p. 62 location is damaged.]
scope: P1 definitional. Darwin's own definition of struggle for existence already includes reproduction as the more important half — predating Hamilton's formalization of inclusive fitness by a century. Cor cites this as the justification for treating P1 as dual-headed (survival + reproduction) from the outset.

content: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase. Every being, which during its natural lifetime produces several eggs or seeds, must suffer destruction during some period of its life, and during some season or occasional year, otherwise, on the principle of geometrical increase, its numbers would quickly become so inordinately great that no country could support the product. Hence, as more individuals are produced than can possibly survive, there must in every case be a struggle for existence. It is the doctrine of Malthus applied with manifold force to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms.
author_quote: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase. Every being, which during its natural lifetime produces several eggs or seeds, must suffer destruction during some period of its life, and during some season or occasional year, otherwise, on the principle of geometrical increase, its numbers would quickly become so inordinately great that no country could support the product. Hence, as more individuals are produced than can possibly survive, there must in every case be a struggle for existence, either one individual with another of the same species, or with the individuals of distinct species, or with the physical conditions of life. It is the doctrine of Malthus applied with manifold force to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms; for in this case there can be no artificial increase of food, and no prudential restraint from marriage.
caveats: Darwin's Malthusian derivation of the struggle for existence from the geometric-increase-vs-finite-resources mismatch. This is the quantitative backbone of P1: because organisms reproduce at geometric rates but resources do not, differential survival and reproduction is inevitable, which in turn drives selection.
scope: The quantitative grounding of P1. The loss function exists because geometric reproduction against finite resources forces differential survival — the selection pressure is inescapable, not contingent.

content: if any slight innate change of habit or of structure benefited an individual wolf, it would have the best chance of surviving and of leaving offspring. Some of its young would probably inherit the same habits or structure, and by the repetition of this process, a new variety might be formed which would either supplant or coexist with the parent-form of wolf.
location: Chapter IV, 'Natural Selection,' wolf illustration, p. 90
author_quote: if any slight innate change of habit or of structure benefited an individual wolf, it would have the best chance of surviving and of leaving offspring. Some of its young would probably inherit the same habits or structure, and by the repetition of this process, a new variety might be formed which would either supplant or coexist with the parent-form of wolf.
caveats: Darwin's concrete illustration of natural selection acting on both structural AND behavioral variation in wolves. This matters for Cor because it shows Darwin was already treating behavioral dispositions ('habit') as heritable and under selection alongside anatomy — not something discovered by later behavioral geneticists. [OCR corrected in author_quote: 'sheht' → 'slight'. Source file line 4428 contains 'sheht innate change'; the author_quote above restores Darwin's canonical 'slight innate change' — 'sheht' is not a word and is unambiguously an OCR artifact.]
scope: Shows Darwin treating behavioral/habit variation as heritable and under selection from the outset. Relevant to P2 (domain-sensitive architecture) because it establishes that behavioral tendencies are legitimate targets of selection, not just morphology.

content: if variations useful to any organic being do occur, assuredly individuals thus characterised will have the best chance of being preserved in the struggle for life; and from the strong principle of inheritance they will tend to produce offspring similarly characterised. This principle of preservation, I have called, for the sake of brevity, Natural Selection.
location: Chapter IV, 'Natural Selection,' formal statement and naming, p. 127
author_quote: if variations useful to any organic being do occur, assuredly individuals thus characterised will have the best chance of being preserved in the struggle for life; and from the strong principle of inheritance they will tend to produce offspring similarly characterised. This principle of preservation, I have called, for the sake of brevity, Natural Selection.
caveats: Darwin's formal naming and definition of Natural Selection. This is the sentence that the entire evolutionary-biology edifice rests on.
scope: P1 foundational. The formal Darwinian definition: variation + advantage + inheritance → differential preservation → natural selection. Cor's P1 is this claim in modern inclusive-fitness vocabulary.

content: Sexual Selection. This depends, not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females; the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring. Sexual selection is, therefore, less rigorous than natural selection. Generally, the most vigorous males, those which are best fitted for their places in nature, will leave most progeny.
author_quote: This depends, not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females; the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring. Sexual selection is, therefore, less rigorous than natural selection. Generally, the most vigorous males, those which are best fitted for their places in nature, will leave most progeny.
caveats: Darwin's original distinction between natural selection and sexual selection. Sexual selection is a second selective force operating on reproductive access rather than survival. Relevant to M14 (Reproductive Motivation) because Darwin establishes the theoretical legitimacy of treating reproductive architecture as a distinct target of selection — which M14 formalizes as a separate mechanism rather than a subset of M2 pursuit.
scope: Dual-force selection framework: natural selection acts on survival; sexual selection acts on reproductive access. M14 in Cor inherits its legitimacy as a distinct mechanism (not absorbed into M2) from this Darwinian distinction.

content: Close study of innate releasing mechanisms reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal. This is the phenomenon of supernormal sign stimuli — an evolved response fires harder in reaction to an exaggerated artificial stimulus than to the natural cue it was shaped to detect.
location: Chapter III, 'Behaviour as a Reaction to External Stimuli,' section 'Supernormal sign stimuli,' pp. 44-46
author_quote: close study of IRMs reveals the remarkable fact that it is sometimes possible to offer stimulus situations that are even more effective than the natural situation. In other words, the natural situation is not always optimal.
caveats: Tinbergen's founding statement of the supernormal sign stimuli phenomenon. This is THE primary source for DA4 (Proxy Hijacking via Open Loops). The idea that an evolved mechanism can be over-activated by an artificial stimulus that exceeds the parameters of the natural cue is the architectural root of every modern proxy-exploitation case Cor flags: ultra-processed food, variable-reward apps, pornography, companion AI.
scope: DA4 foundational claim. Establishes the existence of an open loop in evolved response systems: the cue-detection architecture can be exceeded by stimuli that did not exist in the ancestral environment, producing disproportionate response without the resolution conditions the response evolved to track.

content: Oystercatchers preferred a clutch of five eggs to the normal clutch of three. Still more astonishing is the oystercatcher's preference for abnormally large eggs: when presented with an egg of normal oystercatcher size, one of herring gull's size, and one double the linear size of a herring gull's egg, the majority of choices fall upon the largest egg. The bird reliably chooses the giant egg it cannot have evolved to recognize over the one it actually laid.
location: Chapter III, 'Supernormal sign stimuli,' pp. 44-45, Figs. 42-43
author_quote: we found that oystercatchers preferred a clutch of five eggs to the normal clutch of three. Still more astonishing is the oystercatcher's preference for abnormally large eggs. If presented with an egg of normal oystercatcher size, one of herring gull's size, and one double the (linear) size of a herring gull's egg, the majority of choices fall upon the largest egg.
caveats: The canonical oystercatcher supernormal-egg experiment, reported by Tinbergen as a direct empirical result. evidence_quality='replicated' because Tinbergen's supernormal-stimuli findings across oystercatchers, ringed plovers, grayling butterflies, and sticklebacks constitute a multi-species replication within a single research program. [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): evidence_quality downgraded from 'replicated' to 'clinical'. Codex audit (msg #332) flagged inflation — the oystercatcher supernormal-egg finding is a single Tinbergen experiment, not a multi-study replication at this row's specific finding. The program-level convergence (across oystercatchers, ringed plovers, grayling butterflies, sticklebacks) that I originally invoked to justify 'replicated' reaches beyond this specific row's scope; the row-specific finding is one behavioral-experiment result reported by Tinbergen himself, which maps to 'clinical' in the expanded v2 evidence_quality enum.]
scope: The most famous single empirical demonstration of proxy hijacking. Directly grounds DA4 and provides the template for Cor's analysis of every modern engineered-proxy case: when the exaggerated artificial cue outcompetes the natural cue, the organism is not malfunctioning — its evolved response is working exactly as designed on an input that did not exist in the EEA.

content: Newly hatched chicks of the herring gull beg for food by pecking at the tip of the parent's bill, which is yellow with a red spot at the end of the lower mandible. Systematic dummy experiments demonstrated that the red patch is the effective releasing stimulus: a dummy lacking the red patch elicits far fewer pecks, a dummy with a red patch on any background elicits strong pecking, and models in which bill colour, head colour, and head shape are varied show that the chick reacts specifically to the red patch against the bill. The pecking response is tied to a specific sign stimulus rather than to a gestalt of the parent bird.
location: Chapter III, 'Sign stimuli,' herring gull chick experiments, pp. 29-30, Figs. 22-24
author_quote: The bill of the herring gull is yellow, with a red spot at the end of the lower mandible. By comparing the chicks' reactions towards (1) a flat cardboard dummy in natural colours and (2) a similar dummy lacking the red patch, it was found that the red patch was of great importance.
caveats: The herring-gull red-spot experiment is one of the founding empirical demonstrations of sign-stimulus control of innate behaviour. Grounds P2 (domain-sensitive architecture: the chick has a specific detector for the red spot, not a general perceptual-categorization system) and DA4 (the existence of a narrow detector is what makes the downstream supernormal-stimulus vulnerability possible). [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): evidence_quality downgraded from 'replicated' to 'clinical'. Codex audit (msg #332) flagged inflation — the herring-gull red-spot dummy-chick experiment is a single behavioral experiment reported by Tinbergen, not a replicated multi-study finding at this specific row's scope. 'clinical' is the accurate grade for a single behavioral-experiment observation in a single species.]
scope: Supports P2 (domain-sensitive evolved response systems) and the necessary precondition for DA4 (narrow detectors can be hijacked by stimuli exceeding the natural parameter range).

content: A territory-holding male English robin will threaten a mere bundle of red feathers much more readily than a complete mounted young robin which shows all the characteristics of a robin except the red breast. The red breast alone is sufficient to release the threat response; the rest of the bird is irrelevant. The male's aggression system runs on a single feature of the stimulus, not on a species-level recognition.
location: Chapter III, 'Sign stimuli,' robin example, p. 28, Fig. 21
author_quote: a territory-holding male of this species would threaten a mere bundle of red feathers much more readily than a complete mounted young robin which showed all the characteristics of a robin except the red breast. Again, the red breast is the effective stimulus
caveats: Lack (1943) as reported by Tinbergen. Classic demonstration that an innate aggressive response can be fully triggered by a minimal feature (red breast) without any gestalt recognition of the opponent species. Relevant to M1 (Threat Management) in the narrow sense that threat-detection systems operate on feature filters rather than full-object recognition. [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): Codex audit (msg #332) flagged SOURCE_TYPE_DRIFT — Tinbergen is explicitly reporting Lack (1943) in this passage ('Much the same condition exists in the English robin. Lack (1943) discovered that a territory-holding male of this species would threaten...'). The primary source is Lack 1943, not Tinbergen 1951. PATCH: source_type='primary' → 'propagation'. Also downgrading evidence_quality='replicated' → 'clinical' for the same reason as rows 114 and 115 (single behavioral experiment, specific-finding scope).]
scope: Illustrates P2 (domain-sensitive mechanism with a narrow input filter) and M1 (threat/aggression response triggered by feature-level rather than object-level stimuli).

content: It is the dependence of innate behaviour on sign stimuli that renders it possible to evoke reactions in an animal by presenting it with dummies. As a matter of fact, when any animal readily responds to a dummy, this is a certain indication that its reaction is dependent on sign stimuli. The animal's perceptual world is not the full sensory world its sense organs can receive — it is a restricted world composed of sign stimuli, at least as long as we are dealing with innate responses.
location: Chapter III, end of 'Sign stimuli' section, pp. 37-38
author_quote: It is the dependence of innate behaviour on sign stimuli that renders it possible to evoke reactions in an animal by presenting it with dummies. As a matter of fact, when any animal readily responds to a dummy, this is a certain indication that its reaction is dependent on sign stimuli.
caveats: The generalized principle behind the specific experiments: innate behaviour operates on a restricted set of sign stimuli rather than on full sensory input. This is Tinbergen's version of the interface-theory-of-perception claim (OF1) at the behavioural-response level: the organism's effective world is a species-specific set of fitness-relevant cues, not a window on objective reality.
scope: P2 (the architecture is domain-sensitive and operates on restricted input filters) and OF1 (the organism's perceptual world is a fitness-filtered interface, not veridical reality).

content: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities. Our collective brains arise from the synthesis of our cultural and social natures — from the fact that we readily learn from others (are cultural) and can, with the right norms, live in large and widely interconnected groups (are social). The striking technologies that characterize our species, from the kayaks and compound bows used by hunter-gatherers to the antibiotics and airplanes of the modern world, emerge not from singular geniuses but from the flow and recombination of ideas, practices, lucky errors, and chance insights among interconnected minds and across generations.
author_quote: The secret of our species' success resides not in the power of our individual minds, but in the collective brains of our communities. Our collective brains arise from the synthesis of our cultural and social natures—from the fact that we readily learn from others (are cultural) and can, with the right norms, live in large and widely interconnected groups (are social).
caveats: The book's thesis statement in Henrich's own words. Grounds the P3 constraint (culture is part of the human expected environment, not an alternative to it) and P2 (domain-sensitive evolved cognition includes specific architecture for social/cultural transmission). Relevant to M11 Cooperation/Alliance because the collective-brain thesis rests on large interconnected cooperative networks.
scope: Thesis-level claim. The P3 constraint that Cor inherits from Boyd/Richerson is here stated in its strongest form: human cognition is fundamentally a distributed cultural phenomenon, and removing the distributed layer removes the organism's ability to meet environmental demands.

content: Franklin's expedition sent 105 big-brained and highly motivated primates, with three years of Arctic experience and nineteen months stuck in the ice, into an environment humans have lived in as foragers for over 30,000 years — and they all died. The Netsilik Inuit spent winters out on the pack ice and summers on King William Island, just like Franklin's men. They lived in snow houses, hunted seals using harpoons, hunted caribou and musk ox with compound bows and kayaks, and speared salmon using leisters. None of the 105 big brains figured out how to use driftwood (which was available on the west coast where they camped) to make the recurve composite bows the Inuit used. They further lacked the vast body of cultural know-how about building snow houses, creating fresh water, hunting seals, making kayaks, spearing salmon, and tailoring cold-weather clothing. Humans don't adapt to novel environments the way other animals do or by using our individual intelligence.
author_quote: Franklin's men were 105 big-brained and highly motivated primates facing an environment that humans have lived in as foragers for over 30,000 years. They'd had three years in the Arctic, and nineteen months stuck in the ice, with their supplies slowly dwindling, to experience the environment and put those big brains to work.
caveats: The Franklin Expedition is a historical natural experiment, not a controlled study, but the evidence is solid: 105 motivated educated primates died in an environment the Inuit thrived in. evidence_quality='clinical' (single-case historical demonstration). Henrich pairs this with the Ross (1829) and Amundsen (1903) counter-examples: both survived by learning from the Inuit. Together these form a natural triple-comparison that grounds the P3 constraint claim. [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): original author_quote combined two non-contiguous source fragments via ellipsis. Fragment 1 at source lines 1135-1139 ('Franklin's men were 105 big-brained... put those big brains to work.') and Fragment 2 at source lines 1144-1147 ('Yet the crew vanished, defeated by the hostile environment... humans don't adapt to novel environments the way other animals do or by using our individual intelligence.') are separated by ~5 sentences about group cohesion and the 105-Netsilik-encampment comparison. Option B PATCH: author_quote now contains only Fragment 1 verbatim. The Fragment 2 punchline ('humans don't adapt to novel environments by using our individual intelligence') is load-bearing for the Henrich cultural-evolution argument and is preserved in the content field above as paraphrase. The full source passage at lines 1135-1147 supports the content; author_quote anchors only the contiguous Fragment 1 portion per Wave 1-B verbatim-quote discipline.]
scope: The most powerful single case study for the P3 constraint. Demonstrates that human evolved cognition is insufficient without the cultural scaffolding it co-evolved with. Cor uses this case as the canonical example for why 'matched' must include cultural scaffolding, not just ancestral environment.

content: Cultural practices and beliefs are often (implicitly) MUCH smarter than we are, as neither individuals nor groups could figure them out in one lifetime. Cultural evolution, through selective attention and learning processes, is fully capable of generating complex adaptive products which no one designed or had a causal mental model of before they emerged. Since the rise of cumulative cultural evolution, natural selection has lost its status as the only 'dumb' process capable of creating complex adaptations well fit to local circumstances. People often don't even know what their practices are actually doing, or that they are 'doing' anything — spicy-food lovers in hot climates don't know that recipes involving garlic and chili peppers protect their families from meat-borne pathogens. They just culturally inherited the tastes and recipes.
location: Chapter 7, 'Teaching, Language, and... Cultural Learning,' sections 'Culture Is Smarter Than We Are' and 'Move Over, Natural Selection,' pp. 124-127
author_quote: These practices and beliefs are often (implicitly) MUCH smarter than we are, as neither individuals nor groups could figure them out in one lifetime.
caveats: Henrich's formal claim that cultural evolution is a second dumb optimization process that creates complex adaptive products independently of individual cognition. This is the theoretical backbone of the P3 constraint: the 'matched' environment for humans includes cultural scaffolding that the organism cannot reconstruct from first principles. [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): original author_quote was a fabrication — opening clause said 'cultural practices and beliefs' but source line 4269 reads 'These practices / and beliefs' (verbatim); and the second clause ('At least since the rise of cumulative cultural evolution, natural selection has lost its status as the only dumb process...') was spliced via ellipsis from source lines 4339-4342 which are in a different section ('Move Over, Natural Selection,' ~70 lines later). The two fragments were not contiguous. PATCH: author_quote now contains only Fragment 1 verbatim from source lines 4269-4271 (Chapter 7 'Culture Is Smarter Than We Are' section, p. 126). The 'Move Over, Natural Selection' argument (Fragment 2 content) remains captured in the content field above as paraphrase but is no longer presented as a direct quote. Option B selected per dispatch preference for PATCH over DELETE where possible; content field already captured both architectural claims as paraphrase.]
scope: Deep theoretical grounding for the P3 constraint. Positions cultural evolution as architecturally distinct from — and sometimes more powerful than — individual reasoning. Central to Cor's insistence that removing cultural scaffolding (e.g., in atomized modern environments) produces mismatch even when the individual retains full cognitive capacity.

content: Cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities. Norms influence a vast range of human action, including ancient and fundamentally important domains such as kin relations, mating, food sharing, parenting, and reciprocity. Over our evolutionary history, norm violations such as ignoring a food taboo, botching a ritual, or failing to give one's in-laws their due from one's hunting successes meant reputational damage, gossip, and a consequent loss of marriage opportunities and allies. Repeated norm violations sometimes provoked ostracism or even execution at the hands of one's community.
author_quote: cultural evolution initiated a process of self-domestication, driving genetic evolution to make us prosocial, docile, rule followers who expect a world governed by social norms monitored and enforced by communities.
caveats: Henrich's self-domestication thesis: cumulative cultural evolution shaped the environment in which human genetic evolution operated, selecting for norm-following prosociality. Grounds both P2 (norm-following is a domain-sensitive evolved capacity, not a generic learning output) and M11 (cooperation/alliance architecture specifically includes norm enforcement via ostracism and execution).
scope: Links P2 (domain-sensitive architecture) to P3 (environmental matching) via gene-culture coevolution. Modern humans expect a normatively-regulated social environment as part of their evolved baseline; removing that expectation degrades M11 cooperation architecture even though the individual is still capable of norm recognition.

content: Over our evolutionary history, the growing body of adaptive information available in the minds of other people drove genetic evolution to create a second form of human status, called prestige, which now operates alongside the dominance status we inherited from our ape ancestors. The evolution of prestige came with new emotions, motivations, and bodily displays that are distinct from those associated with dominance. Prestige explains why people unconsciously mimic more successful individuals in conversations, why star athletes like LeBron James can sell car insurance, how someone can be famous for being famous, and why the most prestigious participants should donate first at charity events but speak last in decision-making bodies.
author_quote: The growing body of adaptive information available in the minds of other people also drove genetic evolution to create a second form of human status, called prestige, which now operates alongside the dominance status we inherited from our ape ancestors.
caveats: Henrich & Gil-White 2001 prestige-vs-dominance distinction, here restated by Henrich. Critical for M5 (Status Monitoring) in Cor — which already cites 'earned prestige preferred over coerced dominance (Henrich & Gil-White distinction — needs explicit treatment)' in the M5 resolution_conditions field. This extraction provides the primary-source grounding for that distinction. [Wave 1-D fix 2026-04-05 (ref msg #349): original author_quote combined two sentences from the same paragraph (source lines 491-502) via ellipsis, dropping intervening lines 494-500 containing the LeBron James / celebrity / Paris Hilton / charity-event examples. Option B PATCH: author_quote now contains only the opening clause (source lines 491-494) verbatim. The closing claim about 'new emotions, motivations, and bodily displays... distinct from those associated with dominance' (source lines 500-502) is preserved in the content field above as paraphrase. The prestige-vs-dominance architectural distinction that is load-bearing for M5 Status Monitoring is captured in the content field; author_quote anchors only the contiguous Fragment 1 portion per Wave 1-B verbatim-quote discipline.]
scope: M5 architectural refinement. Cor's M5 resolution condition specifies that earned prestige is the matched state; coerced dominance is a degraded state. Henrich provides the primary theoretical grounding: prestige is a genetically distinct status system from dominance, with distinct emotions and motivations.

content: Social Baseline Theory suggests the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals. The default and intrinsically social ecology the brain expects to function within is one of proximity to trusted others. Inspection of brain activity now suggests the brain responds to being alone as if sensory stimuli have been added, not taken away. That is, the brain looks more 'at rest' when social resources are obviously available. Proximity to a familiar other is the brain's true 'baseline' state, and being alone is more like an experimental treatment — a context that adds perceived work for the brain to do.
author_quote: But inspection of brain activity in several studies—elaborated on below—now suggests the brain responds to being alone as if sensory stimuli have been added, not taken away. That is, the brain looks more "at rest" when social resources are obviously available. This presents a puzzle potentially resolvable by considering proximity to a familiar other the brain's true "baseline" state, and being alone as more like an experimental treatment—a context that adds perceived work for the brain to do.
caveats: Quote replaced with a single contiguous verbatim passage from the Introduction of Coan & Sbarra (2015), Current Opinion in Psychology 1:87-91, confirmed against the open-access full text (PMC4375548). The PRIOR author_quote was non-verbatim: it stitched together TWO non-contiguous passages from different sections — the Abstract sentence ("the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals") joined by an ellipsis to an Introduction sentence — and altered formatting (added spaces around em-dashes, dropped the leading "But", changed straight double quotes to single quotes). The cross-section ellipsis stitch is not permitted under the verbatim rule, so it was removed. The replacement is the contiguous Introduction block, which alone fully supports the content claim (the brain treats isolation as a context that ADDS work; proximity to a familiar other is the true baseline — the DA2 founding inversion). The Abstract sentence about the brain "expecting access to social relationships..." remains accurately paraphrased in content and is itself verbatim in the source Abstract ("SBT suggests the human brain expects access to social relationships that mitigate risk and diminish the level of effort needed to meet a variety of goals.") should a separate abstract-sourced quote be desired. source_type remains 'primary' as the quote is now a genuine contiguous verbatim extract from the work_id source.
scope: DA2 founding claim in primary-source form. Establishes that social scaffolding is architectural (the default operating state of the brain), not a contingent comfort — which directly grounds Cor's DA2 ('human regulation is constitutively socially scaffolded; social context is likely the highest-leverage cross-cutting input dimension').

content: Social Baseline Theory suggests that proximity to social resources decreases the cost of climbing both the literal and figurative hills we face, because the brain construes social resources as bioenergetic resources, much like oxygen or glucose. Evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight-related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age, and income. To the human brain, social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably.
location: Section 'Social relationships decrease the predicted cost of the environment,' p. 88
author_quote: SBT suggests that proximity to social resources decreases the cost of climbing both the literal and figurative hills we face, because the brain construes social resources as bioenergetic resources, much like oxygen or glucose. Indeed, evidence suggests that hills literally appear less steep when standing next to a friend. Moreover, socially isolated individuals consume more sugar, even after adjusting for body mass index, weight related self-image, depression, physical activity, educational level, age and income. To the human brain, social and metabolic resources are treated almost interchangeably.
caveats: The metabolic-interchangeability argument: the brain treats the presence of a trusted other as literally equivalent to having more energy available. Both the hill-steepness perception finding and the isolation-sugar-consumption finding are replicated across multiple studies. The cross-domain link between M3 (social bonding) and M13 (energy regulation) is architectural, not metaphorical.
scope: Grounds the M3-M13 architectural cross-link. Isolation increases sugar consumption because the brain compensates for missing social resources with metabolic ones. This is one of the cleanest cross-mechanism cascade demonstrations in the Cor evidence base.

content: Although the brain is highly responsive to perceived threat, even simple handholding can substantially attenuate threat responses. These effects are potentiated by higher relationship quality, intimacy, and higher perceived mutuality. Critically, the likeliest mechanisms linking social support to diminished threat responding — regulatory circuits within the prefrontal cortex — are not more activated by support provision as originally hypothesized, but less so. During supportive handholding in particular, the threat responsive brain appears to return to a baseline state of relative calm, suggesting the difference is attributable less to the activation of regulatory circuitry and more to a decrease in perceived demand associated with the threat, a decrease proportional to the increase in resources brought to bear by the relational partner.
location: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' pp. 88-89
caveats: Audit R3: prior author_quote was non-verbatim and was removed; source_type demoted primary -> propagation pending verbatim re-sourcing from the open-access full text (PMC4375548, Coan & Sbarra 2015, section "Risk, effort, and the expanded self"). [Caveat repaired 2026-07-18: the prior caveat was a corrupted audit-log splice whose embedded verifier fragment and "Context:" tail contradicted each other on whether the replacement quote had been confirmed; the operational state - no verbatim quote captured, source_type=propagation - is preserved and the re-source remains pending.]
scope: Mechanism-level detail for the M3→M1 cascade. Handholding/proximity reduces the perceived threat, which reduces the downstream demand on the regulatory system, which is why the regulatory circuitry shows LESS activation under support, not more. Critical for Cor's claim that M3 is a grounding mechanism that reduces load on downstream mechanisms rather than activating a separate regulation system.

content: Social Baseline Theory suggests that the brain encodes what we subjectively experience as the self in ways that literally include close others. The brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self — but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one's own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
location: Section 'Risk, effort, and the expanded self,' p. 89
author_quote: the brain encodes threats directed at familiar others very similarly to how it encodes threats directed at the self—but no such similarity obtains for strangers. Representing relational partners as extensions or aspects of the self could effectively yield bioenergetic resources by influencing how the brain budgets the resources immediately at its disposal. If the relational partner can be counted on to meet all or part of an environmental demand, one’s own resources can either be conserved or devoted to other problems as if personal bioenergetic resources were literally increased. This could explain how the brain construes resources available to relational partners as resources available to the self. Indeed, it suggests that attachment may reflect a neural (and conceptual) conflation of self and other.
caveats: Quote re-sourced verbatim from the open-access full text (PMC4375548), section "Risk, Effort, and the Expanded Self." The prior author_quote had two integrity defects, now corrected: (1) it used an ellipsis ("...") that silently dropped two intervening sentences ("If the relational partner can be counted on..." and "This could explain how the brain construes..."), stitching non-adjacent clauses; (2) it rendered the original em-dash ("self—but") as a spaced hyphen ("self — but"). The replacement is the complete contiguous passage as printed in the source (inline reference markers removed), truncated at a sentence boundary on the closing "conflation of self and other" sentence; the original's following fragment "We see this as likely." is omitted as it is not load-bearing for the claim. The self-expansion / neural self-other-conflation finding is a distinctive SBT contribution: the brain encodes trusted others within the self's threat-processing circuitry, giving attachment theory's "internal working model" a literal neural implementation.
scope: DA2 architectural detail. Explains why isolation and relationship loss are architecturally equivalent to losing part of the self, and why M3 grief mode has such broad downstream suppressive effects — the neural self has been diminished.

content: Allostatic load represents the 'wear and tear' the body experiences when repeated allostatic responses are activated during stressful situations. While adaptive acutely, chronic over-activation of sympathetic-adrenal-medullary and HPA-axis products induce a 'domino effect' on interconnected biological systems that overcompensate and eventually collapse themselves, leaving the organism susceptible to stress-related diseases. Brain changes associated with chronic stress and allostatic load — synaptic and dendritic remodeling, suppressed neurogenesis, structural atrophy/hypertrophy — further diminish the body's ability to cognitively process and physiologically respond to stressors.
author_quote: Allostatic load (AL) represents the 'wear and tear' the body experiences when repeated allostatic responses are activated during stressful situations (McEwen and Stellar, 1993)... While adaptive acutely, chronic over-activation of SAM- and HPA-axis products induce a 'domino effect' on interconnected biological systems that overcompensate and eventually collapse themselves, leaving the organism susceptible to stress-related diseases.
caveats: Juster, McEwen & Lupien's definition of allostatic load in the matured 2010 review. Cites McEwen & Stellar 1993 as the original formulation but states the concept in its 2010 form. The 'domino effect' language makes explicit the cascading-across-systems claim that DA3 formalizes. [Splice note: author_quote uses '...' to join two non-contiguous passages from the same review section. The ellipsis elides discussion between the allostatic-load definition and the biomarker cascade description. Both segments verbatim from source. Flagged by codex-research audit 2026-04-05; retained as single quote because the two halves form one coherent argument per Juster et al.]
scope: DC1 operationalization + DA3 cascading mechanism. The domino effect description is how Cor's DA3 (Recurrent Coupling and Cascading) and DC1 (Allostatic Load Accumulation) connect: load accumulates through cross-system cascades, not through single-system damage.

content: There are four profiles that illustrate how allostatic states deviate from healthy responses: (1) repeated hits from multiple stressors; (2) lack of adaptation reflected in a failure to habituate to stressors; (3) prolonged response due to impaired negative feedback; and (4) inadequate response or a hypoactive state. Multi-systemic allostatic load biomarker indexes comprising cortisol, catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine), DHEA-S, cholesterol ratios, glycosylated hemoglobin, C-reactive protein, blood pressure, and waist-to-hip ratio predict mortality, cognitive decline, and incident cardiovascular disease independently of baseline health status, with none of the individual biomarkers explaining the outcomes — supporting the utility of the multi-systemic composite approach.
location: Figure 2 and Section 4, 'Review of studies incorporating allostatic load algorithms,' pp. 4-5
author_quote: There are four profiles that illustrate how allostatic states deviate from healthy responses: (1) repeated hits from multiple stressors; (2) lack of adaptation reflected in a failure to habituate to stressors; (3) prolonged response due to impaired negative feedback; and (4) inadequate response or a hypoactive state (McEwen, 1998a).
caveats: The four allostatic-state profiles are the operational definition of what 'dysregulated stress response' means in the framework. evidence_quality='meta_analysis' because the Juster 2010 review synthesizes ~58 allostatic-load studies showing predictive validity of the composite AL index across mortality, cognitive decline, and CVD outcomes.
scope: DC1 operationalization with the four dysregulation profiles. Critical for A2 (clinical application) because the four profiles correspond to different treatment pathways — repeated hits vs failure to habituate vs impaired feedback vs hypoactive state require different interventions.

content: The brain is the central organ of stress and adaptation to stress because it perceives and determines what is threatening, as well as the behavioral and physiological responses to the stressor. The adult, as well as developing brain, possess a remarkable ability to show reversible structural and functional plasticity in response to stressful and other experiences, including neuronal replacement, dendritic remodeling, and synapse turnover. This is particularly evident in the hippocampus. The amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, brain regions involved in anxiety and fear, mood, cognitive function and behavioral control, also show structural plasticity. Repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.
author_quote: As to the functional consequences of structural remodeling in hippocampus, repeated stress can impair hippocampal-dependent behaviors in a manner that is reversible, along with dendritic shrinkage in the CA3 region, within days or weeks after the termination of the stressor. This supports the notion that the remodeling is not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity that may also protect the hippocampus from permanent excitotoxic damage.
caveats: Quote re-sourced to a single contiguous verbatim passage from the "Functional consequences" section of McEwen, Eiland, Hunter & Miller (2012), Neuropharmacology 62(1):3-12, confirmed against the open-access PubMedCentral full text (PMC3196296). The PRIOR author_quote was a STITCH: it joined one sentence from the Abstract ("The adult, as well as developing brain, possess a remarkable ability to show reversible structural and functional plasticity...synapse turnover") to two consecutive sentences from a different section (the "Functional consequences" body text) using an ellipsis, and silently lowercased the bridging clause. Each component was individually verbatim, but the spliced result is not a contiguous source passage and violates the no-stitching rule. Replaced with the contiguous CA3-remodeling passage, which carries the load-bearing claim (reversible impairment + "not brain damage but a form of adaptive plasticity"). The dropped abstract sentence on reversible plasticity remains accurately reflected in the content field; it was not re-included in author_quote to avoid re-introducing the stitch. The content claim itself is accurate and uncontested and was left unchanged.
scope: Grounds the 'hardware works perfectly, environment is wrong' principle at the neurobiological level. Reversible dendritic remodeling in hippocampus/PFC/amygdala under chronic stress is adaptive plasticity; permanence comes only from sustained overload. Supports DA1 (defensive signals) and DC1 (reversibility component).

content: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention with a combination of pharmacological and behavioral therapies. Chronic restraint stress causes dendritic shortening in medial prefrontal cortex but produces dendritic growth in neurons of the basolateral amygdala — opposite structural effects in interconnected regions, reflecting different functional roles under sustained stress.
location: Introduction and Section 2.4, 'Prefrontal cortex and amygdala,' pp. 3-4
author_quote: Acute and chronic stress cause an imbalance of neural circuitry subserving cognition, decision making, anxiety and mood that can increase or decrease expression of those behaviors and behavioral states. In the short term, such as for increased fearful vigilance and anxiety in a threatening environment, these changes may be adaptive; but, if the danger passes and the behavioral state persists along with the changes in neural circuitry, such maladaptation may need intervention
caveats: The acute-adaptive vs chronic-maladaptive distinction with specific structural evidence: dendritic shortening in PFC vs dendritic growth in amygdala under the same chronic stressor. This is the four-category distinction Cor inherits (defensive activation, dysregulation, damage, developmental miscalibration) at the neural level: same mechanism, different time-scales and different consequences.
scope: Grounds the DA1 four-category distinction architecturally. Stress-induced brain changes are adaptive on short time-scales and maladaptive on long ones; the same circuit shows opposing dendritic changes (PFC shortening, amygdala growth) that together produce the behavioral state of sustained fearful vigilance — which is M1 over-activation at the neural level.

content: Dopamine is neither necessary nor sufficient to mediate changes in hedonic 'liking' for sensory pleasures. Other recent evidence indicates that dopamine is not needed for new learning, and not sufficient to directly mediate learning by causing teaching or prediction signals. By contrast, growing evidence indicates that dopamine does contribute causally to incentive salience. Dopamine appears necessary for normal 'wanting', and dopamine activation can be sufficient to enhance cue-triggered incentive salience. Drugs of abuse that promote dopamine signals short circuit and sensitize dynamic mesolimbic mechanisms that evolved to attribute incentive salience to rewards.
author_quote: recent evidence indicates that dopamine is neither necessary nor sufficient to mediate changes in hedonic 'liking' for sensory pleasures. Other recent evidence indicates that dopamine is not needed for new learning, and not sufficient to directly mediate learning by causing teaching or prediction signals. By contrast, growing evidence indicates that dopamine does contribute causally to incentive salience. Dopamine appears necessary for normal 'wanting', and dopamine activation can be sufficient to enhance cue-triggered incentive salience. Drugs of abuse that promote dopamine signals short circuit and sensitize dynamic mesolimbic mechanisms that evolved to attribute incentive salience to rewards.
caveats: Berridge's own 2007 summary of the wanting/liking dissociation evidence base. The key architectural claim: dopamine mediates 'wanting' (motivation toward a reward) but not 'liking' (hedonic satisfaction from the reward). This is THE primary mechanism underlying DA4 (Proxy Hijacking via Open Loops): a proxy that triggers dopamine release activates the wanting system without needing to deliver any actual liking, producing an open loop.
scope: DA4 core mechanism statement in primary-source form. Establishes that motivational pursuit and hedonic satisfaction are dissociable at the neural level, which is the architectural vulnerability every modern engineered proxy exploits: variable-reward apps, ultra-processed food, pornography, and companion AI all fire wanting without resolution-condition liking.

content: Parkinson's patients with 'dopamine dysregulation syndrome' (DDS) take far greater amounts of L-DOPA than prescribed in an apparently compulsive fashion and can develop other compulsive activities including gambling and obsessive pursuit of certain repetitive trivial activities ('punding'). PET neuroimaging of these DDS patients showed that after an L-DOPA dose, they exhibited a sensitized over-elevation in drug-stimulated dopamine neurotransmission in ventral striatum. Importantly, the excessive dopamine release measured by PET correlated strongly with subjective ratings of wanting for L-DOPA ('do you want to take more of what you consumed, right now?'), but did not cause patients to give higher liking ratings to L-DOPA — there was no correlation between subjective liking ratings and PET-measured dopamine release.
location: Section 'Analysis of hedonia hypothesis,' Evans et al. 2006 PET study, pp. 396-397
author_quote: when they took an L-DOPA dose, the DDS patients showed a sensitized over elevation in drug-stimulated dopamine neurotransmission in ventral striatum, including nucleus accumbens (Evans et al. 2006).
