Importantly for understanding dopamine's role, the excessive dopamine release measured by PET correlated strongly with subjective ratings of wanting for L-DOPA ('do you want to take more of what you consumed, right now?'). However, excessive dopamine release did not cause patients to give higher liking ratings to L-DOPA, and there was no correlation found between subjective liking ratings ('do you like the effects you feel right now?') and PET-measured dopamine release
caveats: Human neuroimaging confirmation of the wanting/liking dissociation in a clinical population (Parkinson's DDS). evidence_quality='clinical' because Evans et al. 2006 is a single-study clinical population result; the broader Berridge program combining this with animal evidence is 'replicated'. This extraction captures the human evidence specifically.
scope: Critical clinical evidence for the architectural dissociation. DDS patients experience compulsive wanting WITHOUT enhanced liking — the exact pattern predicted by the wanting/liking dissociation and the exact pattern Cor attributes to every modern engineered proxy. The human evidence closes the gap between animal neuroscience and real-world implications.

content: In normal human volunteers, temporary dietary manipulation to deplete brain dopamine levels (via ingestion of a deficient amino acid mixture) caused a dopamine-induced dissociation between subjective liking and wanting for intranasally administered cocaine. Dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged. Several psychopharmacological studies have similarly reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched. Dopamine appears to correspond more closely to ratings of reward wanting than to reward liking.
location: Section 'Analysis of hedonia hypothesis,' Leyton et al. 2005 and Brauer/de Wit studies, pp. 397-398
author_quote: dopamine depletion caused a suppression of subjective ratings of wanting/desire to take more cocaine, but left subjective liking ratings for cocaine pleasure essentially unchanged (Leyton et al. 2005)... In several psychopharmacological studies, Brauer and colleagues (especially deWit) reported that dopamine blockade by neuroleptic antagonists may suppress wanting ratings or behavioral consumption of amphetamine or cigarettes, yet leave subjective liking ratings for the drugs untouched
caveats: Multi-study replication of the dopamine-wanting-not-liking dissociation in healthy humans. Dietary depletion (Leyton et al.) and pharmacological blockade (Brauer/deWit studies) converge on the same result: dopamine manipulation suppresses wanting without affecting liking. evidence_quality='replicated' because multiple independent research programs (Leyton dietary depletion + Brauer/deWit pharmacological blockade) converge on the same finding.
scope: Strong cross-method replication of the architectural dissociation in healthy humans. Together with the Parkinson's DDS clinical evidence and the animal-model evidence, the wanting/liking dissociation is among the best-replicated findings in reward neuroscience.

content: Many functions have been suggested for low mood or depression, including communicating a need for help, signaling yielding in a hierarchy conflict, fostering disengagement from commitments to unreachable goals, and regulating patterns of investment. A more comprehensive evolutionary explanation may emerge from attempts to identify how the characteristics of low mood increase an organism's ability to cope with the adaptive challenges characteristic of unpropitious situations in which effort to pursue a major goal will likely result in danger, loss, bodily damage, or wasted effort. In such situations, pessimism and lack of motivation may give a fitness advantage by inhibiting certain actions, especially futile or dangerous challenges to dominant figures, actions in the absence of a crucial resource or a viable plan, efforts that would damage the body, and actions that would disrupt a currently unsatisfactory major life enterprise when it might recover or the alternative is likely to be even worse.
author_quote: Many functions have been suggested for low mood or depression, including communicating a need for help, signaling yielding in a hierarchy conflict, fostering disengagement from commitments to unreachable goals, and regulating patterns of investment. A more comprehensive evolutionary explanation may emerge from attempts to identify how the characteristics of low mood increase an organism's ability to cope with the adaptive challenges characteristic of unpropitious situations in which effort to pursue a major goal will likely result in danger, loss, bodily damage, or wasted effort.
caveats: The paper's abstract statement of the multi-subtype thesis. Nesse enumerates four proposed functions of low mood (communication, yielding, disengagement, investment regulation) and frames them as complementary rather than competing — different aspects of a common architectural response to 'unpropitious situations.' This is the primary-source grounding for Cor's DA1 treatment of depression as a family of defensive signals, not a single disease.
scope: DA1 foundational statement for depression specifically. Establishes that low mood has multiple adaptive functions corresponding to different types of unpropitious situations, and that pathological depression results when low mood is 'excessive, prolonged, or expressed in the wrong situation.'

content: Natural selection may have gradually and partially differentiated a generic state of inhibition into subtypes specialized to cope with particular kinds of situations. Sadness, depression, guilt, and grief may be partially differentiated members of a 'fuzzy set' whose commonalities are explained partially by phylogeny and partially by the benefits certain responses offer in any unpropitious situation. Depression is painful and interferes with normal function, so it seems obviously maladaptive. However, other useful capacities, such as pain, nausea, and fatigue, are also aversive and disruptive. In fact, their very aversiveness is likely a product of natural selection, probably because they promote escape and avoidance of situations that decrease fitness. From this perspective, the intrinsic aversiveness of most low mood and depression suggests that they may be related to a defense.
author_quote: Natural selection may have gradually and partially differentiated a generic state of inhibition into subtypes specialized to cope with particular kinds of situations. Sadness, depression, guilt, and grief may be partially differentiated members of a 'fuzzy set' whose commonalities are explained partially by phylogeny and partially by the benefits certain responses offer in any unpropitious situation.
caveats: The 'fuzzy set' framing is important for Cor because it directly supports the 'not one thing' treatment of depression: sadness, grief, guilt, and clinical depression are partially differentiated subtypes of a common ancestral inhibition state, shaped by phylogeny plus situation-specific selection. This justifies Cor's four-category distinction (defensive activation, dysregulation, damage, developmental miscalibration) — within defensive activation alone, there are multiple subtypes that map to different situations.
scope: Architectural refinement of DA1. Not only are aversive outputs defensive signals rather than defects, but different aversive outputs (sadness, grief, guilt, depression) are partially differentiated adaptations to different situations, with overlapping phylogenetic origins.

content: Price and others have suggested the utility of depression as a yielding signal in hierarchy conflicts. Basing their theory on animal models, they recognized that many of their patients with depression were unwilling to yield to a more powerful adversary. If they did finally yield, this signaled to the dominant figure that the person was no longer a threat, ended the conflict, and resolved the depression. This theory suggests a possible role for high as well as low mood in negotiating hierarchies and is supported by clinical evidence of episodes of depression precipitated by social competition and resolved by reconciliation.
location: Section 'Possible Functions of Low Mood and Depression,' p. 15
author_quote: Price and others have suggested the utility of depression as a yielding signal in hierarchy conflicts. Basing their theory on animal models, they recognized that many of their patients with depression were unwilling to yield to a more powerful adversary. If they did finally yield, this signaled to the dominant figure that the person was no longer a threat, ended the conflict, and resolved the depression.
caveats: Nesse endorses the Price/Gilbert involuntary defeat / social competition hypothesis of depression. This maps depression onto M5 (Status Monitoring) — specifically the rank-regulation failure mode where inability to yield produces prolonged defensive activation. Critical for Cor because it links depression (DA1 subtype) to M5 mechanism output and predicts that environmental correction (reconciliation, status restoration) resolves the depression.
scope: The social-competition subtype of depression. Maps a specific depression presentation to M5 (Status Monitoring) mechanism and predicts rank-resolution as the therapeutic lever. Provides primary-source grounding for Cor's M5-driven status-defeat cascade.

content: The role of depression in disengaging motivation from an unreachable goal was specified explicitly in the incentive-disengagement theory of Klinger. If a commitment to pursue a goal encounters an obstacle, efforts increase and become aggressive. If the obstacle cannot be overcome, low mood helps to disengage the commitment and end the cycle. If the individual cannot disengage, low mood escalates. Klinger concludes, 'depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive.' Many other researchers also see a close relationship between depression and difficulty in disengaging from major commitments. Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources — toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
location: Section 'Possible Functions of Low Mood and Depression,' pp. 15-16
author_quote: depression is ordinarily, therefore, a normal, adaptive part of disengaging oneself from an incentive... Mood thus regulates the allocation of effort and resources—toward enterprises, strategies, and times likely to give a high payoff and away from unprofitable enterprises and times when efforts will likely be wasted or dangerous.
caveats: The Klinger incentive-disengagement subtype of depression. Maps depression onto M2 (Pursuit/Exploration) failure and M6 (Controllability/Agency) degradation: when a pursued goal is unreachable but the individual cannot disengage, low mood escalates. This is the DA1 framing of the M6 cascade — learned helplessness via unreachable goals produces depressive symptoms as a motivational-disengagement signal that failed to terminate pursuit.
scope: The unreachable-goal subtype of depression. Maps to M2 (Pursuit/Exploration) and M6 (Controllability/Agency) cascade failure. Provides primary-source grounding for one of Cor's core cascade chains: goal blockage → M6 degradation → M2 anhedonia → DA1 defensive signal.

content: Social pain, also known as loneliness, evolved because it protected the individual from the danger of remaining isolated. Our forebears depended on social bonds for safety and for the successful replication of their genes. Feelings of loneliness told them when those protective bonds were endangered or deficient. In the same way that physical pain serves as a prompt to change behavior — the pain of burning skin tells you to pull your finger away from the frying pan — loneliness developed as a stimulus to get humans to pay more attention to their social connections, and to reach out toward others, to renew frayed or broken bonds.
location: Chapter 1 'Lonely in a Social World,' p. 7
author_quote: Social pain, also known as loneliness, evolved for a similar reason: because it protected the individual from the danger of remaining isolated. Our forebears depended on social bonds for safety and for the successful replication of their genes in the form of offspring who themselves survived long enough to reproduce. Feelings of loneliness told them when those protective bonds were endangered or deficient. In the same way that physical pain serves as a prompt to change behavior — the pain of burning skin tells you to pull your finger away from the frying pan — loneliness developed as a stimulus to get humans to pay more attention to their social connections, and to reach out toward others, to renew frayed or broken bonds.
caveats: Cacioppo's founding statement of the loneliness-as-evolved-signal thesis. source_type='propagation' because this is framework synthesis building on Bowlby/Panksepp rather than a primary research finding from Cacioppo's own lab. No OCR issues at this passage — text is clean modern-book scan. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): retroactive caveat per new quote-normalization policy (effective 2026-04-05). Contiguous-verbatim anchoring of the quote otherwise confirmed by codex-research audit; no splices, no rewording, no semantic substitutions, no tense/pronoun adjustments.

Directly grounds M3 Social Bonding's grief-mode operating condition (pain-grade distress when bonds are lost or endangered) and supports DA1 (aversive outputs as intelligible defensive signals) applied specifically to the social domain.

content: In English, we have a word for pain and a word for thirst, but no single, specific terms that mean the opposite. We merely reference the absence of these aversive conditions, which makes sense, because their absence is considered part of the normal state. 'Not lonely' — there is no better, more specific term for it — is also, like 'not thirsty' or 'not in pain,' very much part of the normal state. Health and well-being for a member of our species requires, among other things, being satisfied and secure in our bonds with other people, a condition of 'not being lonely' that, for want of a better word, we call social connection.

content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows that the emotional region of the brain activated when we experience rejection is the same region — the dorsal anterior cingulate — that registers emotional responses to physical pain. The discovery that feelings of social rejection (isolation) and reactions to physical pain share the same hardware begins to suggest why, once loneliness becomes chronic, you cannot escape it merely by 'coming out of your shell,' losing weight, getting a fashion makeover, or meeting Mr. or Ms. Right.

author_quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) shows us that the emotional region of the brain that is activated when we experience rejection is, in fact, the same region — the dorsal anterior cingulate — that registers emotional responses to physical pain
caveats: Cacioppo is reporting Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams 2003 Science paper findings here — this is not Cacioppo's primary data, hence source_type='propagation' and evidence_quality='clinical' (single fMRI study of n≈13 at publication). The Eisenberger 2003 paper itself has since been replicated and critiqued; the specific ACC-pain overlap claim is contested in the reverse-inference literature but the basic neural-overlap finding has held up. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): retroactive caveat per new quote-normalization policy (effective 2026-04-05). content: Between 1991 and 2003, Dorret Boomsma of the Free University Amsterdam tracked thousands of identical twins in the Netherlands Twin Register on items measuring loneliness. When one member of an identical twin pair was lonely, loneliness in the second member could be predicted approximately 48% of the time — a heritability coefficient around .48 that holds true for most major personality characteristics including neuroticism, agreeableness, and anxiety. The genes set the course, but the environment still strongly influences the final destination.
location: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 23-24
author_quote: when we found loneliness in one member of a pair of these identical twins, our prediction of loneliness in the second member of the pair was right approximately forty-eight percent of the time. To understand the significance of that predictive ability, consider that whether an individual is lonely or not lonely is a fifty-fifty proposition, like a coin toss. But our forty-eight percent predictive accuracy was not based on a one-shot flip of the coin. This was a case of being able to predict the outcome forty-eight percent of the time throughout the whole series of several thousand twin pairs. The odds of being right by chance half the time in a series of thousands of fifty-fifty propositions are virtually nil. So what our ability to predict indicated was the influence of heredity. It so happens that a heritability coefficient around .48 also holds true for most of the other genetically influenced major personality characteristics such as neuroticism, agreeableness, and anxiety.
caveats: Cacioppo uses 'we found' here, indicating he was a collaborator on the Boomsma twin-register analysis — source_type='primary' for Cacioppo via his co-investigator role. evidence_quality='longitudinal' (1991-2003 panel) plus the Netherlands Twin Register is one of the largest behavioral-genetics samples in existence. Note: the .48 heritability coefficient is for the disposition to feel lonely, not for loneliness as a state — standard behavior-genetics trait heritability estimate. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). The Boomsma-introduction text (1154-1167) was moved to content as paraphrase in the original extraction and retained. Line-break hyphenation joined throughout per quote-normalization policy (e.g. 'fifty-/fifty'). No other normalization.
scope: Supports the 'elastic leash' framing: M3's sensitivity to social deprivation has a substantial heritable component (variation in set-point sensitivity to the same social input), consistent with an evolved architecture rather than a cultural construction. P2 (domain-sensitive architecture) grounding via twin-register behavioral genetics.

content: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. When our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force.
location: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 31-32
author_quote: For creatures shaped by evolution to feel safe in company and endangered when unwillingly alone, feelings of isolation and perceptions of threat reinforce each other to promote a higher and more persistent level of wariness. To prepare us to react efficiently when confronting threats to life and limb, nature provided us with the ability to be cognitively hypervigilant, along with a chain of physiological reactions known as the fight-or-flight response. But the neurological wiring we depend on today evolved in response to the kinds of hit-and-run stressors we faced millions of years ago. As a result, our stress response ('fight or flight') includes a prompt to immediate action that increases resistance in the cardiovascular system and floods the body with hormones that rev us up. If we were fending off wild dogs, those hormones could help save our lives. However, when our stressors consist of feeling isolated and unloved, the constant presence of these excitatory chemicals acts as a corrosive force that accelerates the aging process.
caveats: Cacioppo & Hawkley's hypervigilance-to-threat cascade framing: loneliness does not just sit next to threat detection; it drives threat detection into a self-reinforcing over-activation. This is the M3→M1 cascade path Cor treats as core. source_type='propagation' (framework synthesis of multiple findings). | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). content: Cacioppo frames loneliness as a functional evolved signal rather than a defect: loneliness, like hunger, is an aversive warning whose adaptive function is to prompt corrective action (return to social bonds). Depression is a distinct state that suppresses action rather than motivating it — the two states operate in functional opposition but can both be present at chronic intensity. Cacioppo elsewhere in the chapter (pp. ~85, lines 3360-3362) proposes that depression itself may have an adaptive social role as the complementary pole of this push-pull regulation system.
location: Chapter 5 'The Universal and the Particular,' pp. 83-85
author_quote: Although both are aversive, uncomfortable states, loneliness and depression are in many ways opposites. Loneliness, like hunger, is a warning to do something to alter an uncomfortable and possibly dangerous condition. Depression makes us apathetic. Whereas loneliness urges us to move forward, depression holds us back.
caveats: The explicit 'loneliness like hunger' signal-framing passage. Cacioppo pairs loneliness (forward-prompting alarm) with depression (backward-holding conservation) as complementary architectural responses in a go/stop regulation system. source_type='propagation' (conceptual framework, not primary data). | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). content: The body's ability to maintain stability through change — allostasis — has a physiological cost, and the total cost of all these adjustments is called the allostatic load. The stress of having only limited power in a hierarchy, or the stress of feeling isolated in your community, your school, or your marriage, increases wear and tear throughout the system. Loneliness causes ill health through a grinding process of wear and tear that proceeds along five intersecting pathways: health behaviors, exposure to stressors, perceived stress and coping, physiological response to stress, and rest/restoration/repair.
location: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' pp. 98-99, citing McEwen allostasis framework
author_quote: The standard operating procedure—staying within the tightly prescribed boundaries—is called homeostasis. The process of making special adjustments of those boundaries according to the broader needs of the organism is called allostasis. Homeostasis is like the first chair violinist: vitally important, but wedded to playing the musical score faithfully as it is written. Allostasis is more like a conductor, responsible for the entire orchestra, who brings a particular interpretation to the performance, and who may, within certain broader limits, alter the tempo or volume or other dynamics of the score as written by the composer. Both ways of proceeding are necessary and desirable, but every time a body system responds to a stressor, whether the response is homeostatic or allostatic, there is a physiological cost to making the adjustment. The more complex the allostatic adjustment, the greater the number of bodily systems—endocrine, cardiovascular, immune—that become involved. The more systems, the larger the needed adjustments, and the more frequently these adjustments are required, the higher the physiological cost of bringing your body back to normal. The total cost of all these adjustments, the rigidly constrained and the more broadly orchestrated, is called the allostatic load.
caveats: Cacioppo applies McEwen's allostasis/allostatic-load framework specifically to chronic loneliness. source_type='propagation' (McEwen's concept, not Cacioppo's). Links the M3 grief-mode cascade to DC1 (Allostatic Load Accumulation) as the route by which chronic social isolation produces measurable cardiovascular/immune wear over time. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). content: In our studies, the lonely, both young and old, perceived the hassles and stresses of everyday life to be more severe than did their nonlonely counterparts, even though the objective stressors they encountered were essentially the same. The lonely also found the small social uplifts of everyday life to be less intense and less gratifying. The presence of and interaction with other people in their lives did not cause them to rate the severity of everyday stressors any less intensely.

content: Our studies showed that loneliness on a given day predicted a higher rise in cortisol the next morning. When we drew blood from our older adults and analyzed their white cells, we found that loneliness somehow penetrated the deepest recesses of the cell to alter the way genes were being expressed. Loneliness predicted changes in DNA transcription that, in turn, made changes in the cell's sensitivity to circulating cortisol, dampening the ability to shut off the inflammatory response.

content: In our Ohio State studies we found that the greater the degree of loneliness of the student volunteers, the higher their total peripheral resistance (TPR), even when their overall blood pressure remained normal. Active coping raises blood pressure primarily by revving up cardiac output. Coping passively — which is what we do when we feel isolated — raises blood pressure primarily by constricting the small arteries, also known as increasing TPR. Higher TPR forces the heart muscle to work harder to distribute the same amount of liquid through the blood vessels.
location: Chapter 6 'The Wear and Tear of Loneliness,' Pathway 4, pp. 103-104
author_quote: In our Ohio State studies we found that the greater the degree of loneliness of the student volunteers, the higher their TPR, even when their overall blood pressure remained normal. This was the case even when we added a bit of stress by asking the students to get up and speak in public, and also when we beeped them during the course of a normal day. In these situations, stress caused blood pressure, TPR, and cardiac output to go up for everyone. But because the lonely group started out with higher TPR, their TPR under stress was higher still.
caveats: Primary finding from Cacioppo's Ohio State lab studies with undergraduate samples. source_type='primary'. evidence_quality='clinical' — single-lab undergraduate samples, one population, not yet replicated across labs at the 2008 publication date. content: In a study at the University of Chicago Brain Imaging Center, volunteers viewed photographs of objects or people, selected to have positive or negative emotional impact. Nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum — one of the brain's reward centers — when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being meant something special. Lonely participants, however, when viewing positive images of people, did not register the same boost: the activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers.
location: Chapter 9 'A Concerto for Two (or More) Voices,' Brain Imaging Center study, pp. 162-163
author_quote: As indicated in Figure 14, nonlonely participants showed greater activity in the ventral striatum, one of the brain's 'reward centers,' when they saw a pleasant image of a person (a smiling farmer) than when they saw an equally pleasant picture of an object (a flower arrangement). For the nonlonely, a positive image of another human being obviously meant something special—it gave them a specific emotional boost as evidenced by changes in this specific area that registers pleasure. Lonely participants, however, when they viewed positive images of people, did not register the same boost: The activation of the ventral striatum in response to a happy face was in fact a bit weaker than when they saw the pleasant picture of the flowers. This finding aligns with self-reports in which lonely individuals said that they found positive social interactions to be less of an uplift than did their nonlonely counterparts.

This is the 'DA4 proxy-failure' route applied to the M3 → M2 pathway: lonely individuals get less reward from social contact even when it is available, which is why 'just meet people' advice fails — the reward machinery is already downregulated.

content: In the same Chicago Brain Imaging Center fMRI study, when participants viewed negative images, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing. Nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects. Lonely individuals, however, paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people — measured by visual cortex activation. When observing the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and perspective taking, lonely individuals appeared more likely to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.
author_quote: In the same study, when the photographs were negative, the patterns of brain activation were equally revealing about the experience of loneliness, moment to moment. Whereas nonlonely participants paid comparable attention to negative images of people and objects, lonely individuals paid far more attention to the negative images depicting people. In both cases, the measure was activation of their visual cortex. When we observed the temporoparietal junction, an area involved in theory of mind and in perspective taking, the pattern of activation was the opposite. Lonely individuals appeared more likely than their nonlonely counterparts to respond to pictures of people in peril from their first-person perspective (as indicated by weaker activation of the temporoparietal junction). When we feel lonely, we tend to scan the horizon for any possibility of social danger, but with an eye toward protecting ourselves rather than with genuine concern for what others may be thinking or feeling.
caveats: Same Chicago Brain Imaging Center study as previous extraction. source_type='primary'. evidence_quality='clinical' (single fMRI study). The theory-of-mind/perspective-taking attenuation finding is important because it shows M3 deprivation degrades prosocial cognition — which explains why loneliness is self-reinforcing: the cognitive apparatus for connecting to others is impaired. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). content: Human stressors no longer come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of fight-or-flight. We can have the same overbearing boss, the same long commute, the same worries about health care and retirement, and the same feelings of social isolation, hour after hour, year after year. Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. The environment is entirely different now than it was in our environment of evolutionary adaptation, but our sympathetic / parasympathetic architecture has not changed.

content: A genetic thermostat for connection sets different individuals at different points along a social-need spectrum, but the thermostat is highly elastic — genes set the course, but the environment still strongly influences the final destination. The elastic-leash framing (E. O. Wilson) captures this: heritability in human behavior means genes bias outcomes without fully determining them. The organism mediates between genes and environment, and subjective social perception plays a determining role in the net outcome.
location: Chapter 2 'Variation, Regulation, and an Elastic Leash,' pp. 24-25
author_quote: As E. O. Wilson's image of the elastic leash suggests, heritability in human behavior means that the genes set the course, but that the environment still strongly influences the final destination. The influence of genes on a purely physical characteristic such as eye color is generally 100 percent, as is the influence of genes on certain conditions such as Huntington's disease. In those cases, genes are in fact destiny; the environment is never going to change the outcome. With the genetic bias toward a greater need for feelings of connection, however, a genetic contribution of forty-eight percent allows for a fifty-two percent contribution from the world we encounter. Mediating between the genes and the environment is the organism—which is to say, you and me. And here is where social cognition—our subjective perceptions—plays such an important role in determining the net outcome.

content: Loneliness and depression share a diminished sense of personal control, which leads to passive coping. This induced passivity is one of the reasons that, despite the pain and urgency that loneliness imposes, it does not always lead to effective action. Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'

Loss of executive control leads to lack of persistence, and frustration leads to what the psychologist Martin Seligman has termed 'learned helplessness.'

content: Loneliness is a perpetrator that uses five different modus operandi to damage health: (1) health behaviors; (2) exposure to stressors; (3) perceived stress and coping; (4) physiological response to stress; and (5) rest, restoration, and repair. Using loneliness as a window on sociality provides a unified account of why chronic social disconnection produces the pattern of morbidity and mortality observed in the epidemiological literature.
location: Chapter 7 'Sympathetic Threads,' pp. 126-127 recap of the five-pathways framework introduced in Chapter 6
author_quote: As we have just seen, loneliness is a perpetrator that uses five different modus operandi to undermine our health. Once we see loneliness on the list of serious risk factors for illness and early death, right alongside smoking, obesity, and lack of exercise, that context should heighten our motivation to improve our level of social satisfaction, both as individuals and as a society. But in a broader sense, the power we can now assign to loneliness, and conversely the power we can now assign to social connection, illuminates human nature itself, underscoring the 'obligatorily gregarious' aspect of our species that is too often overlooked. Our sociality is central to who we are.
caveats: Cacioppo's five-pathways summary framework for how chronic loneliness translates to physical morbidity/mortality. source_type='propagation' (synthesis of the preceding chapter's primary findings). Parallels and complements the Holt-Lunstad meta-analytic 50% mortality finding.

content: Among people above a threshold of material well-being, the higher their status in the pecking order the healthier they are likely to be. In other words, health follows a social gradient. I call this the status syndrome. For people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being is central. Autonomy — how much control you have over your life — and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.
author_quote: The answer that I shall lay out in this book, is that for people above a threshold of material well-being, another kind of well-being 1s central. Autonomy — how much control you have over your life — and the opportunities you have for full social engagement and participation are crucial for health, well-being and longevity. It is inequality in these that plays a big part in producing the social gradient in health. Degrees of control and participation underlie the status syndrome.

Marmot names two distinct causal mechanisms — autonomy/control (M6) and social engagement/participation (M3/M11) — both operating on top of a status-gradient phenomenon (M5). source_type='propagation' because this is framework synthesis after 25 years of research; the primary Whitehall papers carry the 'primary' tag where quoted directly. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). The pecking-order finding is preserved in content as paraphrase. The two-mechanism answer (autonomy + participation) is critical because it means the M5 status-signal operates through downstream M6 controllability and M3 social engagement, not as an independent variable.

The diseases of the status syndrome are those of rich societies that have dealt with absolute deprivation: heart disease, diabetes, mental illness.

content: The Whitehall I occupational-grade mortality gradient: the Administrators (top grade) have about half the average civil-service mortality at age 40-64, while the office support grades (bottom) have about twice the average — a four-fold top-vs-bottom mortality difference. This exceeds the national 1.8-fold difference between top and bottom social classes (measured by grouping occupations), showing that the gradient is STEEPER within the relatively homogeneous civil service than in the country as a whole. Figures taken from Marmot & Shipley (1996); summarised at source lines 1752-1760 (figure-caption text).
location: Chapter 2 'Men and Women Behaving Badly?' Figure 2.1 and surrounding text, pp. 39-40, citing Marmot and Shipley (1996)
author_quote: Both the gradient and the four-fold difference between top and bottom are dramatic. National figures at the time showed a 1.8-fold difference between top and bottom social classes, formed by grouping occupations together. What is this civil-service organisation that there should be a steeper gradient in Whitehall than in the country as a whole?
caveats: Marmot and Shipley (1996) is the primary citation. source_type='primary' because Marmot is the principal investigator. evidence_quality='longitudinal' (25-year civil-servant cohort with near-complete mortality follow-up). The four-fold within-civil-service gradient is the headline Whitehall finding: stratification within a white-collar population produces a bigger mortality gradient than stratification across the country as a whole. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). The numerical content from the figure caption (Administrators half the average, office support twice, four-fold ratio) is preserved in content as paraphrase with explicit source-line attribution. scope: The empirical core of M5: mortality follows occupational grade step-wise, even in a population where everyone has adequate housing, food, medical care, and job security. This is why M5 is a signaling mechanism rather than a proxy for resources — the resources are controlled for and the gradient remains.

content: Whitehall II included women as well as men and was designed to investigate the psychosocial mechanisms underlying the gradient found in Whitehall I. The simple answer from Whitehall II is that where you come from (family background, parents' education, father's social class) does matter for heart disease risk, but it is not the reason for the health gradient: even taking into account differences in family background, your position in the job hierarchy is closely linked with your risk of heart disease.
location: Chapter 2 'Men and Women Behaving Badly?' p. 58, citing Whitehall II
author_quote: The simple answer from the second Whitehall study, Whitehall II, is: yes, but. Where you come from does matter for your health, but it is not the reason for the health gradient. Family background, measured as parents' education and father's social class, are related to risk of heart disease. In the above example, Bob, from humble origins, is at higher risk of heart disease than Ted, from a more privileged background, despite the fact that they have the same occupational prestige. Background matters. There is then a different question: given that people in lower-status jobs are likely to come from more humble origins than those in high-status jobs, is this the main reason why low-status people have higher risk of heart disease? Whitehall II shows that it is not. Even taking into account differences in family background, your position in the job hierarchy is closely linked with your risk of heart disease.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II result. source_type='primary' (Marmot is principal investigator). evidence_quality='longitudinal'. Rules out the 'early-life disadvantage explains everything' alternative hypothesis: current occupational grade predicts heart disease risk independently of where you started. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). Original author_quote spliced the 'yes, but' opening (source lines 2480-2486) with the 'Even taking into account' conclusion (source lines 2494-2496), eliding the Bob/Ted example and the methodological question bridge (lines 2487-2493). author_quote REPLACED with the full contiguous source passage at Marmot pp. ~57-58 (lines 2480-2496), one continuous paragraph. Page-header artifact '58 / STATUS SYNDROME' at lines 2483-2484 excised (allowed per policy); citation marker '*' on line 2482 removed; OCR repair: 'ongins' at source line 2487 is an OCR artifact for 'origins' and has been repaired in author_quote (allowed per policy with this caveat).
scope: Strengthens the M5-as-current-signal claim: the status syndrome is not a residual effect of early-life deprivation; current hierarchy position produces its own physiological signal even controlling for background. This is critical for treating M5 as a mechanism with present-environment resolution conditions rather than a developmental-calibration phenomenon.

content: A large body of evidence supports the demand/control model: people whose jobs are characterised by high demands and low control have a higher risk of developing coronary heart disease than others in jobs with more control. The Whitehall II study showed stronger support for the effects of low control on heart disease than for the adverse effects of high demand alone. Other studies in the US and Sweden show that a combination of high demand and low control is harmful to health. A strong relation was also found between low control at work and depressive symptoms.
location: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 127-128, citing Karasek demand/control model and Whitehall II heart-disease outcomes
author_quote: A large body of evidence now exists that supports the demand/control model: people whose jobs are characterised by high demands and low control have a higher risk of developing coronary heart disease than others in jobs with more control. Our own Whitehall II study in the British civil service showed stronger support for the effects of low control on heart disease than for the adverse effects of high demand. Other studies in the US and Sweden, however, do show that a combination of high demand and low control is harmful to health. We also found a strong relation between low control at work and depressive symptoms.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II finding. source_type='primary'. evidence_quality='longitudinal'. Maps directly to M6 Controllability/Agency (Maier & Seligman's core mechanism): low decision latitude is a specific signal that predicts disease. This is the bridge from M5 (status) to M6 (agency) at the empirical level. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). Original author_quote had an ellipsis eliding the 'Other studies in the US and Sweden' sentence (source lines 5230-5232) and the intervening citation markers. author_quote REPLACED with the full contiguous source passage at Marmot pp. ~127-128 (lines 5221-5233). Page-header artifact '127 / WHO'S IN CHARGE?' at lines 5223-5224 excised (allowed per policy); citation markers 40, 41, 42, 43 removed; OCR repair: 'Bnitish' at source line 5228 is an OCR artifact for 'British' and has been repaired in author_quote (allowed per policy with this caveat); line-break hyphenation joined.
scope: Critical M5→M6 cross-mechanism grounding. The status gradient operates partly through the fact that lower-grade jobs structurally offer lower decision latitude, which is the M6 operating condition Karasek/Maier/Seligman identify as a cascade-break point. Supports Cor's treatment of Whitehall findings as co-grounding M5 AND M6.

content: People at the same level in the occupational hierarchy with differing amounts of control had markedly different rates of disease — low control consistently led to more disease. In Whitehall II, within-grade variation in control predicted heart disease: it was not simply grade per se doing the work, but the low control that tended to accompany lower grades.
location: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' p. 128, Whitehall II analysis
author_quote: People at the same level in the occupational hierarchy with differing amounts of control had markedly different rates of disease — low control consistently led to more disease.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II finding. The within-grade analysis is the sharpest test of the control-as-active-ingredient hypothesis: if low control predicts disease even when grade is held constant, then control is not just a correlate of grade but a distinct causal factor. source_type='primary', evidence_quality='longitudinal'.
scope: The strongest single statistical argument that M6 (Controllability/Agency) is architecturally distinct from M5 (Status Monitoring), not just its correlate: within-grade variation in control predicts disease. Cor treats both mechanisms as separate Tier 1 systems; this finding justifies that architectural separation empirically.

content: Marmot addresses the subjective-vs-objective control measurement problem in Whitehall II by asking both managers (to rate jobs for degree of control) and civil servants (to self-report perceived control). The correlation between the two measures was surprisingly low — they captured different things about the job — yet both independently predicted heart disease. The methodological framing ('In the Whitehall II study, we wrestled with this problem in relation to low control at work') is at source lines 5271-5273, pp. ~128, and leads through a colour anecdote to the finding at 5291-5297.
location: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 128-129, Whitehall II methodology
author_quote: It turns out the answer is both. We asked managers to rate jobs for their degree of control, and we asked civil servants themselves to tell us how much control they had. The correlation between them was surprisingly low. It seemed that subjective perception and external ratings of control were capturing something different about the job. Yet these two measures, the one more or less independent of the other, both predicted heart disease.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II methodological finding. source_type='primary', evidence_quality='longitudinal'. The subjective/objective measure independence-with-convergent-prediction pattern is important: both the felt experience and the structural features of low-control work predict the health outcome, so M6 resolution conditions cannot be satisfied by pure cognitive reframing or pure structural change alone. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). Original author_quote spliced the methodological-framing opening (source lines 5271-5273) with the managers-vs-self-reports finding (source lines 5291-5297) across a ~18-line parking-bicycle colour anecdote. author_quote narrowed to the finding fragment (source lines 5291-5297, contiguous), which is the load-bearing claim. Opening framing preserved in content as paraphrase with source line reference. Citation marker '**' on line 5297 removed; smart quotes normalized.
scope: Has direct implications for Cor's A2 clinical application and A3 environment design: restoring M6 requires BOTH giving people actual decision latitude AND supporting their subjective sense of control. Either one alone is insufficient per the Whitehall II findings.

content: In Whitehall II, lower control appeared in lower grades whether we consider people's self-reports or managers' 'objective' assessment of how much control each job entails. Statistically, low control was an important contributor to the higher rate of heart disease in the lower grades. The nature of the hierarchy is less control the lower you go.
location: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' p. 129, Whitehall II structural finding
author_quote: In Whitehall II, we found lower control in lower grades whether we consider people's self-reports or managers' 'objective' assessment of how much control each job entails. In Whitehall II, this gradient in control over work appears to have strong implications for the gradient in heart disease and mental illness. Statistically, low control was an important contributor to the higher rate of heart disease in the lower grades.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II finding quantifying how much of the grade-health relationship is explained by control. source_type='primary', evidence_quality='longitudinal'. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B, trivial — no narrowing needed). Citation marker on line 5338 removed; smart quotes normalized.
scope: Operationalizes the M5→M6 cascade step: lower position in the status hierarchy → lower decision latitude → higher heart disease risk. The 'important contributor' language indicates partial but substantial explanation of the total gradient.

content: In Whitehall II, the metabolic syndrome increased in frequency as the civil-service hierarchy was descended: the lower the employment grade, the lower the HDL cholesterol, the higher the plasma triglyceride, the higher the fasting levels of glucose and insulin. The lower the grade, the higher the waist:hip ratio. This central adiposity may be the result of a complex series of reactions involving cortisol metabolism; central obesity occurs in Cushing's Syndrome, a disorder characterised by over-secretion of cortisol.
location: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 121-122, citing Whitehall II metabolic markers
author_quote: in our Whitehall II study of British civil servants we also found: the lower the rank, the lower the HDL cholesterol. All things considered, we thought better of trying to adopt Sapolsky's darting technique for our civil servants. We did, however, find that the metabolic syndrome increased in frequency as the hierarchy was descended: the lower the employment grade, the lower the HDL cholesterol, the higher the plasma triglyceride, the higher the fasting levels of glucose and insulin. The lower the grade, the higher the waist:hip ratio. It is important to make the distinction between this central pattern of obesity and simple overweight, where the excess body fat is more widely distributed.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II metabolic data. source_type='primary', evidence_quality='longitudinal'. The waist:hip ratio / metabolic-syndrome gradient is one of the cleanest demonstrations of M5 → downstream metabolic consequences via chronic cortisol elevation. Specifically maps onto the DA3 cascade pathway (M5 → M8 chronic low-grade inflammation → M13 altered metabolism) at a measurable biomarker level. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): retroactive caveat per new quote-normalization policy (effective 2026-04-05). Normalization applied to author_quote vs source: OCR spacing repair and removal of inline citation numerals. All applied normalizations are within the policy's allowed list (line-break hyphenation joining, inline citation numeral removal, page-header / running-header excision, smart-quote -> straight-quote glyph normalization). Contiguous-verbatim anchoring of the quote otherwise confirmed by codex-research audit; no splices, no rewording, no semantic substitutions, no tense/pronoun adjustments.
scope: Biomarker-level grounding for the M5 cascade. Whitehall II provides the human replication of Sapolsky's baboon findings — the same pattern (lower rank, higher morning cortisol, worse metabolic markers) in a non-darting human civil-servant population. Parallel data across species supports Cor's treatment of M5 as an evolutionarily conserved signaling system.

content: Sapolsky's studies of wild baboons in the Serengeti show that all the biological stress markers follow the social hierarchy: the lower the rank of the baboon, the higher the level of cortisol early in the morning, and the lower the HDL cholesterol. Under conditions of hierarchical instability, stress hormones rise particularly in higher-ranking males being challenged by someone below them. The same HDL pattern appears in the Whitehall II British civil servants. Animal studies from lab and field give us biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease.
location: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 120-121, citing Sapolsky and parallel Whitehall II findings
author_quote: Sapolsky finds, in general, that all the biological stress markers follow the social hierarchy. He has studied, in particular, the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis that is responsible for regulating glucocorticoids. For example, the lower the rank of the baboon, the higher is the level of cortisol early in the morning. You may wonder how Sapolsky determines the cortisol level of a baboon early in the morning. Anaesthetic darts. He creeps up on the target baboon and darts it. He has a few minutes before the blood cortisol level changes. He quickly takes a blood sample and, voila, he has the basal cortisol level. He also finds that the lower the baboon's rank, the lower the HDL cholesterol level — a low level being associated with an increased risk of heart disease. The higher the morning cortisol, the lower is the HDL cholesterol. Interestingly, in our Whitehall II study of British civil servants we also found: the lower the rank, the lower the HDL cholesterol.
caveats: Marmot reports Sapolsky's primate findings alongside his own Whitehall II results, establishing cross-species convergence on the same pattern. source_type='propagation' (Sapolsky's data cited by Marmot). evidence_quality='cross_species' using the expanded v2 enum — this is exactly the kind of finding that justifies the cross_species tag. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). Original author_quote had an ellipsis eliding the anaesthetic-darts methodology passage (source lines 4993-4998) between the cortisol claim and the HDL claim. author_quote REPLACED with the full contiguous source passage at Marmot pp. ~120-121 (lines 4989-5004), one continuous passage. The methodology detail is retained because it is part of the same argument; line-break hyphenation joined ('hy-/pothalamic'); smart quotes normalized; no page-header excision needed in this range.
scope: Direct cross-species grounding for M5 as a phylogenetically deep mechanism: the same rank-cortisol-HDL pattern appears in wild baboons and British civil servants. Supports Cor's treatment of M5 as an evolved mechanism (primate ancestry ~50-100Myr) rather than a culture-specific human phenomenon.

content: Animal studies, from lab and field, give us biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease. In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes — but the physiological stress response is similar in many different species. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that puts out cortisol operates similarly across mammals, and chronic activation of this system has systemic health consequences regardless of species.
location: Chapter 4 'Stress in the Jungle? Stress in the Office?' pp. 115-116
author_quote: In case it needs re-emphasis, we are not monkeys or even apes. We should not look to them, necessarily, to understand how people behave in the workplace, in the benefits office, on the local council, or the church committee. What these animal studies, from lab and field, give us are biologically plausible ways that social experience can be translated, via biological stress pathways, into disease.
caveats: Marmot's methodological framing of why animal hierarchy studies are relevant to human social gradients. source_type='propagation' (framework claim).
scope: Supports the use of Sapolsky's primate data and Bowman Gray primate hierarchy studies as cross-species evidence for the M5 mechanism while maintaining appropriate distance from naive 'humans are baboons' extrapolation.

content: People whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between efforts put in and rewards received had higher risk of disease, independently of low control at work. Two distinct psychosocial features — low control and effort/reward imbalance — both contribute to the work-health gradient in Whitehall II.
location: Chapter 7 'Health and Work' p. 190-191, Whitehall II effort/reward analysis, citing Siegrist model
author_quote: We used measures of effort/reward imbalance in the workplace in our studies in Poland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Hungary. This study confirmed the importance for poor health of low control at work and generally. In addition, people whose work was characterised by a high degree of imbalance between effort and reward had a 60 per cent greater chance of being in poor health than those with an appropriate balance.
caveats: Primary Whitehall II finding on Siegrist's effort/reward imbalance model. source_type='primary'. evidence_quality='longitudinal'. The effort/reward imbalance construct adds a reciprocity dimension (M11 Cooperation / Alliance) to the status+control account, consistent with Cor's architecture where social reciprocity is a distinct evolved expectation. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous, extension). Original author_quote was catastrophically truncated — it ended mid-sentence at 'imbalance between' with no closing clause, and had a prior ellipsis that reordered fragments. author_quote REPLACED with the full contiguous source passage at Marmot pp. ~205-206 (lines 8798-8804), which gives the complete Poland/Czech Republic/Lithuania/Hungary effort-reward-imbalance study + the 60% poor-health finding. Citation marker '~*' removed; line-break hyphenation joined ('work-/place' and similar).
scope: Adds M11 (Cooperation/Alliance) to the M5 cascade: the status syndrome operates not only through hierarchy position and decision latitude but also through violated reciprocity norms. Relevant to Cor's A6 policy application (workplace design, effort-reward calibration).

content: The chronic-stress-pathway translation from social experience to disease in humans. Marmot's synthesis draws on Sapolsky's fight-or-flight account (source lines 4763-4793, pp. ~115-116) — the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axes, with immune function inhibited as 'another feature of the stress response' (line 4783) — and adds the critical observation that these biological stress pathways can be triggered by purely psychological stimuli, whether or not the person consciously experiences fear. Chronic activation of these pathways in the low-status, low-control condition translates perceived social experience into elevated cortisol, insulin resistance, central adiposity, dyslipidemia, immune suppression, and cardiovascular disease.
location: Chapter 4 pp. 116-118, synthesizing the HPA/cortisol stress-disease pathway
author_quote: There is little doubt, however, that purely psychological stimuli can arouse the physiological stress response, whether or not we experience an emotion such as fear.
caveats: Marmot synthesizing the HPA-axis stress-to-disease pathway in his own voice. source_type='propagation' (framework synthesis). | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). Original author_quote stitched THREE non-adjacent fragments: (1) 'As another feature of the stress response, immune function is inhibited' at source lines 4783-4784, (2) 'the body system that puts out cortisol — the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis' at source line 4793, (3) 'arouse the physiological stress response, whether or not we experience' at source lines 4843-4844. The three fragments span ~60 lines across multiple paragraphs. author_quote narrowed to Fragment 3 (source lines 4842-4844, contiguous), which is the most load-bearing claim for the DA1/DC1 stress-response-as-unconscious-signal extraction. Fragments 1 and 2 preserved in content as paraphrase with source line references.
scope: Connects M5 (signal) to M8 (immune regulation) and downstream DC1 (allostatic load) via chronic HPA activation. This is the main mechanistic chain by which the status-gradient signal produces the observed morbidity/mortality pattern.

content: Much of the evidence for the importance of control in health comes from the observation that where people are unable to direct the circumstances of their own lives, health suffers. The social gradient in health affects everyone — it is not simply a question of 'them and us'. Understanding the social gradient requires focusing not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
location: Introduction, p. 4, and Chapter 5 opening framing
author_quote: The discovery of how important control and participation are for health leads in a different direction: to the circumstances in which we live and work. In other words, this is health research that leads us to focus, not on access to the latest medical technology, but on the way we think about the sort of lives we want for ourselves, and the sort of society in which we want to lead them.
caveats: Marmot's policy framing of the Whitehall findings. source_type='propagation' (framework application).
scope: Supports Cor's A6 Policy application: the Whitehall gradient implies that population health cannot be improved primarily via medical technology; it requires changes to the environment-level resolution conditions for M5 (status), M6 (control), and M11 (reciprocity). Marmot's policy framing anticipates the A6 argument Cor builds.

content: Health-related social mobility is not the cause of the social gradient in health. People who rise up the social scale are healthier than those in the social class they left behind, but they are less healthy than others in their class of destination. Those who are downwardly mobile are more unhealthy than those who stayed in a high social class but not as unhealthy as those who were always in a lower class. Health-related social mobility is blurring the social gradient in health, not increasing it. This effect works precisely because social position is related to health.
location: Chapter 2 'Men and Women Behaving Badly?' pp. 59-60, citing Bartley and Blane
author_quote: It is true that people who rise up the social scale are healthier than those in the social class they left behind. But these upwardly-mobile people are less healthy than others in their class of destination. Conversely, those who are downwardly mobile are, indeed, more unhealthy than those who stayed in a high social class, but not as unhealthy as those who were always in a lower class. It works the same way as misclassification. The healthier top-rank people are having the average health of their group reduced by recruitment to their ranks of some people who were less healthy. The less healthy low-rank people are having the average health of their group improved by recruitment to their ranks of some who are healthier than they were. This health-related social mobility is blurring the social gradient in health, not increasing it. This effect works precisely because social position is related to health.
caveats: Marmot citing Bartley and Blane's medical-sociology analysis. The directionality argument rules out the 'healthy people rise to the top' alternative hypothesis. source_type='primary' because Marmot treats this as a key finding from Whitehall longitudinal analyses; the Bartley/Blane citation is the methodological frame. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous). Original author_quote spliced the 'rise up / downwardly mobile' comparison (source lines 2581-2586) with the 'blurring the gradient' conclusion (source lines 2591-2594), eliding the misclassification-analogy bridge (lines 2586-2590). author_quote REPLACED with the full contiguous source passage at Marmot pp. ~60-61 (lines 2581-2594), one continuous paragraph including the misclassification analogy that makes the argument intelligible. Smart quotes normalized; line-break hyphenation joined; no page-header excision needed.
scope: Establishes the direction of causality: status → health, not health → status. Critical for treating M5 as a mechanism that produces physiological consequences, rather than a correlate of underlying health. Strengthens the claim that the status signal itself is doing the work.

content: The social gradient in health is as big as, if not bigger than, it is in Britain in North America and Australia, despite those countries believing themselves to be egalitarian. Even in Japan, whose overall health record is the envy of the world, the status syndrome is found. The findings of a health gradient are remarkably general across developed countries with different health systems, cultures, and political arrangements.
author_quote: Americans and Australians believed their countries were egalitarian so there would be no social-class difference there. They were wrong. In North America and Australia the differences are as big as, if not bigger, than they are in Britain. Scandinavians said they had no class differences in health, until they looked and found that this phenomenon went deeper and wider than class-ridden Britain. Many continental European countries were slower at picking up on this story, because they did not have the data systems in place. When they looked, they too found a clear social gradient in health. When the doors opened on the former communist countries of Europe, we found big and growing social differences in health within those countries as well as a growing gap in health between them and the flourishing countries of Western Europe. Even in Japan, whose health record is the envy of the world, we find evidence of the status syndrome.
caveats: Cross-cultural / cross-country generalization of the Whitehall social-gradient finding. source_type='propagation' (synthesis across multiple national datasets). evidence_quality='replicated' — the status gradient appears across dramatically different political-cultural arrangements (UK, North America, Australia, Scandinavia, continental Europe, former Eastern Bloc, Japan), which is cross-POPULATION replication (not cross-species biological). The breadth of the replication is the strongest evidence for an underlying mechanism rather than a cultural artifact. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH + EVIDENCE_QUALITY_DRIFT MEDIUM combined fix. (1) PARAPHRASE_LEAK: original author_quote started with 'The findings of a health gradient are, however, remarkably general...' (source lines 307-308) and then jumped to 'Americans and Australians believed...' (source line 320), eliding the British civil service context at lines 309-319. author_quote narrowed to the cross-country comparison fragment (source lines 320-337, contiguous) at Marmot pp. ~4-5, which is the load-bearing claim for the cross-population gradient replication. The 'remarkably general' thesis statement is preserved in content. Page-header artifact '4 / STATUS SYNDROME' at lines 330-332 excised (allowed per policy); line-break hyphenation joined; citation marker '*' removed. (2) EVIDENCE_QUALITY_DRIFT: changed cross_species -> replicated. The Whitehall status-gradient finding replicated across UK, North America, Australia, Scandinavia, continental Europe, former Eastern Bloc, and Japan is CROSS-POPULATION / CROSS-COUNTRY replication, not cross-species biological replication. This was the issue originally self-flagged in Wave 2 report #348. | Wave 2-D (corherence #386, 2026-04-05): leading caveat prose rewritten to reflect current machine state (evidence_quality='replicated', no longer 'cross_species'). Dated audit trail preserved verbatim.
scope: Cross-population replication strengthens the case that M5 is an evolved architectural feature rather than a British-civil-service peculiarity or a Western-capitalist artifact. The gradient appears in every developed country examined — different cultures, different health systems, different political-economic arrangements, same gradient.

content: Marmot explicitly generalises the workplace-control finding to non-workplace spheres of life: low control in domestic, economic, and other spheres is also a causal exposure for disease, not an ancillary correlate of workplace conditions. The Whitehall II extension (asking civil servants about perceived control at home and in life in general) is what he uses to ground this generalisation empirically.
author_quote: Low control at work is an important contributor to disease, but there are ways of depriving people of control other than subjecting them to difficult conditions at work. The Rick and Maria story makes plain that low control over life circumstances is not confined to work. Low control in these other spheres, too, may be important for health.
caveats: Marmot's generalization from workplace control to broader autonomy and participation. The quoted author_quote is short because the surrounding text is policy argumentation rather than a compact thesis statement; the verbatim portion captures Marmot's pivot from workplace-specific to general-population claims. source_type='primary' because Marmot is stating his own program's conclusion. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): OVERSTATEMENT fix. Original author_quote was truncated mid-sentence at 'but there' (16 words, ending without a period) while content claimed a broader generalisation including civil-servant gradient mechanics and autonomy/participation causal framing. Option B: author_quote EXTENDED to the contiguous verbatim passage at Marmot pp. ~132, source file lines 5441-5445 (dehyphenated 'refer-/ence' and similar line-break hyphens; no other normalisation). Content NARROWED to exactly what this verbatim passage supports — the workplace-to-domestic-to-life-in-general generalisation plus the Whitehall II grounding. The earlier broader reading (stratified-population extrapolation + explicit autonomy/participation labelling) was reading beyond the quoted verbatim text and has been removed from content. Dehyphenation applied per 2026-04-05 quote-normalization policy.
scope: Generalizes the M5/M6 cascade beyond the workplace to any hierarchical environment. Critical for Cor's A3 Environment Design application: any designed environment that imposes status gradients with low decision latitude will produce M5/M6 degradation regardless of whether it's a civil service, corporation, school, or housing development.

content: Marmot integrates Siegrist's effort/reward model into his control/participation hypothesis by treating 'reward' (esteem, recognition, appropriate return for effort) as a mode of full social participation. Lack of appropriate reward therefore maps onto the same autonomy/participation pathway that drives the health gradient; it is not a third distinct factor but an extension of the participation axis through the workplace reciprocity channel.
location: Chapter 5 'Who's in Charge?' pp. 131-132 synthesizing Karasek + Siegrist

content: Humans have evolved three primary brain systems that guide mating and reproduction: the sex drive; romantic love; and the feelings of deep attachment. These three basic neural systems interact with one another (and many other brain systems) in myriad flexible combinations to provide the range of motivations, emotions and behaviors necessary to orchestrate our complex human reproductive strategy. However, these three brain systems are not always well connected. So it is biologically possible to express deep feelings of attachment for a primary partner while one feels intense romantic love for another individual, while one feels the sex drive for even more extra partners.

However, these three brain systems are not always well connected. So it is biologically possible to express deep feelings of attachment for a primary partner while one feels intense romantic love for another individual, while one feels the sex drive for even more extra partners.

content: The sex drive motivates us to seek a range of mating partners. Romantic love drives us to focus our mating energy on a single individual at a time. And feelings of deep attachment enable us to remain with this special other at least long enough to rear a single child through infancy together. Each of these basic drives produces different behaviors, feelings, hopes, and dreams. And each is associated primarily with different neurochemical systems. Lust is associated primarily with the hormone testosterone, in both men and women. Romantic love is linked with the natural stimulant, dopamine, and perhaps also with norepinephrine and low activity of serotonin. While feelings of deep attachment are produced principally by the neuropeptides, oxytocin and vasopressin.

This is the architectural basis for why Cor treats M14 as one mechanism with three components rather than as three separate mechanisms — they are designed to work together and co-fail together.

content: Fisher and colleagues put seventeen new lovers into the fMRI scanner — ten women and seven men who had been madly and happily in love for an average of 7.4 months. The scans showed blobs of activity in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a tiny factory near the base of the brain that makes dopamine and sends this natural stimulant to many brain regions. This factory is part of the brain's reward system, the brain network that generates wanting, seeking, craving, energy, focus, and motivation. The VTA was particularly important. Men showed just as much activity in the VTA and other neural pathways for romantic passion as women did.
location: Chapter 2 'Why Him? Why Her?' Romantic Attraction fMRI study, pp. 33-34, with Lucy Brown, Art Aron, and colleagues
author_quote: Then, with neuroscientist Lucy Brown, psychologist Art Aron, and others, I put seventeen new lovers into the brain scanner: ten women and seven men who had been madly and happily in love for an average of 7.4 months. I will never forget the moment I first saw the results. I was standing in a darkened lab at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine. I felt like jumping in the sky. Before my eyes were scans showing blobs of activity in the ventral tegmental area, or VTA, a tiny factory near the base of the brain that makes dopamine and sends this natural stimulant to many brain regions. We found activity in many other brain regions, but the VTA was particularly important. This factory is part of the brain's reward system, the brain network that generates wanting, seeking, craving, energy, focus, and motivation.

Romantic love activates the same VTA-dopamine reward system that drives general goal pursuit — confirming Cor's treatment of M14 as a distinct mechanism that interacts with M2's infrastructure rather than being absorbed into M2.

content: When Fisher's colleagues redid the brain scanning experiment in China, their Chinese participants showed just as much activity in the VTA and other dopamine pathways — the neurochemical pathways for wanting. Almost everyone on earth feels this passion. Because the VTA lies near primitive brain regions associated with thirst and hunger, romantic love is a basic human drive. Romantic love is a survival mechanism as crucial as the craving for water.

content: With a reanalysis of the Fisher/Brown/Aron fMRI data, activity was found in the nucleus accumbens — a brain region that is part of the reward system, is fueled by dopamine, and is associated with all of the addictions — including the cravings for heroin, cocaine, nicotine, alcohol, amphetamines, gambling, sex, and food. Romantic love is, in this architectural sense, a natural addiction, running through the same reward pathways that pathological addictions hijack.

content: Cross-species evidence: when a female prairie vole begins to express attraction to a male vole, she experiences a 50% increase of dopamine activity in parts of the reward system. An increase of dopamine in the brain is also associated with mate attraction in female sheep. This neural mechanism for attraction must have evolved in many species of birds and mammals — to enable individuals to prefer and focus on specific mating partners, thereby conserving valuable courtship time and energy.

Hence, this neural mechanism for attraction must have evolved in many species of birds and mammals—to enable individuals to prefer and focus on specific mating partners, thereby conserving valuable courtship time and energy.
