content: The duration of intense romantic love varies but is bounded. Tennov concluded that 'the most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' A study of serotonin activity in blood suggests 12 to 18 months. In the Match.com survey of over 5,000 men and women, 29% reported the passion lasting for two to five years; 8% for six to ten years; and 18% for over ten years. Either the nerve pathways for dopamine and related neurochemicals become habituated to these natural stimulants, or the production and distribution of dopamine decline.
author_quote: Tennov measured the duration of romantic love from the moment infatuation hit to when a 'feeling of neutrality' for one's love object began. She concluded, 'The most frequent interval, as well as the average, is between approximately 18 months and three years.' But data vary. A study that indicates serotonin activity in the blood suggests that this intoxication lasts twelve to eighteen months. And in our 2012 national Match.com survey of singles, 29% of over 5,000 men and women of every age group, background, and sexual persuasion reported that this passion lasted for two to five years; 8% remained intensely in love for six to ten years, and 18% reported that they remained madly in love for over ten years.
caveats: Fisher reports Tennov's observational data and her own Match.com convenience-sample data. source_type='propagation' (synthesis of multiple datasets). evidence_quality='thin' because the Tennov survey is based on self-report retrospective recall with no control for response bias and the Match.com samples are internet-survey convenience populations rather than representative samples. The 18-month-to-3-year bound is the classic Fisher number, even though the underlying data are thin.

content: In Acevedo et al.'s fMRI brain scanning experiment, seventeen long-married women and men were scanned while viewing photos of their spouse. Average length of marriage was twenty-one years; most had grown children; all said they were still in love with their spouse. The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among newly-in-love younger men and women. One exception: newly-in-love participants showed activity in a brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.

The results were astonishing: the VTA and other basic brain regions associated with early-stage intense romantic love were just as active among these long-term lovers as among our newly-in-love younger men and women. With one exception: Our newly-in-love participants showed activity in a specific brain region associated with anxiety, whereas in our long-term lovers this angst was replaced by new activity in brain regions linked with calm and pain suppression.

This is the 'matched state' for M14 in Cor's framework: sustained VTA activation + calm attachment + pair bond stability. The anxiety-replaced-by-calm pattern is a key architectural signature of the romantic-love → attachment transition done well.

content: When prairie voles first engage in sex, copulation triggers activity in oxytocin receptors (in the nucleus accumbens) among females and vasopressin receptors (in the ventral pallidum) among males. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions — producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation — driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. Specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.

author_quote: Please recall the prairie vole. These individuals form lifelong pair-bonds soon after puberty and raise several litters as a team. This stimulates dopamine release in several brain regions—producing feelings of wanting, seeking, focus, energy, pleasure, and motivation—driving these furry little creatures to prefer a particular mate, initiate a pair-bond, and express enduring attachment behaviors. But specific variations in a particular gene in the vasopressin system contribute to variability in the strength of a male prairie vole's pair-bond, including the degree to which a male expresses sexual fidelity to his partner.

Prairie voles show the full three-system interaction (dopamine attraction + vasopressin/oxytocin attachment + mate preference) with genetic variation producing the sexual fidelity gradient. This is critical because it means M14's sex-differentiated architecture is not a human-specific cultural pattern but a mammalian pair-bonding substrate.

content: A Swedish study of 552 men, all either married or living with a partner for at least five years, investigated whether a vasopressin-receptor gene affects pair-bonding behavior. Men who inherited this gene scored significantly lower on the Partner Bonding Scale. Scores were dose-dependent: men carrying two copies of this gene showed the lowest scores; those carrying one copy expressed more feelings of attachment; and men who had no copies of this gene were the most attached to their partner. Men carrying this vasopressin gene had also experienced more marital crises during the previous year, including threats of divorce. Spouses of men with one or two copies of this gene scored significantly lower on questionnaires measuring marital satisfaction.
location: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' pp. 93-94, Walum et al. 2008 AVPR1A finding

Moreover, scores were dose-dependent. Men carrying two copies of this gene showed the lowest scores on the Partner Bonding Scale; those carrying one copy expressed more feelings of attachment; and men who had no copies of this gene were the most attached to their partner. Men carrying this vasopressin gene had also experienced more marital crises during the previous year, including threats of divorce. Once again, these results were dose-dependent. Last, the spouses of men with one or two copies of this gene scored significantly lower on questionnaires measuring marital satisfaction.

Critical for Cor's claim that M14 is a conserved mammalian architecture with measurable genetic variation in humans.

content: Larry Young and colleagues modified a harmless virus to carry the genetic code for vasopressin receptors and injected the virus into males of meadow voles — creatures that do not normally form pair-bonds. These animals then began to make solid attachments to their current sexual partners. This direct genetic manipulation from non-monogamous to monogamous behavior at the single-gene level is one of the strongest demonstrations that the vasopressin system is causally involved in mammalian pair-bonding.

And most important to this book: men with related genes for vasopressin transmission also tend to make more stable partnerships.

content: In the 'sweaty T-shirt' experiment, women sniffed the T-shirts of anonymous men and selected the T-shirts of those they felt were the sexiest. They selected the T-shirts of men with genes that were different from their own in a specific region of the immune system — the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). These women were unconsciously attracted to men with different MHC genes because similarity between partners in this part of the immune system can lead to complications of fertility and pregnancy. In a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. The more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.
location: Chapter 4 'Why Adultery?' The Sweaty T-Shirt Experiment, pp. 94-95, citing Wedekind et al. 1995 and follow-up
author_quote: In the now classic 'sweaty T-shirt' experiment, women sniffed the T-shirts of several anonymous men and selected the T-shirts of those they felt were the sexiest. Interestingly, they selected the T-shirts of men with genes that were different from their own in a specific region of the immune system, the major histocompatibility complex. Perhaps these women were unconsciously attracted to men with different genes because similarity between partners in this part of the immune system can lead to complications of fertility and pregnancy. Tellingly, in a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. And the more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.

The MHC-adultery correlation adds a functional dimension: women in mismatch conditions (similar-MHC pairing) show behavioral compensation via extra-pair mating, which Fisher interprets as an evolved response to fitness-suboptimal pairings.

content: Fisher's cross-cultural / cross-species framing of human reproductive architecture. The pair-bonding species claim is grounded in two distinct empirical observations from different parts of the book: (a) the cross-cultural pattern — 85% of cultures permit polygyny but most men have only one wife at a time (Fisher prologue, source lines 100-106); and (b) the cross-species rarity — only 3% of mammals form pair-bonds to rear their young, while ~90% of avian species do (Fisher Chapter 3 on adultery in other species, source line 1710). The two findings jointly establish pair-bonding as part of human architecture while showing it is a robust but distinctive mammalian pattern.
location: Prologue and Chapter 3 'Is Monogamy Natural?' pp. 1 and 39-40
author_quote: We are a pair-bonding species. Some 85% of cultures permit a man to have several wives, but few men actually build a harem. A man has to have a lot of goats, cows, land, money, or other impressive resources to get several women to share his wedding bed. Even then, having more than one wife can be a toothache. Co-wives fight; sometimes they even poison one another's children. We are built to rear our babies as a team of two—with a lot of helpers near the nest.
caveats: Standard Fisher cross-cultural statistics (85% polygynous-permitting / de facto monogamous practice) and the 3% of mammals pair-bonding figure. source_type='propagation' (synthesis of ethnographic and mammalogy data). author_quote is fragmentary because the 85% and 3% figures appear in different paragraphs of the book; the compact quote captures the key phrases. evidence_quality='cross_species'. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option B narrow-to-contiguous). Original author_quote catastrophically spliced Fragment 1 at source line 100 ('We are a pair-bonding species. Some 85% of cultures permit a man to') — which was ALSO truncated mid-sentence — with Fragment 2 at source line 1710 ('Only 3% of mammals form a pair-bond to rear their young'), across a ~1,610-line gap spanning multiple chapters. The two fragments are from completely different sections of the book (prologue vs Chapter 3). author_quote narrowed to Fragment 1 completed — full contiguous source passage at Fisher prologue (lines 100-106). The 3%-of-mammals cross-species fact is preserved in content as paraphrase with explicit source line reference.
scope: Grounds M14's pair-bonding component as a species-typical human trait against the backdrop of mammalian mating-system variation. Humans are one of only ~3% of mammals that pair-bond — this is what makes M14 architecturally distinctive and why Cor treats pair-bonding as a load-bearing mechanism rather than a cultural option.

content: Love is distinguished by men and women around the world. The Taita of Kenya say that love comes in two forms: an irresistible longing, a 'kind of sickness'; and a deep, enduring affection for another. Brazilians say, 'Love is born in a glance and matures in a smile.' For the Koreans, sarang is a word close to the Western concept of romantic love, while chong is more like feelings of long-term attachment. Nisa, the !Kung woman of the Kalahari Desert, explained the arc of love: 'When two people are first together, their hearts are on fire and their passion is very great. After a while, the fire cools and that's how it stays. They continue to love each other, but it's in a different way — warm and dependable.'
author_quote: The Taita of Kenya say that love comes in two forms: an irresistible longing, a 'kind of sickness'; and a deep, enduring affection for another. Brazilians say, 'Love is born in a glance and matures in a smile.' For the Koreans, sarang is a word close to the Western concept of romantic love, while chong is more like feelings of long-term attachment.

content: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with Bowlby and Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver. Extensive research has shown that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course — serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring. The adult pair-bond attachment system is an extension of, not a replacement for, the infant-caregiver attachment system.
author_quote: The contemporary psychological investigation of human attachment began with a British psychiatrist, John Bowlby, and an American psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, who proposed that, to promote the survival of their young, primates have evolved an innate attachment system designed to motivate infants to seek comfort and safety from their primary caregiver, generally mother. Since then extensive research has been done on the behaviors, feelings, and biological mechanisms associated with this attachment system in human adults and other creatures. Moreover, researchers have proposed that these attachment circuits remain active throughout the life course—serving as a foundation for emotional commitment between pair-bonded partners for the purpose of raising offspring.
caveats: Fisher's integration of Bowlby/Ainsworth attachment theory into the M14 architecture. source_type='propagation' (Fisher synthesizing Bowlby/Ainsworth into her three-component model). | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): OCR + citation repair documentation (caveat-gap from original extraction). Source file line 4931 reads 'adults and other creaturess.8 Moreover' — two silent edits were applied to the author_quote: (a) 'creaturess' -> 'creatures' (single-letter OCR repair, clearly a scanning artifact of the plural form), and (b) removal of inline citation numeral '8'. Both edits are within the 2026-04-05 quote-normalization policy allowed list, but the caveat was missing from the original extraction and is added here retroactively.
scope: Links M14's attachment component to M3's Social Bonding architecture at the mechanistic level. Fisher's M14 attachment component is not a separate system but a repurposing of the infant-caregiver attachment circuitry (M3 developmental substrate) for adult pair-bonds. Cor's architectural choice to treat M14 as a distinct mechanism rather than collapsing it into M3 reflects this: M14 is the reproductive-motivation-specific use of circuits that also serve M3.

content: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These satisfaction hormones undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.
author_quote: Like vasopressin, oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus. Unlike vasopressin, oxytocin is released in all female mammals (including women) during the birthing process. It initiates contractions of the uterus and stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk. But oxytocin also stimulates bonding between a mother and her infant. And more and more data now indicate that oxytocin can also produce feelings of attachment to a preferred mating partner. You have undoubtedly felt the power of these 'cuddle chemicals,' as vasopressin and oxytocin are sometimes called. At orgasm, the activities of oxytocin spike in men and women. These 'satisfaction hormones' undoubtedly contribute to your sense of fusion, closeness, and attachment after sweet sex with a beloved.

content: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, reproduced himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children. Women's adultery has separate evolutionary logic: four hypotheses include (1) resource supplementation via gifts/food from lovers, (2) insurance policy against death or desertion of a primary mate, (3) 'upgrade' of genetic quality when the primary mate is deficient, and (4) genetic diversity of offspring against unpredictable environments.
author_quote: From a Darwinian perspective, it is easy to explain why men are—by nature—interested in sexual variety. If an ancestral man bore children with one woman, he had, genetically speaking, 'reproduced' himself. But if he also engaged in dalliances with another woman and, by chance, sired another child, he doubled his contribution to the next generation. So those men who sought sexual variety throughout deep history also tended to have more children.
caveats: Fisher's evolutionary-logic arguments for sex-differentiated mating strategies. source_type='propagation' (theoretical framework grounded in Trivers parental investment and Buss sexual strategies, which Fisher extends with her own four female-adultery hypotheses). evidence_quality='theoretical' — these are adaptive hypotheses, not direct empirical findings. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): retroactive caveat per new quote-normalization policy (effective 2026-04-05). content: After a while the fire cools and that's how it stays. The three basic brain systems for mating generally transition: feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment — what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.' But the three systems can also ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her.
author_quote: In spite of this common course of love, the three basic brain systems for mating that I have elsewhere proposed—lust, romantic love, and attachment—can actually ignite in any order. Some people have sex first, then fall in love. Some fall madly in love with someone they just met, then have sex several weeks down the road. Some even build a deep attachment to a friend at work or in their social circle, then later fall madly in love and have sex with him or her. Yet, generally, feelings of lust and passionate romantic love are triggered first, followed by feelings of deep attachment — what psychologist Theodor Reik called the warm 'afterglow.'
caveats: The typical-but-not-obligatory sequence of the three M14 components. source_type='propagation' (theoretical synthesis with cross-cultural observational support). | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): retroactive caveat per new quote-normalization policy (effective 2026-04-05). The flexibility of ordering is why M14 can produce diverse phenomenology (love-at-first-sight vs attachment-first romances) while still reflecting one underlying architecture. Relevant to Cor's treatment of M14 as a multi-component system with internal interactions.

content: When my colleagues redid the brain scanning experiment to look at rejection, we found that feelings of romantic rejection lit up activity in several brain regions linked with profound attachment, deep addiction, and physical pain. When you are rejected in love, many brain systems go to work, and rejection is one of the most painful experiences a human being can endure.
location: Chapter 5 'Blueprint for Divorce' pp. 127-128, Fisher/Brown rejection fMRI study
author_quote: Brain activations occurred in several regions of the reward system. Included were regions of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) associated with feelings of intense romantic love; the ventral pallidum, associated with feelings of deep attachment; the insular cortex and the anterior cingulate, associated with physical pain, anxiety, and the distress associated with physical pain; and the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, brain regions associated with assessing one's gains and losses—as well as craving and addiction. Most relevant to our story, activity in several of these brain regions has been correlated with the craving for cocaine and other drugs.
caveats: Fisher/Brown/Aron fMRI study of rejected lovers. source_type='primary' (Fisher's lab). evidence_quality='clinical' (small-sample fMRI). The overlap of romantic-rejection neural activation with physical-pain and addiction-withdrawal networks parallels the Eisenberger/Cacioppo social-pain overlap from Book 1 (Cacioppo), reinforcing the 'social pain is real pain' architectural claim. | Wave 2-B audit (codex-research #365, 2026-04-05): PARAPHRASE_LEAK HIGH fix (Option A full contiguous, pseudoquote replacement). Romantic rejection is not just a cognitive disappointment; it activates the same physical-pain and attachment-loss machinery that M3 grief uses. Critical for Cor's treatment of M14 breakdowns as architectural events, not merely emotional preferences.

content: Several serotonin-enhancing antidepressants, such as Prozac, Zoloft, and the newer serotonin boosters, can suppress dopamine pathways, dull the emotions, and potentially kill romantic passion. The romantic-love component of M14 depends on the dopamine-norepinephrine-low-serotonin neurochemical profile; increasing serotonin chemically disrupts this profile and may interfere with the normal operation of the romantic-love system.

content: The three basic brain systems for lust, romantic love and attachment began to take their human forms soon after our forebears descended from the fast-disappearing trees of Africa to walk on two feet and form pair-bonds to rear their helpless young at least through infancy as a team. Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate — a symphony, sometimes a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.

Lucy loved, some 3.2 million years ago. She felt sexual craving, passionate rapture, and deep feelings of attachment toward her mate — a symphony, sometimes even a cacophony of joyous, exciting, and calming sensations.

content: In our fMRI studies of romantic love, men and women showed equivalent activation in the core romantic-love brain regions (VTA and related dopamine pathways). Tennov reported that men and women experience this passion in roughly equal proportions from her 800+ informants. In contrast to folk belief that men are less emotional or less capable of romantic love, the neural data show men and women feel this passion equivalently.
author_quote: And men feel this passion just as powerfully as women. Tennov wrote of her 800+ informants that men and women experienced this intense passion 'in roughly equal proportions.' My colleagues and I have now confirmed this. In our fMRI study of young happy lovers, men showed just as much activity in the VTA and other neural pathways for romantic passion as women did.

Although M14 is sex-differentiated in substrate (VMH vs POA, estrous cycling vs tonic testosterone), the romantic-love COMPONENT is experienced with equivalent intensity across sexes. Sex differences exist in the specific selection criteria and timing, not in the intensity or presence of romantic love itself.

content: Lieberman's first-person observation of a Hadza hunter-gatherer camp in 2013 contradicts the standard Western assumption about hunter-gatherer activity levels. Upon arrival he found Hadza men, women, and children sitting on the ground, doing light chores, with no one engaged in hard work. This became the load-bearing empirical touchstone for M10's resolution-conditions framing: 'normal' human physical activity is embedded in daily life rather than set aside as 'exercise', and includes substantial rest and sitting.
location: Chapter 1 'Are We Born to Rest or Run?' pp. ~15-17
author_quote: Many things surprised me when I first walked into a Hadza camp mid-morning on a torrid, sunny day in 2013, but I remember being especially struck by how everyone was apparently doing nothing. Hadza camps consist of a few temporary grass huts that blend in with the surrounding bushes. I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. The women and children were relaxing on one side, and the men on another. One fellow was straightening some arrows, and a few children were toddling about, but no one was engaged in any hard work. To be sure, the Hadza weren't lounging on sofas, watching TV, munching potato chips, and sipping soda, but they were doing what so many health experts warn us to avoid: sitting.
