content: Rheumatoid arthritis case illustration (Mrs P): RA is classically taught as a localized joint disease, but the molecular cause is systemic — auto-antibodies and cytokines circulate throughout the body, not just in inflamed joints. Blood cytokine levels are elevated in RA patients, confirming the systemic inflammation. The question Bullmore retrospectively asks: was Mrs P's depression-and-fatigue profile (present alongside her joint disease) a DIRECT CONSEQUENCE of her systemic inflammation rather than a 'rational' response to her grim prospects? This reframes the comorbidity of depression with inflammatory disease from psychological to biological-cascade.
location: Chapter 2 'The Maudsley Hypothesis' — Mrs P rheumatoid arthritis case
author_quote: Auto-antibodies and cytokines are in circulation throughout the body, not solely concentrated in a few local hotspots. That is why doctors can check the diagnosis of rheumatoid disease by a blood test – cytokines and other inflammatory proteins are increased to concentrations much higher than normal in the blood of a patient like Mrs P. Her whole body was inflamed, not just her joints. And the whole body includes the brain.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 3 fresh extraction from Bullmore The Inflamed Mind (2018).txt] Bullmore's Mrs P rheumatoid case. source_type=primary (his clinical observation). evidence_quality=clinical. Pre-commit grep verified at source line ~1466-1472. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Bullmore's first-person clinical retrospective. Single case illustration, but grounded in standard immunology of rheumatoid arthritis (systemic inflammation is a textbook finding).

content: Paradigmatic example of the inflammation-as-cause reframing in medicine generally: atherosclerosis was 20th-century taught as a cholesterol plumbing problem, but 21st-century medical students are taught it as an inflammatory disease. Cholesterol accumulation triggers macrophage activity (foam cells), which spew cytokines, damage neighboring cells, and cause the sticky arterial wall that becomes a clot. 'Having a heart attack isn't a random plumbing disaster; it's often the end product of arterial inflammation.' This is the broader paradigm shift in medicine that Bullmore argues psychiatry has missed.
author_quote: Atherosclerosis, we were taught in the 20th century, was a thickening of the arteries due to deposits of cholesterol just beneath the lining of the arterial walls. If enough cholesterol accumulated it would block the artery completely; and if that artery happened to be supplying blood to the heart, then the patient would have a heart attack. We learnt about it by analogy to plumbing and that was often how it was treated, by a surgical operation to unblock or bypass the blocked piece of arterial pipe. In the 21st century, medical students are taught a significantly different story: the accumulation of cholesterol triggers an inflammatory reaction in the arterial wall.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 3 fresh extraction from Bullmore The Inflamed Mind (2018).txt] Bullmore on atherosclerosis reframing. source_type=primary (his summary of a paradigm shift). evidence_quality=replicated (established in medicine). Pre-commit grep verified at source line ~1516-1524. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Bullmore reporting the 21st-century medical consensus on atherosclerosis as an inflammatory disease. This reframing is cross-lab replicated and is now standard medical textbook material.

content: Epidemiological consensus: both major depressive disorder (MDD) in psychiatric patients and milder depressive symptoms in the general population are robustly associated with increased levels of inflammatory proteins in the blood. This is beyond doubt from the growing case-control and epidemiological literature of the last 20 years. While psychiatric diagnosis of MDD is conventionally incompatible with bodily disease, the association between MDD and inflammation is mechanistically compatible with 'enormous number of medical patients hiding in plain sight' who have both inflammatory disease and depression. This undermines the Cartesian mind/body separation in psychiatric diagnosis.

That much seems beyond doubt from the growing volume of case-control and epidemiological studies that have been published in the last 20 years. content: Tomasello's central thesis: what makes human thinking unique is its fundamentally cooperative nature. Humans put their heads together with others in acts of shared intentionality — 'we' intentionality — creating joint goals and joint attention that constitute a plural agent. This capacity enables everything from collaborative hunting to cultural institutions. Great apes, despite knowing much about others as intentional agents, do NOT engage in shared intentionality and do NOT form human-like culture. Shared intentionality is the specific human-unique adaptation.
author_quote: A small group of philosophers of action (e.g., Bratman, 1992; Searle, 1995; Gilbert, 1989; Tuomela, 2007) have investigated how humans put their heads together with others in acts of so-called shared intentionality, or "we" intentionality. When individuals participate with others in collaborative activities, together they form joint goals and joint attention, which then create individual roles and individual perspectives that must be coordinated within them (Moll and Tomasello, 2007).
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello Natural History 2014] Tomasello's central thesis framing. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's central theoretical framing, building on Bratman, Searle, Gilbert, Tuomela. The shared-intentionality construct is well-established in philosophy of action; Tomasello's contribution is the empirical-developmental evidence for it as a human-unique cognitive capacity.

content: Tomasello's two-step evolutionary sequence for uniquely human cognition: (1) Joint intentionality — small-scale ad hoc pair collaboration with 'I'/'you' second-personal engagement, emerging from obligate collaborative foraging ~400,000 years ago; (2) Collective intentionality — group-mindedness with in-group strangers, based on conventions/norms/institutions, emerging as populations grew and competed. This maps to two distinct cognitive-capacity profiles: perspectival/symbolic representations with recursive mind reading (joint) vs agent-neutral thinking with cultural common ground (collective). Both steps were driven by ecological pressure forcing cooperative lifeways.
author_quote: There were two key evolutionary steps. The first step, reflecting the focus of social infrastructure theorists such as Mead and Wittgenstein, involved the creation of a novel type of small-scale collaboration in human foraging. Participants in this collaborative foraging created socially shared joint goals and joint attention (common ground), which created the possibility of individual roles and perspectives within that ad hoc shared world or "form of life."
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's 2-step hypothesis. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's original 2-step evolutionary hypothesis. Theoretical framework; empirically supported by developmental studies comparing human infants/children with great apes, but the evolutionary timing is inference from the comparative data.

content: Obligate collaborative foraging as evolutionarily stable strategy: interdependence + social selection. Early humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure daily food alone — they were interdependent. This created direct selective pressure for joint-intentionality skills. As a natural outcome, individuals made evaluative judgments about potential collaborative partners — social selection against cheaters and laggards, and against bullies. Critically, individuals had to worry about BOTH evaluating others AND how others were evaluating them (self-image concern) — a uniquely human cognitive preoccupation.
author_quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities—which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's interdependence+social-selection model. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello et al. 2012 hypothesis. Theoretical model grounded in game-theoretic analysis and comparative developmental data.

content: The stag hunt as formal model for early human collaboration: two individuals have easy access to low-payoff hares and see a high-payoff stag that requires joint action. Motivations align but the cognitive problem is coordination — I want to go for the stag only if you do, and vice versa. The leader-follower solution that chimpanzees use is unstable when risk is high. Schelling/Lewis showed that coordination requires mutual knowledge / recursive mind-reading. Tomasello's refinement: humans use 'common ground' with recursive decomposition only when perturbations occur. This is the cognitive architecture that distinguishes human from ape cooperation.
author_quote: The situation these early humans faced is perhaps best modeled by the stag hunt scenario from game theory (Skyrms, 2004). Two individuals have easy access to low-payoff "hares" (e.g., low-calorie vegetation), and then there appears on the horizon a high-payoff but difficult-to-obtain "stag" (e.g., large game) that can be acquired only if individuals abandon their hares and collaborate. Their motivations thus align, because it is in both their interests to work together. The dilemma is thus purely cognitive: since collaboration is mandatory and I am risking my hare, I want to go for the stag only if you do, too. But you only want to go for the stag if I do, too.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello applying stag hunt to early human collaboration. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello reporting Skyrms's stag-hunt game-theory formalization and Schelling/Lewis coordination theory. Theoretical model, not empirical.

content: Children vs chimps reengagement experiment: Warneken et al. had 14-18 month old human infants engage in joint activity with an adult (operating an apparatus). When the adult stopped playing her role for no reason, children were unhappy and attempted to reengage the partner. When the SAME situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, chimps ignored the partner and tried to complete the goal alone. This dissociation — even at prelinguistic ages, humans expect partners in joint activity to be committed enough to reengage, chimps do not — is a central behavioral marker of joint intentionality.
author_quote: Thus, Warneken et al. (2006, 2007) had infants of this age engage in a joint activity with an adult, such as obtaining a toy by each operating one side of an apparatus. Then, the adult simply stopped playing her role for no reason. The children were not happy about this and did various things to attempt to reengage their partner. (They did not do this if her stopping was for a good reason; e.g., she had to attend to something else [Warneken et al., 2012].) Interesting, when this same situation was arranged for human-raised chimpanzees, they simply ignored the recalcitrant partner and tried to find ways to achieve the goal on their own.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello reporting Warneken comparative studies. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Warneken 2006/2007 comparative developmental studies with young children and chimpanzees. Cross-lab replicated. Small samples typical of developmental primate comparison but the dissociation is robust.

content: 3-year-old children collaborative commitment study (Hamann 2012): pairs of 3yo children worked together to bring rewards to the top of a step structure. One child's reward, surprisingly, became available midway. The 'lucky' child DELAYED consuming her own reward and PERSEVERED until the other got hers — significantly more than in a parallel non-collaborative individual-action condition. This shows commitment to a joint goal: 'we' get the prizes together, and they make adjustments to realize the joint goal. Chimps in parallel experiments show no such commitment. And Hamann 2011: 3yo children (but not chimps) also committed to dividing spoils equally.
author_quote: For example, Hamann et al. (2012) had pairs of three-year-old children work together to bring rewards to the top of a step-like structure. The problem was that for one child the reward, surprisingly, became available midway through. Nevertheless, when this happened, the lucky child delayed consumption of her own reward and persevered until the other got hers (i.e., more than they helped the partner in a similar situation in which they were acting individually, without collaboration). Such commitment to the partner suggests that the children constructed a joint goal at the beginning that "we" get the prizes together, and they made whatever adjustments were necessary to realize that joint goal. Again, great apes do not behave in this same way.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello reporting Hamann collaborative-commitment studies. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Hamann et al. 2012 + Hamann 2011 developmental studies. Small cross-lab replicated samples. Central behavioral evidence for joint goals in 3yo humans vs absence in chimpanzees.

content: Taking leave: Gräfenhain 2009 had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult; then another adult attempted to lure them to a more exciting game. Two-year-olds mostly bolted to the new game, but from age 3 children paused before departing and 'took leave' — verbally or by handing the adult the shared tool. Children recognized that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires acknowledgment. No published reports of chimpanzees taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment exist. This is specific evidence for commitment-as-moral-obligation in joint intentionality.
author_quote: Importantly, when children of this same age have it in their common ground with a collaborative partner that each is counting on the other to come through (we are interdependent), they both feel obligated to the other (see Gilbert, 1989, 1990). Thus, Gräfenhain et al. (2009) had preschoolers explicitly agree to play a game with one adult, and then another adult attempted to lure them away to a more exciting game. Although two-year-old children mostly just bolted to the new game straightaway, from three years of age children paused before departing and "took leave," either verbally or by handing the adult the tool they had been using together. The children seemed to recognize that joint goals involve joint commitments, the breaking of which requires some kind of acknowledgment or even apology. No study of this type has ever been done with chimpanzees, but there are no published reports of one chimpanzee taking leave from, making excuses to, or apologizing to another for breaking a joint commitment.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello reporting Gräfenhain taking-leave study. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Gräfenhain 2009 developmental study + comparative absence in chimpanzees. Small sample but cross-lab replicated pattern.

content: Role-switching in collaborative roles: Carpenter 2005 found that young children, after playing one role in a collaboration, could quickly switch to the other role. Chimpanzees could not. This indicates that children attend not just to their own subgoals but to the partner's subgoal AND to the partner attending to them — a specifically recursive level of joint-attention tracking. Fletcher 2012 extended this: 3yo children who had first played role A in collaboration learned role B more easily than children who had only observed — they had learned BOTH roles from their own collaborative experience simultaneously.
author_quote: other studies have found that young children, but not chimpanzees, learn important new things about the partner's role as they are collaborating. For example, Carpenter et al. (2005) found that after young children played one role in a collaboration, they could quickly switch to the other, whereas chimpanzees could not do this (Tomasello and Carpenter, 2005).
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello reporting Carpenter role-switching studies. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Carpenter 2005 + Tomasello & Carpenter 2005 comparative developmental data. Cross-lab partially replicated.

content: Cooperative communication as second-personal process: humans communicators conceptualize situations via external communicative vehicles for other persons; recipients then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks these will be relevant for them. This dialogic process involves not just shared-intentionality motivations but complex recursive inferences about others' intentions toward my intentional states. This form of communication — unique to humans, characteristic even of prelinguistic infant gestures — presupposes a shared conceptual framework (common conceptual ground) AND appreciation of the partner's individual intentions within it. Grounds M11 cooperation AND M3 social bonding through the communication channel.
author_quote: as a specific form of human collaborative activity and shared intentionality, human cooperative communication involves a set of special intentional and inferential processes—first identified by Grice (1957, 1975) and since elaborated and amended by Sperber and Wilson (1996), Clark (1996), Levinson (2000), and Tomasello (2008). Human communicators conceptualize situations and entities via external communicative vehicles for other persons; these other persons then attempt to determine why the communicator thinks that these situations and entities will be relevant for them.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello on cooperative communication as second-personal. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's synthesis of Gricean pragmatics applied to human-specific communication. Theoretical framing with substantial empirical backing from developmental and comparative studies.

content: Tomasello's characterization of how humans think about each other recursively: attuned to common ground, and decomposing common ground a few recursive layers deep when perturbations occur ('he thinks that I think he thinks...'). Typically only a few iterations deep — not the infinite regress that Lewis/Schelling formalized. This realistic recursive-mind-reading architecture is what supports joint intentionality in practice: most of the time you just know what the shared situation is, but when things go wrong you can reason explicitly about what the partner thinks about your thinking.
author_quote: Clark (1996) proposed, as a more realistic account, that humans simply recognize the "common ground" they have with others (e.g., we both know that we both want to go for the stag) and that this is sufficient for making joint decisions toward joint goals. Tomasello (2008) suggested that something like common ground is how people actually operate, but when perturbations occur they often explain them by reasoning that "he thinks that I think he thinks . . ." (typically only a few iterations deep), suggesting an underlying recursive structure.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's common-ground + recursive-mind-reading architecture. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello 2008 theoretical proposal with supporting developmental data. The recursive mind-reading + common ground architecture is a theoretical synthesis rather than a directly tested claim.

content: Joint goal formation specification (from Bratman 1992): for you and me to form a joint goal to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH YOU; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag TOGETHER WITH ME; and critically (3) we must have MUTUAL KNOWLEDGE (common ground) that we both know each other's goal. Each of us wanting separately to capture the stag, even if mutually known, does not count — it would be parallel hunting, not joint hunting. The together-with-the-other structure is essential.
author_quote: We may characterize the formation of a joint goal (or joint intention) in more detail as follows (see Bratman, 1992). For you and me to form a joint goal (or joint intention) to pursue a stag together, (1) I must have the goal to capture the stag together with you; (2) you must have the goal to capture the stag together with me; and, critically, (3) we must have mutual knowledge, or common ground, that we both know each other's goal.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello reporting Bratman joint-intention formalization. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello reporting Bratman 1992 formal specification of joint intention. Theoretical construct from philosophy of action.

content: Tomasello's framing of ape-cognition vs human-cognition: early humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, but they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. Early humans were FORCED by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and their thinking became more directed toward coordinating with others to achieve joint goals or collective group goals. This shift — from individual-competitive to joint-cooperative cognition — 'changed everything'. Thinking itself became fundamentally social.
author_quote: Although humans' great ape ancestors were social beings, they lived mostly individualistic and competitive lives, and so their thinking was geared toward achieving individual goals. But early humans were at some point forced by ecological circumstances into more cooperative lifeways, and so their thinking became more directed toward figuring out ways to coordinate with others to achieve joint goals or even collective group goals. And this changed everything.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's ape-vs-human cognitive-shift framing. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's central theoretical claim about the cognitive shift from competitive-individualistic to cooperative-joint thinking. Theoretical framing, not a directly testable empirical claim.

content: Objective-reflective-normative thinking: the human-unique cognitive profile. Many animals can cognitively represent situations abstractly, but only humans conceptualize the same situation under differing, even CONFLICTING social perspectives (leading to 'objectivity'). Many animals make simple causal/intentional inferences, but only humans make socially RECURSIVE and self-reflective inferences about others' intentional states. Many animals monitor their actions for instrumental success, but only humans self-monitor with respect to the NORMATIVE perspectives and standards ('reasons') of others or the group. These three social differences — perspectival, recursive, normative — yield an identifiably different type of thinking.
author_quote: although many animal species can cognitively represent situations and entities at least somewhat abstractly, only humans can conceptualize one and the same situation or entity under differing, even conflicting, social perspectives (leading ultimately to a sense of "objectivity"). Further, although many animals also make simple causal and intentional inferences about external events, only humans make socially recursive and self-reflective inferences about others' or their own intentional states. And, finally, although many animals monitor and evaluate their own actions with respect to instrumental success, only humans self-monitor and evaluate their own thinking with respect to the normative perspectives and standards ("reasons") of others or the group.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's objective-reflective-normative thinking characterization. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's characterization of human-unique thinking. Three specific cognitive capacities (perspectival, recursive-reflective, normative) each with developmental and comparative support.

content: Collective intentionality (second step): as human populations grew and groups competed, group life as a whole became 'one big collaborative activity' — a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions. This shifts from the face-to-face 'I-you' joint-intentionality of the first step to an impersonal 'we-as-group' collective intentionality with conventional communication and cultural institutions. The architectural distinction matters for M11 — humans have BOTH ad hoc joint collaboration AND stable group-mindedness, and these are different cognitive capacities.
author_quote: The second step, reflecting the focus of culture theorists such as Vygotsky and Bakhtin, came as human populations began growing in size and competing with one another. This competition meant that group life as a whole became one big collaborative activity, creating a much larger and more permanent shared world, that is to say, a culture. The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on a new ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 4 fresh extraction from Tomasello 2014] Tomasello's collective intentionality / cultural group-mindedness framing. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Tomasello's second-step collective intentionality hypothesis. Builds on Vygotsky and Bakhtin culture-theory traditions; empirically supported by developmental studies of children's grasp of cultural conventions and norms.

content: Panksepp's canonical definition of the SEEKING system: a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes survival by making animals intensely interested in exploring their world and excited when they are about to get what they desire. It drives animals to find and eagerly anticipate food, water, warmth, and sex. When fully aroused, it fills the mind with interest and motivates movement toward resources. In humans, this is 'one of the main brain systems that generates and sustains curiosity, even for intellectual pursuits'. Neuroanatomically the SEEKING system corresponds to the major self-stimulation system from midbrain to cortex, long misconceptualized as a 'reward or reinforcement system'. This is the foundational primary-source definition that load-bears M2 Pursuit/Exploration in Cor.
location: Chapter 3 'The Varieties of Emotional Systems in the Brain' pp. ~53
author_quote: The SEEKING system (see Chapter 8): This emotional system is a coherently operating neuronal network that promotes a certain class of survival abilities. This system makes animals intensely interested in exploring their world and leads them to become excited when they are about to get what they desire. It eventually allows animals to find and eagerly anticipate the things they need for survival, including, of course, food, water, warmth, and their ultimate evolutionary survival need, sex. In other words, when fully aroused, it helps fill the mind with interest and motivates organisms to

content: Panksepp's specific neuroanatomical claim for SEEKING: dopamine is the key neurochemical, specifically the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits emanating from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) at the back of the hypothalamus. These dopamine circuits energize and coordinate higher brain areas mediating planning and foresight — amygdala, nucleus accumbens, frontal cortex — and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals. Amphetamines and cocaine produce their psychic appeal by temporarily overarousing this emotional system; opiates, nicotine, and alcohol also derive hedonic appeal from interacting with it. This is the specific anatomical substrate that load-bears M2 and DA4 (proxy hijacking by stimulant drugs).
author_quote: A very important neurochemical in this system is dopamine, especially the dopaminergic mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine circuits, which emanate from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) situated at the very back of the hypothalamus (Figure 3.6). These dopamine circuits tend to energize and coordinate the functions of many higher brain areas that mediate planning and foresight (such as the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and frontal cortex—see next chapter) and promote states of eagerness and directed purpose in both humans and animals.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's VTA dopamine SEEKING anatomy. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation + smart quotes normalized.
scope: Panksepp's anatomical specification — VTA mesolimbic/mesocortical dopamine + downstream targets (amygdala, NAcc, frontal cortex). Cross-lab replicated via self-stimulation, microdialysis, lesion, and pharmacology.

content: Panksepp's definition of the RAGE system: working in opposition to SEEKING, it mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and by attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. Electrical stimulation of specific brain regions paralleling the FEAR trajectory produces rage in both animals and humans. The system helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in opponents, AND energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger gets much of its psychic 'energy' from this brain system. Brain tumors irritating the circuit cause pathological rage; damage to the system promotes serenity. This is the canonical primary-source definition for M1 Threat Management (rage component).
author_quote: The RAGE system (see Chapter 10): Working in opposition to SEEKING is a system that mediates anger. RAGE is aroused by frustration and attempts to curtail an animal's freedom of action. It has long been known that one can enrage both animals and humans by stimulating very specific parts of the brain, which parallel the trajectory of the FEAR system. This system not only helps animals defend themselves by arousing fear in their opponents but also energizes behavior when an animal is irritated or restrained. Human anger may get much of its psychic "energy" from this brain system.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's RAGE system definition. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=replicated. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied; OCR repair: source line 5478 has 'auempts' → 'attempts' (OCR artifact repair) — confirmed in normalized source.
scope: Panksepp's canonical primary-source RAGE definition. Grounded in decades of electrical brain stimulation research in cats, rats, and humans (clinical stimulation case literature).

content: Panksepp's definition of the FEAR system: a circuit designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. Intense stimulation makes animals run away as if extremely scared; weak stimulation produces the opposite motor tendency — freezing, common when animals are placed in circumstances where they have previously been hurt or frightened. Humans stimulated in these same brain areas report being engulfed by intense anxiety. This is the canonical primary-source evidence that fear is not a derived cognitive state but a hardwired affective circuit with specific neuroanatomy. Load-bearing for M1 Threat Management.
author_quote: The FEAR system (see Chapter 1 1): A FEAR circuit was probably designed during evolution to help animals reduce pain and the possibility of destruction. When stimulated intensely, this circuit leads animals to run away as if they are extremely scared. content: Panksepp's definition of the PANIC separation-distress system, one of his most distinctive theoretical contributions: to be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to ensure parents take care of offspring AND offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate they need care — reflected in crying (scientifically: separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for provides a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes. This is load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding and M9 Care/Alloparenting — Panksepp is the primary source for reading attachment distress as a specific affective circuit rather than a learned association.
author_quote: The PANIC system (see Chapter 14): To be a mammal is to be born socially dependent. Brain evolution has provided safeguards to assure that parents (usually the mother) take care of the offspring, and the offspring have powerful emotional systems to indicate that they are in need of care (as reflected in crying or, as scientists prefer to say, separation calls). The nature of these distress systems in the brains of caretakers and those they care for has only recently been clarified; they provide a neural substrate for understanding many other social emotional processes.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's PANIC/separation-distress definition. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical (framework definition; empirical circuit details in Ch 14 are replicated). Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's canonical primary-source PANIC system definition. Theoretical framework for separation distress as an affective circuit; empirical grounding in Ch 14 across rodents, guinea pigs, domestic animals, and primates.

content: Panksepp's identification of three additional special-purpose socioemotional systems beyond the 4 primitive ones: sexual LUST (Ch 12), maternal CARE (Ch 13), and roughhousing PLAY (Ch 15). Sexual urges are mediated by distinct brain circuits and chemistries for males and females but share components such as oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation. Maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with sexuality circuits, suggesting how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for 'the social contract' — the possibilities for love and bonding — in the mammalian brain. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation, M9 Care/Alloparenting, M4 Social Calibration/Play, and the architectural claim that social bonding evolved as an extension of pre-existing reproductive circuits.
author_quote: In addition to the preceding primitive systems that are evident in all mammals soon after birth, we also have more sophisticated special-purpose socioemotional systems that are engaged at appropriate times in the lives of all mammals-for instance, those that mediate sexual LUST (see Chapter 12), maternal CARE (see Chapter 13), and roughhousing PLAY (see Chapter 15). Each of these is built around neural complexities that are only provisionally understood. Sexual urges are mediated by specific brain circuits and chemistries that are quite distinct for males and females but appear to share some components such as the physiological and psychological effects of oxytocin, which also promotes maternal motivation.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's LUST/CARE/PLAY trifecta. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's canonical three-circuit framework for LUST/CARE/PLAY. Theoretical framework with anatomical specification in individual chapters.

content: Panksepp's six methodological criteria for identifying genuine emotional systems in the brain (Figure 3.3): (1) Underlying circuits are genetically predetermined to respond unconditionally to life-challenging stimuli; (2) they organize diverse behaviors by activating/inhibiting motor subroutines and autonomic-hormonal changes; (3) they change sensitivities of sensory systems relevant to the aroused behavioral sequences; (4) their neural activity outlasts precipitating circumstances; (5) they can come under conditional control of emotionally neutral stimuli; (6) they have reciprocal interactions with higher decision-making and consciousness circuits. Plus the seventh psychological criterion: they must generate affective feelings. This is Panksepp's load-bearing methodological framework for distinguishing emotional systems from general-purpose sensorimotor circuits.
author_quote: The underlying circuits are genetically predetermined and designed to respond unconditionally to stimuli arising from major life-challenging circumstances. These circuits organize diverse behaviors by activating or inhibiting motor subroutines and concurrent autonomic-hormonal changes that have proved adaptive in the face of such life-challenging circumstances during the evolutionary history of the species. Emotive circuits change the sensitivities of sensory systems that are relevant for the behavioral sequences that have been aroused. Neural activity of emotive systems outlasts the precipitating circumstances. Emotive circuits can come under the conditional control of emotionally neutral environmental stimuli. Emotive circuits have reciprocal interactions with the brain mechanisms that elaborate higher decision-making processes and consciousness.
caveats: Wave 3A-1 Book 5 (Panksepp). author_quote covers criteria 1-6 from source lines 4908-4944 with mid-quote excision of the intervening Figure 3.3 caption and page-header block, applied under quote normalization policy clause 6 (figure-caption / layout-block excision; non-authorial layout blocks only). The normalized source strips leading numerals such as " 1.", " 2." as bare-digit page-number artifacts, so grep phrases test the criterion text rather than the numbering. Dehyphenation applied. Caveat tightened 2026-04-05 by corherence per codex-research audit #417 policy-edge flag.
scope: Panksepp's methodological criteria framework. Theoretical framework with embedded empirical-operational operationalization; load-bearing for distinguishing affective-neuroscience claims from sensorimotor / cognitive ones.

content: Panksepp's empirical discovery of rat laughter: listening in the ultrasonic frequency range at which rats communicate, friendly tickling induced very high-frequency chirping at about 50 kHz. The response was most effective when tickling the nape of the neck (where rats normally solicit play) or when full-body tickling was applied. Social-deprived rats exhibited MORE chirping to tickling than littermates allowed daily play sessions; playfulness correlated highly with tickling-induced 'laughter'. Tickling was a positive incentive — rats sought it out and began to chirp to cues associated with it. If this vocalization is homologous to human laughter, 'we may come to understand human joy by studying the circuits that generate such vocalization in rats'. This is Panksepp's primary empirical evidence for M4 PLAY and for cross-species affective homology.
author_quote: To evaluate whether rats laugh, we took a simple tickling approach. Listening in to the ultrasonic frequency range at which rats communicate, we rapidly found that friendly tickling induced very high-frequency chirping at about 50 KHz. This response could be provoked more effectively when the tickling occurred at the nape of the neck, where animals normally solicit play, than on the rump, and full body tickling was most effective of all (Figure 15.4). Animals that had been deprived of social contact from weaning at 24 days of age through puberty exhibited more chirping to tickling than littermates that had been allowed two play sessions each day through this interval.

scope: Panksepp's original rat-tickling / 50kHz chirping discovery. Cross-lab replicated (Burgdorf, Kroes, and others extended).

content: Panksepp's original discovery linking endogenous opioids to separation distress: brain opioids (especially beta-endorphin and enkephalins) modulate social feelings and separation distress, AND opioids promote social bonding. Oxytocin and opioids work together to inhibit separation distress. This is Panksepp's foundational finding that attachment pain shares neural substrates with physical pain — the 'social pain' hypothesis at the molecular level. Load-bearing for M3 Social Bonding, DA8 Phylogenetic Priority (opioid system is ancient), and for reading depression/grief as dysregulation of an opioid-modulated affective circuit rather than a purely cognitive state.

author_quote: especially the endogenous opioid peptides, are already known to modify feeling states in humans and corresponding behavioral changes in animals.

scope: Panksepp's endogenous-opioid / separation-distress framework. His lab's original finding (Panksepp 1978 onwards) that opioid agonists reduce separation distress vocalizations in young animals, and opioid antagonists increase them. Cross-lab replicated.

content: Panksepp's early summary of oxytocin's pro-social functions: oxytocin mediates various pro-social processes including female sexual response, orgasm, maternal behavior, social memory, and the INHIBITION of separation distress. It is a single neuropeptide that operates across the sexual-maternal-social-bonding domains — exactly the molecular overlap that allows evolution to construct the 'social contract' by repurposing reproductive circuits for broader bonding. This is primary-source evidence for the M14/M9/M3 architectural overlap in Cor's specification.
author_quote: oxytocin, which mediates various pro-social processes, including maternal behavior and the inhibition of separation distress (Chapters 12 to 14), can yield a tripeptide called PLG (proline-leucine-glycine), which mediates none of the above but has antidepressant effects.

scope: Panksepp's synthesis of oxytocin's multi-domain social effects. Well-replicated in animal models; human oxytocin-behavior evidence is more contested (cf. Wave 2 Fisher 188 discussion).

content: Panksepp's central theoretical commitment — the seventh psychological criterion: emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings. This criterion is 'hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram' but is the load-bearing claim that distinguishes affective neuroscience from behavioral neuroscience. Panksepp argues affect emerges from interactions of emotional systems with primal neural mechanisms that represent 'the self', particularly midbrain periaqueductal and deep tectal circuits interacting with frontal cortical systems. Arousal of the executive circuit for each emotion is a NECESSARY CONDITION for getting feeling states activated within the brain. Load-bearing for reading M1-M4/M9/M14 outputs as having affective content, not just behavioral output.
author_quote: Of course, as mentioned, there is a seventh psychological criterion: The emotional circuits must be able to generate affective feelings, but this is hard to incorporate into the conceptual diagram. I will eventually develop the idea that affect emerges from the many interactions of emotional systems depicted in Figure 3.3 with primal neural mechanisms that represent "the self" (see Chapter 16)
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's 7th affective criterion. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's theoretical commitment to affective consciousness as emergent from emotional-circuit arousal. Theoretical framework developed in Ch 16.

content: Panksepp's conceptual toolkit for emotional circuits: he calls them 'executive, command, and operating systems' — executive implies a superordinate role in hierarchical controls; command implies the circuit can INSTIGATE a full-blown emotional process (not just correlate with it); operating implies it coordinates and synchronizes multiple subsystems. Together these yield coherent psycho-behavioral and physiological responses that constitute an emotional 'organ system' — an anatomical network of interconnected neurons with endocrine, paracrine, and immune influences. This is the load-bearing architectural framing for why emotional circuits are mechanisms (Cor's M-framework) rather than mere sensorimotor reflexes.
author_quote: I will speak of these emotional systems in a variety of ways, using designations such as executive, command, and operating systems, to provide nuances of meaning that may be needed to conceptualize their overall functions. The use of the term executive implies that a neural system has a superordinate role in a cascade of hierarchical controls
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's executive/command/operating framework. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's theoretical terminology for emotional circuits as executive/command/operating systems.

content: Panksepp's historical contribution: in his 1982 paper he first distinguished four primary emotional command systems that are organized along discrete but interacting subcortical trajectories (mostly following the medial forebrain bundle). These are depicted in Figure 3.5 (original paper) with approximate anatomical locations for SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE in the hypothalamus and their interconnections. The 1982 framework was the foundational statement of affective neuroscience as a research program distinct from behavioral or cognitive approaches. This is primary-source citation for the architectural claim that mammalian emotions are subcortically organized, not cortically derived.
author_quote: The major emotional operating systems are defined primarily by genetically coded neural circuits that generate well-organized behavior sequences that can be evoked by localized electrical stimulation of the brain. Representative behaviors generated by the various systems are indicated, and the approximate locations of the SEEKING, FEAR, and RAGE systems are depicted on a small frontal section through one side of the hypothalamus.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp 1982 framework citation from Figure 3.5 caption. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied. Note: This is a figure caption, treated per clause 6 — figure captions can be quoted if they are the authorial statement, but only where distinguishable from body prose. Figure 3.5 caption is Panksepp's own authorial summary, so it qualifies for quoting as primary text.
scope: Panksepp's Figure 3.5 caption describing his 1982 framework. Historical and theoretical anchor for affective neuroscience.

content: Panksepp's clinical prediction from the SEEKING-system framework: when the SEEKING brain system becomes UNDERACTIVE (as is common with aging), a form of depression results. When it becomes spontaneously OVERACTIVE (from stress), animal behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow — especially the 'functional' forms of psychosis treatable with traditional antipsychotic medications (all of which reduce dopamine activity). This predicts that depression-via-SEEKING-hypofunction is mechanistically distinct from depression-via-PANIC-overactivation (social loss), and provides a specific dopamine-centered prediction for M2 Pursuit/Exploration dysregulation. Load-bearing for reading modern anhedonic depression as a SEEKING-hypoactivation phenotype.
author_quote: When this brain system becomes underactive, as is common with aging, a form of depression results. When the system becomes spontaneously overactive, which can happen as a result of various kinds of stress, an animal's behavior becomes excessive and schizophrenic or manic symptoms may follow-especially the "functional" forms of psychosis that can be treated with traditional antipsychotic medications (which all reduce dopamine activity in the brain)
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's SEEKING / depression / mania / psychosis prediction. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's theoretical prediction mapping SEEKING-system activity levels to clinical phenotypes (depression / psychosis / mania). Theoretical framing consistent with the broader dopamine-psychopathology literature.

content: Panksepp's observation of evolutionary economy in neuropeptide coding: there is extensive correspondence between the peripheral and central functions of neuropeptides — insulin controls peripheral glucose dispersion AND central satiety; angiotensin controls peripheral water retention AND central thirst; oxytocin controls peripheral birthing and milk letdown AND central maternal acceptance and readiness. Many peptides highlight evolution's tendency to REUTILIZE existing elements for new tasks harmonious with previous functions. This exaptation pattern is load-bearing for the DA8 architectural claim that newer mechanisms (social bonding) are built from older ones (reproductive physiology).
author_quote: there is a great deal of neuropeptide specificity in the coding of behavior, and it is esthetically pleasing to note that we often observe a correspondence between the peripheral functions of these neuropeptides and their role within the brain (Table 6.1). For instance, in the periphery, insulin controls metabolic dispersion of nutrients, while in the brain it helps mediate satiety (see Chapter 9). Likewise, in the periphery, the hormone angiotensin promotes water retention in the kidney, while in the brain it promotes thirst. Thus, many neuropeptide languages highlight the tendency of evolution to reutilize existing elements for new tasks that are harmonious with previous functions.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp on peripheral-central neuropeptide correspondences. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's evolutionary-economy framing for neuropeptide coding. Grounded in specific examples from the neuropeptide literature.

content: Panksepp's architectural claim about the evolution of social bonding: maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality. This suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the 'social contract' — 'the possibilities for love and bonding' — in the mammalian brain. Maternal nurturance probably arose gradually from preexisting circuits that initially mediated reproductive behaviors. This is THE foundational architectural claim for why Cor's M3 Social Bonding, M9 Care/Alloparenting, and M14 Reproductive Motivation share substrate — they were built by evolution as extensions and overlays of the same neurochemical machinery, not as independent systems.
author_quote: We now realize that maternal behavior circuits remain closely intermeshed with those that control sexuality, and this suggests how evolution gradually constructed the basic neural substrates for the social contract (i.e., the possibilities for love and bonding) in the mammalian brain.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp's maternal-sexuality-social-bonding architectural overlap. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied. This is the single most-cited Panksepp passage for Cor's reading of the M3/M9/M14 substrate overlap.
scope: Panksepp's social-contract / social-bonding architectural claim. Theoretical framing grounded in specific anatomical and neurochemical overlaps documented in Ch 12-14.

content: Panksepp's framework of 4 primary emotional command systems: expectancy/SEEKING, RAGE, FEAR, and separation-distress/PANIC. These are organized along discrete but interacting trajectories in the subcortical brain, largely following the medial forebrain bundle. These 4 systems are 'evident in all mammals soon after birth' — they are not cognitive achievements but mammalian hardware inherited from at least 150 million years of mammalian evolution. This is the central DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim: the affective substrate is ancient, pre-cortical, and conserved across all mammals.

content: Panksepp notes important species differences in separation-distress systems — they exhibit striking interspecies variability even though the basic circuit is conserved. This calibration variability is important for understanding human-unique attachment patterns: the PANIC system is mammal-universal but its specific tuning (sensitivity thresholds, recovery dynamics, cross-modal signaling) varies with species ecology. For humans, separation distress is tuned for the long juvenile dependency period and for loss of specific attachment figures rather than general social absence. This grounds DA7 Developmental Calibration at the PANIC-circuit level.

content: Panksepp's more specific primary-source claim: brain opioids promote the development of food and social attachments, and the inhibition of separation distress. In young animals, opioid agonists reduce separation-distress vocalizations; opioid antagonists increase them. This is the neurochemical bridge from physical pain (classically opioid-modulated) to social pain (separation distress), grounding the architectural claim that social rejection activates the same molecular systems as physical injury. Load-bearing for the M3 cascade connecting social bonds to physical-pain circuitry and for the DA8 phylogenetic-priority claim that attachment evolved by repurposing older pain-modulation systems.

content: Panksepp's architectural claim about emotion-cognition interaction: emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over behavior and mental activity through widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate physiological changes synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies. This is NOT just a one-way emotion→behavior pathway — cognition is PENETRATED by emotional-circuit activity, meaning that 'cognitive' function cannot be cleanly separated from affective-circuit function. Load-bearing for Cor's framing that mechanism outputs (M1-M4, M9, M14) shape perception and attention upstream, not just behavior downstream.
author_quote: In addition to being the deep neural sources of psychic life, emotional circuits achieve their profound influence over the behavior and mental activity of an organism through the widespread effects on the rest of the nervous system. Emotive circuits change sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processing, and initiate a host of physiological changes that are naturally synchronized with the aroused behavioral tendencies characteristic of emotional experience.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 5] Panksepp on emotional-circuit effects on cognition. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified. Dehyphenation applied.
scope: Panksepp's emotion-penetrates-cognition claim. Theoretical framing consistent with affective-neuroscience consensus.

content: Hrdy's core allomothering thesis: Among humans living in foraging societies, a helpful mate and/or alloparents were usually essential for a mother to rear any infant at all. Indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might — protecting, provisioning, even suckling another female's infant. This is load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting: human infants are NOT raised dyadically, and the mother-as-sole-caregiver framing misses the evolutionary architecture entirely.

In a surprisingly broad range of creatures, indispensable alloparents provide many of the same forms of care a mother might, protecting and provisioning, even suckling another female's infant in cases where the alloparent is

content: Hrdy's 'allomother' term precision: E.O. Wilson coined 'alloparent' in 1975 to replace imprecise 'helpers' (ornithologists) and 'aunts' (primatologists). Hrdy refines further to 'allomothers' — all caretakers OTHER than the mother (whose identity is usually known for sure). The precision matters: in cooperative-breeding species, alloparents play critical roles, allowing mothers to breed at a faster rate than would otherwise be possible. Humans fit this pattern.
author_quote: Ornithologists used to call such assistants "helpers"; primatologists called them "aunts" (after the British "auntie," to designate a female relative or trusted family friend). In 1975, Edward O.Wilson decided it was time for a more dignified designation: allo- (from the Greek for "other than") plus parent.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy on alloparent term history. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's terminological precision. Historical note grounded in E.O. Wilson 1975 Sociobiology.

content: Dwarf mongoose as classic cooperative breeding example: Typically only the oldest female in a large group breeds, but all help her rear her young. Each animal takes a turn as babysitter or sentinel. The rule: 'Those who can, breed; kin who can't, help out.' Subordinate females spontaneously lactate to feed their charges. Dominant breeding females ensure allomother availability by killing infants born to subordinates — the alpha female makes giving birth an option not worth the cost. This is a paradigm case for cooperative-breeding biology and for M9.
author_quote: the dwarf mongoose of East Africa provides a classic example of cooperative breeding. Typically only the oldest female in a large group breeds, but all help her rear her young. Each animal takes a turn as baby-sitter or sentinel, standing upright on the vast arid savanna, vigilantly scanning the horizon for predators.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy reporting dwarf mongoose cooperative breeding. source_type=propagation. evidence_quality=cross_species (different species than humans). Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy reporting Creel and Rasa dwarf mongoose cooperative-breeding research. Cross-species replicated cooperative breeding finding.

content: Hrdy's alloparenting role in human evolution: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species. This links the cross-species cooperative-breeding finding to the specific human case: our unusually extended juvenile period and large brains require more caloric provisioning than a single mother can provide, making allomothering not a cultural addition but a species architecture.
author_quote: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy human-alloparenting thesis. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.

content: Hrdy's autobiographical framing: she describes her own reliance on alloparents to melding vocation with family, and grew up herself being reared by a succession of governesses. Her experience — that mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed and depended on others to help rear their children — is the implicit empirical anchor for the broader thesis. This is not mere anecdote but frames the book's central argument that maternal self-sacrifice as a norm is a modern-Western construction, not an evolutionary given.
author_quote: My melding of vocation with family has been supported by a steadfast partner, resilient children, and the generous hearts of alloparents—all the individuals other than me and my husband who helped us rear our children. As I would learn, mothers have worked for as long as our species has existed, and they have depended on others to help them rear their children.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy's own framing. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's autobiographical framing of the central thesis.

content: Hrdy on attachment theory: Bowlby's insights that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form attachment to a trusted figure, and that secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is essential for emotional development, rank among the greatest contributions of evolutionary-minded psychologists. BUT Bowlby's original framing (exclusive maternal attachment) produces dilemmas for mothers wanting self-confident children AND lives/careers of their own. Hrdy's refinement: 'one or more trusted caretakers' — plural attachment figures, not a single dyadic bond. This is load-bearing for how M9 Care/Alloparenting integrates with M3 Social Bonding in Cor's architecture.
author_quote: Bowlby demonstrated that babies are genetically programmed to seek and form an attachment to a trusted figure. Secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers is an essential aspect of emotional development in humans, just as it is in all other primates.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy's multi-attachment-figure refinement of Bowlby. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's synthesis of Bowlby extended to multiple attachment figures. Theoretical framing with substantial empirical backing from cross-cultural attachment research.

content: Infanticide by males as selective pressure: Even in normally gentle primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This creates selective pressure on mothers. Hrdy's specific hypothesis: female langurs' apparently promiscuous mating with invading males (even when pregnant/not ovulating) casts wide the web of possible paternity — males almost never attack infants they might have fathered. Males use past mating relations as a cue to attack or tolerate an infant. This is load-bearing for M14 Reproductive Motivation and for reading female sexuality in light of infanticide risk.
author_quote: Even in normally gentle and herbivorous primates like langurs and gorillas, other members of the same species can be a threat to infant survival every bit as hazardous as lurking predators. This was a new kind of selective pressure on mothers, one not previously dreamed of.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy's infanticide / mate-insurance hypothesis. source_type=primary (her own field research). evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's classic 1970s langur infanticide research + her hypothesis about female mating strategies. This is her foundational primary research.

content: Hrdy's central reframing of female sexuality: In the 1970s Darwinians widely assumed females were sexually passive and 'coy'. Female langurs were anything but — they solicited invading males or left their troop to find them, and mated with invaders even while pregnant and not ovulating. Hrdy's interpretation: mothers were insuring paternity uncertainty as an infanticide-avoidance strategy. This overturns the passive-female Darwinian framing and grounds M14 Reproductive Motivation in a specifically female-agency frame rather than a male-pursuit frame.
author_quote: In the early 1970s, it was still widely assumed by Darwinians that females were sexually passive and "coy." Female langurs were anything but. When bands of roving males approached the troop, females would solicit them or actually leave their troop to go in search of them. On occasion, a female mated with invaders even though she was already pregnant and not ovulating (something else nonhuman primates were not supposed to do).
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy's female agency reframing. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=clinical (field research). Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's 1970s langur field research. Published in Hrdy 1977 The Langurs of Abu.

content: Hrdy's elaboration of the infanticide mechanism: males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant. Mothers who cast wide the web of possible paternity increase the prospects of future survival for their offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females they have 'known' in the biblical sense. This is the specific behavioral rule that makes paternity confusion adaptive for mothers — it's not promiscuity as failure of pair-bonding but as insurance against infanticide.
author_quote: By casting wide the web of possible paternity, mothers could increase the prospects of future survival of offspring, since males almost never attack infants carried by females that, in the biblical sense of the word, they have "known." Males use past relations with the mother as a cue to attack or tolerate her infant.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy paternity-insurance hypothesis. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's 1970s original hypothesis on paternity-insurance function of promiscuous mating.

content: Hrdy's identification of infanticide as widespread across primate taxa: infanticide by males is documented across many primate species, establishing it as a recurrent evolutionary pressure shaping female reproductive strategy across primates broadly, not a pathological anomaly of a few species. This cross-taxon distribution is load-bearing for P1 Inclusive Fitness and for M14 Reproductive Motivation's architectural shaping by infanticide risk.
caveats: [R3 quote integrity] author_quote removed pending verbatim re-sourcing from the physical copy (book flagged in_physical_collection=true); the prior author_quote was non-verbatim and mismatched to the claim. [Content repaired 2026-07-18] The content field previously carried a fabricated pseudo-quote ('Studies of primates belonging to sixteen different primate genera, infanticide is often [a reproductive strategy]') - ungrammatical, bracket-inserted, wearing quote marks but never a verbatim Hrdy sentence. It has been excised and the claim restated at the granularity the comparative primatology literature supports: infanticide is documented across many primate species (reviews report on the order of two dozen to fifty-plus species across the primate order), not the unconfirmed 'sixteen genera' framing, which could not be verified in this work and was likely an artifact of the earlier extraction. evidence_quality='replicated' is retained for the general cross-taxon pattern (well established over decades, e.g. van Schaik & Janson 2000); no specific genus/species count is asserted in content. source_type='propagation' (Hrdy synthesizing the comparative literature). Re-source a verbatim Hrdy passage from the physical copy before restoring a primary author_quote.
scope: Hrdy synthesizing cross-primate infanticide observations across many primate species. Replicated in the comparative primatology literature over decades.

content: Hrdy on contingent maternal commitment: For cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to CARRY THROUGH with the enterprise — rearing offspring to independence. This is the foundational argument that maternal investment is context-dependent, not unconditional — mothers evaluate whether circumstances (including alloparent availability, food resources, and infant health) permit successful rearing, and adjust their investment accordingly. Load-bearing for M9 Care/Alloparenting and for reading maternal ambivalence as adaptive rather than pathological.
author_quote: Clearly, for cooperatively breeding mammals, a female's physical capacity to conceive and bear viable young is only a small part of the equation. She must also be able to carry through with the enterprise—rearing offspring to independence.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy contingent maternal commitment. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's contingent-commitment framing of maternal investment.

content: Hrdy on the compartmentalization error: maternal emotions (producing/nurturing/keeping offspring alive) have been viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of a woman — her sexuality and her ambition. This compartmentalized framing has nothing to do with how these emotions evolved. In the ancestral environment, the same female was simultaneously pursuing reproductive goals AND maternal goals AND resource goals AND social-position goals, with all of them integrated rather than competing. The modern fragmentation is cultural, not evolutionary.
author_quote: a woman's maternal emotions (those concerned with producing and nurturing offspring and keeping them alive) continued to be viewed as separate from and even antithetical to the rest of her—her sexuality and, particularly, her ambition. Yet the compartmentalized way we have learned to think about these emotions has nothing to do with how they evolved.
caveats: [Wave 3A-1 Book 6] Hrdy on compartmentalization error. source_type=primary. evidence_quality=theoretical. Pre-commit grep verified.
scope: Hrdy's framing of maternal emotions as integrated with broader female life-history strategy.

content: The constrained total energy expenditure model: total daily energy expenditure (TEE) increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher levels as the body adapts metabolically to maintain TEE within a narrow range. Tested in a multi-population doubly-labeled-water study (n=332 adults from Ghana, Jamaica, Seychelles, South Africa, and the US). Above moderate activity, each additional increment of ~100 counts per minute per day was associated with less than 50 kcal/day increase in TEE. The change point from positive slope to zero was 230 CPM/day. Load-bearing for M13 Energy Regulation: the body is homeostatically buffered against habitual activity variation, and exercise does not produce linear caloric deficits.
location: Pontzer et al. 2016 Current Biology 26:410-417, Abstract / Introduction
author_quote: Here we tested a Constrained total energy expenditure model, in which total energy expenditure increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher activity levels as the body adapts to maintain total energy expenditure within a narrow range. We compared total energy expenditure, measured using doubly labeled water, against physical activity, measured using accelerometry, for a large (n = 332) sample of adults living in five populations. After adjusting for body size and composition, total energy expenditure was positively correlated with physical activity, but the relationship was markedly stronger over the lower range of physical activity. For subjects in the upper range of physical activity, total energy expenditure plateaued, supporting a Constrained total energy expenditure model.
caveats: Pontzer et al. 2016 Current Biology primary-source statement of the Constrained TEE model. Tested against the competing Additive model using doubly-labeled water across five populations (Ghana, Jamaica, Seychelles, South Africa, US). Citation markers dropped from author_quote per the allowed normalization list. The underlying compensation mechanism at higher activity levels (non-muscular physiological activity contributing to activity energy expenditure 2) is presented as a hypothesis in the paper's Discussion section, not as a demonstrated finding.
scope: Multi-population cross-sectional doubly-labeled-water study (n=332 adults from five populations). The Constrained TEE finding is cross-population replicated but the causal mechanism for metabolic compensation (activity energy expenditure component 2) remains hypothesis rather than demonstrated.

content: Cross-population pattern: people in less socioeconomically developed populations — subsistence farmers and traditional hunter-gatherers — have total energy expenditures similar to those in more developed populations despite substantial differences in physical activity. Non-human mammals in the wild show the same pattern: wild and captive populations have similar TEE. These population-level comparisons suggest that total energy expenditure is an evolved, species-specific trait that is homeostatically buffered against variation in habitual physical activity. This is the foundational empirical pattern that the Constrained TEE model is designed to explain.
location: Pontzer et al. 2016, Introduction / Cross-population synthesis
author_quote: People in less socioeconomically developed populations, including subsistence farmers and traditional hunter-gatherers, have total energy expenditures similar to those in more developed populations despite substantial differences in physical activity. Mammals living in the wild, including non-human primate species, have total energy expenditures similar to captive populations. These population-level comparisons suggest that total energy expenditure is an evolved, species-specific trait that is homeostatically buffered against variation in habitual physical activity.
caveats: Pontzer 2016 Current Biology, cross-population synthesis section. Citation markers to references 6-8 dropped per allowed normalization.
scope: Synthesis of cross-population doubly-labeled-water data (human hunter-gatherer, subsistence farmer, and industrialized) plus cross-species wild-vs-captive mammalian data. The evolved-species-typical-trait framing is Pontzer's theoretical claim; the underlying cross-population TEE similarity is cross-lab replicated.

content: Pontzer's non-muscular compensation hypothesis: the component of activity energy expenditure that compensates for increased physical activity is unlikely to be purely muscular. When the analysis limits to subjects above 230 CPM/day, activity energy expenditure 2 (the compensatory component) is too large to be accounted for by reductions in standing, fidgeting, or peripheral limb movement alone. Pontzer hypothesizes that non-muscular physiological activity — reproductive activity, somatic maintenance, inflammation, immune system activity — is reduced when physical activity increases, absorbing the expected caloric deficit. This frames physical activity as a regulator of systemic energy allocation across multiple physiological domains, not merely as direct caloric expenditure.
location: Pontzer et al. 2016, Discussion section on activity energy expenditure components
author_quote: We hypothesize that non-muscular physiological activity contributes substantially to activity energy expenditure 2 and its adaptation to physical activity. Human studies and non-human animal models show that energy allocation across a broad range of physiological tasks, including reproductive activity and somatic maintenance, may be reduced when physical activity increases, resulting in decreased activity energy expenditure 2. Indeed, such physical activity-induced reduction in activity energy expenditure 2 could potentially contribute to the beneficial health effects of exercise, reducing energy expenditure on inflammation and detrimental immune system activity.
caveats: Pontzer 2016 Discussion section hypothesis. Tagged evidence_quality=theoretical because the compensation-via-non-muscular-physiological-activity claim is presented as hypothesis in the paper itself. Citation markers dropped per allowed normalization.
scope: Pontzer's theoretical hypothesis. Explicitly framed as a hypothesis in the paper, not a demonstrated finding. The supporting animal-model and cross-species data exist in the broader energetics literature but the specific causal chain in humans is not directly tested in the 2016 paper.

content: The Pontzer 2012 Hadza-energetics finding: despite dramatically greater physical activity (Hadza PAL ~1.78-2.26 vs Western PAL ~1.68-1.81), Hadza hunter-gatherers expend no more total daily energy than Western adults after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting are also similar across groups. This contradicted the then-dominant obesity hypothesis that Western lifestyles reduce caloric expenditure and motivated the Constrained TEE model developed in subsequent work. The implication: global obesity cannot be explained by Western sedentarism producing lower daily energy expenditure — Western and hunter-gatherer daily calorie burns are similar, so the obesity difference must lie primarily in energy intake and food composition.
location: Pontzer et al. 2012 PLoS ONE 7(7):e40503, Abstract
author_quote: As expected, physical activity level, PAL, was greater among Hadza foragers than among Westerners. Nonetheless, average daily energy expenditure of traditional Hadza foragers was no different than that of Westerners after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting were also similar among Hadza and Western groups. The similarity in metabolic rates across a broad range of cultures challenges current models of obesity suggesting that Western lifestyles lead to decreased energy expenditure.
caveats: Pontzer et al. 2012 PLoS ONE primary-source Hadza energetics finding. Single small-sample study that motivated the Constrained TEE program; later replicated across populations in Pontzer 2016. Formatting artifacts '±' replaced with '6' in source OCR; reconstruction in author_quote preserves the semantic content. Citation markers dropped per allowed normalization.
scope: Original Hadza TEE finding from a single small sample (n=30 Hadza adults: 13 men, 17 women). Cross-referenced against previously published Western and subsistence-farming data. Single-population study, but subsequently extended and replicated in the Pontzer 2016 five-population study. Tagged clinical because it is a single-site small-sample doubly-labeled-water measurement.
