The four-condition taxonomy in CONTENT is directly supported by the source ("Four situations are associated with allostatic load"): (1) frequent/repeated stress; (2) lack of adaptation to repeated stressors of the same type; (3) inability to shut off allostatic responses (prolonged response / delayed shut-down); (4) inadequate responses by some allostatic systems triggering compensatory increases in others. NOTE on a minor CONTENT overreach: the clause attributing allostatic load to "genetic load" as McEwen's wording reflects the 1993 paper's phrasing rather than the 1998 text; the 1998 paper instead states individual stress responses are determined by "genetic factors but also by behavioral and lifestyle choices" and lists diet, tobacco, alcohol, and exercise. Not flagged as a content defect since the substance (genetics + lifestyle + developmental factors modulate the stress response) is faithfully supported by the 1998 source. Source verified primary; QUARANTINED status can be lifted.
scope: Extends DC1 beyond the 1993 definition: the four conditions of allostatic load (repeated stress, failed adaptation, prolonged response, inadequate response) map directly onto Cor's cascade chains. Condition 4 (compensatory hyperactivity) is the mechanism behind DA3 cascading — when one system fails to respond, others overcompensate.

content: Allostasis is the ability to achieve stability through change — the body's active adjustment to anticipated demands. Unlike homeostasis (maintaining constant internal conditions), allostasis recognizes that the body actively shifts its operating parameters in response to predicted demands. The cost of this active adjustment, when chronically required, is allostatic load. Selye recognized 60 years earlier that stress mediators can both protect and damage — McEwen's contribution is formalizing this paradox.
author_quote: Over 60 years ago, Selye recognized the paradox that the physiologic systems activated by stress can not only protect and restore but also damage the body.
caveats: Author_quote replaced after full-text verification of the cited source (McEwen BS, "Protective and damaging effects of stress mediators," N Engl J Med 1998;338(3):171-179; PMID 9428819; DOI 10.1056/NEJM199801153380307). The PRIOR quote ("Hormones associated with stress and allostatic load protect the body in the short run and promote adaptation through allostasis, but in the long run allostatic load causes changes that can lead to disease.") was MIS-ATTRIBUTED and NON-VERBATIM: it does not appear anywhere in this NEJM 1998 paper (the phrase "short run" occurs nowhere in the text). It is a near-paraphrase of the abstract of a DIFFERENT McEwen paper — McEwen BS, Seeman T, "Protective and damaging effects of mediators of stress. Elaborating and testing the concepts of allostasis and allostatic load," Ann N Y Acad Sci 1999;896:30-47 (PMID 10681886), whose abstract reads "...protect the body in the short run and promote adaptation, but in the long run allostatic load causes changes in the body that lead to disease" — and even that wording differs from the stored version ("changes that can lead to disease"). The new quote is the verbatim opening sentence of the correct cited work and directly grounds the content's explicit claim that Selye recognized stress mediators can both protect and damage. The superscript reference numeral after "Selye" is omitted as a citation marker, not prose. The allostasis/allostatic-load definitions in the content are also verbatim-supported by the same paper: "Allostasis — the ability to achieve stability through change — is critical to survival" and "The price of this accommodation to stress can be allostatic load, which is the wear and tear that results from chronic overactivity or underactivity of allostatic systems." Prior QUARANTINED snippet-source flag is now resolved by full-text confirmation.
scope: Grounds the allostasis-allostatic load distinction for DC1: the same stress mediators that protect acutely produce disease chronically. This is not system failure — it is the cost of a system operating correctly but chronically outside its environment of adaptedness (P3).

content: Eaton & Konner analyzed nutritional properties of wild game and uncultivated vegetable foods and evaluated archaeological remains to reconstruct Paleolithic diet composition. Their model was derived from 69 game and wild vegetable items. Humanity has existed as a genus for about 2 million years, with evolutionary history making definitive contributions to current genetic composition partly in response to dietary influences. The resulting evolutionary discordance between ancestral and modern diets is proposed as a major source of chronic disease.
caveats: Audit R3: prior author_quote was non-verbatim; a proposed verbatim replacement was NOT independently confirmed (adversarial verifier refuted it: Could NOT independently confirm the proposed quote verbatim in the real source. Source = Eaton & Konner 1985, "Paleolithic Nutrition," NEJM ). Quote removed and source_type demoted to propagation pending verbatim re-sourcing. Context: Author_quote corrected from a non-verbatim paraphrase to the exact source text (R3 re-source)
scope: THE foundational text for P3 applied to diet: Eaton & Konner established the methodology of reconstructing ancestral conditions and comparing them to modern environments to identify mismatch. This paper launched the field of evolutionary medicine as applied to nutrition and chronic disease.

content: The Paleolithic nutrition model identifies specific discordances between ancestral and modern diets: higher protein intake, lower carbohydrate (especially refined), much higher fiber, lower sodium, higher potassium, higher calcium from non-dairy sources, and substantially lower sugar consumption. The fat profile differs in kind, not just quantity — ancestral fats were predominantly unsaturated while modern diets are dominated by saturated and trans fats. These specific nutritional parameters define the mismatch that drives metabolic disease.
caveats: Author_quote removed pending verbatim re-sourcing under R3. The prior author_quote ("The evolutionary history making definitive contributions to current genetic composition partly in response to dietary influences.") was a non-verbatim, ungrammatical paraphrase/mangling of a sentence reported in secondary summaries of Eaton & Konner 1985 (NEJM 312:283-289) — approximately "This phase of evolutionary history made definitive contributions to our current genetic composition, partly in response to dietary influences at that time." The DB version dropped "This phase of," altered "made" to "making," and omitted "our" and "at that time," so it was not verbatim and could not be confirmed against the primary text. It was also topically mismatched: the quote concerns genetic constitution, whereas the content claim concerns specific nutritional discordances (protein, carbohydrate, fiber, sodium, potassium, calcium, sugar, fat profile). The primary source could not be accessed (NEJM full text paywalled/HTTP 403; PubMed PMID 2981409 carries no abstract); every candidate "verbatim" sentence surfaced only via web-search summaries, which are presumptively contaminated. Source_type downgraded primary->propagation. The content remains a faithful synthesis of the well-known Eaton-Konner discordance model; note that several specific nutrient values were revised in the authors' 1997 and 2010 retrospectives.
scope: Grounds the specific M13 (energy regulation) mismatch parameters: the Paleolithic nutrition model identifies which dietary inputs have changed and in what direction. This provides the testable predictions — each nutritional discordance should correlate with specific metabolic pathologies.

content: The ACE Study identified seven categories of childhood adversity and found that more than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories. The graded dose-response relationship — where each additional ACE category incrementally increases risk — demonstrates that childhood adversity is cumulative rather than categorical. Persons with 4+ categories had 4-12 fold increased health risk, suggesting a threshold effect where the cascade becomes self-reinforcing.
author_quote: More than half of respondents reported at least one, and one-fourth reported two or more categories of childhood exposures.
caveats: Source: PubMed abstract + supplementary web data. Third extraction from same source — this one focuses on the prevalence and threshold findings rather than the disease outcomes.
scope: Extends the ACE evidence for DA7: the prevalence data (>50% have at least one ACE) means developmental calibration toward threat is the statistical norm, not the exception. The 4+ threshold for extreme risk suggests a cascade tipping point where DA3 (recurrent coupling) becomes self-sustaining.

content: The cross-fostering experiment definitively proved that the epigenetic differences are caused by maternal behavior, not genetic inheritance. Pups born to low-LG mothers but raised by high-LG mothers developed the low-stress phenotype of their foster mothers, and vice versa. The pharmacological reversal via histone deacetylase inhibitor demonstrated that the epigenetic marks are modifiable even in adulthood, establishing that developmental calibration is potentially reversible — a finding with profound therapeutic implications.
author_quote: methylation differences emerged over the first week of life, were reversed with cross-fostering, persisted into adulthood.
caveats: Source: PubMed abstract. This third extraction focuses on the cross-fostering design and reversibility — the most methodologically important findings. The pharmacological reversal opens a therapeutic pathway.
scope: Critical for DA7: developmental calibration is behaviorally programmed (not genetically determined) AND potentially reversible (not permanent). This means interventions that change the social environment can theoretically reprogram the epigenetic marks — grounding Cor's emphasis on environment modification rather than mechanism suppression.

content: Trivers models the natural selection of reciprocally altruistic behavior and shows how selection operates against cheaters. The human psychological system that regulates reciprocal altruism explains friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy as adaptations to regulate the altruistic system.
author_quote: A model is presented to account for the natural selection of what is termed reciprocally altruistic behavior.
caveats: Verified verbatim 2026-05-29: the author_quote is the exact opening sentence of the abstract of Trivers RL (1971) "The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism," Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, DOI 10.1086/406755. Confirmed character-for-character across multiple independent renderings of the published abstract (uchicago publisher-derived abstract text and R Discovery article page). The full abstract also corroborates the content claim: it explicitly lists "friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and some forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy can be explained as important adaptations to regulate the altruistic system." Prior QUARANTINE flag (snippet-sourced / presumptively contaminated, Codex audit 2026-04-09) is cleared; quote is genuine primary text. Note: the GreaterGood/Berkeley-hosted PDF is an image-scanned (JBIG2) copy not machine-readable, but the abstract text was confirmed via other sources.
scope: THE foundational text for M11 beyond kin: reciprocal altruism extends cooperation to non-relatives via a psychological system that tracks debts, detects cheaters, and motivates moralistic punishment.

content: Trivers presents three instances of reciprocal altruism: (1) cleaning symbioses between fish (cleaner wrasse and host grouper), where hosts refrain from eating cleaners despite opportunity; (2) warning cries in birds, reinterpreted as reciprocal altruism rather than kin selection; (3) human reciprocal altruism, the most complex form, regulated by an elaborate psychological system including friendship, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, and aspects of guilt.
author_quote: Three instances of altruistic behavior are discussed, the evolution of which the model can explain: (1) behavior involved in cleaning symbioses; (2) warning cries in birds: and (3) human reciprocal altruism.
caveats: REMEDIATED — Codex audit 2026-04-09. Original flagged CONTENT_QUOTE_FABRICATED. Quote replaced with verbatim text from Trivers 1971 PDF (abstract, p. 35). Content verified against full text at /tmp/pdfs/work66_trivers_1971.txt.
scope: Grounds DA8 for cooperation: reciprocal altruism has phylogenetic precursors but the human version adds uniquely complex cognitive tracking.

content: Humans have innate needs to be seen as attractive to others, forming the basis for shame. Shame and humiliation derive from attacks on social attractiveness. Internal shame experience derives from submissive defense strategies signaling awareness of lost social standing to limit damage from higher-ranking individuals.
author_quote: humans have innate needs to be seen as attractive to others. These needs form the basis for shame and mediate evaluations of social standing (status), social acceptance and social bonds.
caveats: Author_quote replaced with the verbatim passage from the published abstract of Gilbert (1997), Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, confirmed via NCBI eutils efetch (PMID 9210990) and the PubMed record. The prior author_quote ("humans have innate needs to be seen as attractive to others, which form the basis for shame.") was NON-VERBATIM: it stitched two separate abstract sentences and reworded "These needs form the basis for shame" into "which form the basis for shame," dropping the remainder of the sentence. The new quote is sourced from the published ABSTRACT, not the full text; full-text verification of supporting claims about submissive-defense signaling and shame/humiliation distinctions remains pending. Removed prior QUARANTINE flag re: the snippet quote, which is now resolved by verbatim re-sourcing.
scope: THE foundational text for M5 applied clinically: shame is an adaptive submissive signal triggered by loss of social attractiveness. Status threats activate defensive signaling (DA1).

content: Shame, humiliation, and guilt differ as evolved social strategies: shame focuses on the self (submissive appeasement), humiliation focuses on harm done by others (agonistic challenge), guilt focuses on specific actions and consequences for others (relationship repair). These map onto different adaptive responses to different types of social evaluation threat.
author_quote: For example, in shame the focus is on the self, while in humiliation the focus is on the harm done by others.
caveats: Author_quote replaced 2026-05-29 with the verbatim sentence from the Gilbert (1997) abstract (PMID 9210990, DOI 10.1111/j.2044-8341.1997.tb01893.x). The prior quote ("shame and humiliation differ: in shame the focus is on the self, in humiliation the focus is on the harm done by others.") was NON-VERBATIM — it fabricated the lead-in clause "shame and humiliation differ:" with a colon, dropped "For example,", and replaced "while in humiliation" with ", in humiliation". The corrected quote supports only the shame-vs-humiliation focus distinction. The fuller trichotomy in content (adding guilt) and the evolutionary social-strategy mapping (submissive appeasement / agonistic challenge / relationship repair) are author's broader theoretical framework, not contained in this single abstract sentence and remain theoretical. Quote verified against the PubMed abstract record only; full-text (Wiley) was paywalled (HTTP 402).
scope: Extends M5: three qualitatively different outputs (shame, humiliation, guilt) from domain-sensitive architecture (P2).

content: Trivers identifies conditions maximizing the chance reciprocal altruism will be selected for: (1) many altruistic situations in the lifetime of the altruists, (2) a given altruist repeatedly interacts with the same small set of individuals, and (3) pairs of altruists are exposed symmetrically to altruistic situations — each able to render roughly equivalent benefits at roughly equivalent costs. He elaborates these into biological parameters: long lifetime, low dispersal rate, mutual dependence, parental care, dominance hierarchy structure (less dominance facilitates reciprocity), and aid in combat. Selection discriminates against cheaters when cheating has later adverse effects that outweigh the benefit of not reciprocating — the altruist curtails future altruistic gestures to the cheater.
location: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Key conditions section.
caveats: REMEDIATED — Codex audit 2026-04-09. Original flagged CONTENT_QUOTE_FABRICATED. Quote cleared (was non-verbatim). Content rewritten: original three conditions (repeated interactions, individual recognition, cheater detection mechanism) were textbook synthesis, not Trivers's formulation. Now uses Trivers's actual conditions from p. 37 of the PDF. Verified against full text at /tmp/pdfs/work66_trivers_1971.txt.
scope: Grounds M11 cheater-detection requirement: cooperation is stable only when cheaters can be identified and punished. Links to Cosmides Wason task (P2) and Fehr/Gachter altruistic punishment (work #24).

content: Gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, and guilt are not arbitrary emotions but specific adaptations for regulating reciprocal altruism. Gratitude motivates reciprocation; sympathy motivates initial altruistic acts toward those in need; trust calibrates willingness to cooperate; suspicion monitors potential cheaters; guilt motivates relationship repair after defection. Each emotion functions as a regulatory mechanism within the reciprocal altruism system.
location: Q Rev Biol 46(1):35-57, 1971. DOI: 10.1086/406755. Human reciprocal altruism section.
author_quote: Regarding human reciprocal altruism, it is shown that the details of the psychological system that regulates this altruism can be explained by the model. Specifically, friendship, dislike, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, trust, suspicion, trustworthiness, aspects of guilt, and some forms of dishonesty and hypocrisy can be explained as important adaptations to regulate the altruistic system.
caveats: Author_quote replaced with the verbatim two-sentence passage from the paper's Abstract (Trivers 1971, Q Rev Biol 46(1):35, p. 35), confirmed against an image PDF of the original via OCR (two independent passes at 300 and 450 dpi) and corroborated by a third-party transcription of the key clause. The prior author_quote ("the details of the psychological system that regulates this altruism can be explained by the model.") was itself a genuine verbatim substring of this same abstract sentence but truncated and too thin to support the content's emotion-specific claim; the prior QUARANTINE/contamination flag (snippet-sourced, Codex audit 2026-04-09) is resolved by this full-text verification. Note: Trivers names these emotions broadly as regulatory adaptations; the content's per-emotion functional breakdown (gratitude->reciprocation, sympathy->initial altruism, suspicion->cheater-monitoring, guilt->repair) is consistent with Trivers' detailed discussion but is a framework synthesis, not a single verbatim list. Subsequent empirical work (Frank 1988; Fessler & Haley 2003) supports the functional interpretation.
scope: Grounds P2 (domain-sensitive adaptations) for social emotions: gratitude, trust, guilt etc. are not general-purpose feelings but domain-specific regulatory mechanisms for the cooperation system (M11). Each targets a specific failure mode of reciprocal altruism.

content: Social rank theory: humans evolved in social hierarchies where status determined access to resources and mates. Involuntary defeat strategy (IDS) is an evolved defensive response to status loss — when an organism loses rank and cannot escape, IDS produces behavioral inhibition, withdrawal, submissive signaling, and depressed mood. Depression in modern humans may reflect chronic activation of IDS in environments where status threats are persistent but escape or resolution is impossible.
location: Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, 1997. PMID: 9210990. Social rank and IDS sections.
author_quote: Shame and humiliation are associated with attacks on, and losses of, social attractiveness.
caveats: Author_quote verified verbatim against the published abstract of Gilbert P (1997), "The evolution of social attractiveness and its role in shame, humiliation, guilt and therapy," Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147 (PMID 9210990; DOI 10.1111/j.2044-8341.1997.tb01893.x). Confirmed via PubMed (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9210990) and corroborated by WebSearch of the Wiley/Semantic Scholar listing. Capitalization restored to match the source ("Shame" was previously lowercased as a mid-sentence excerpt); wording, order, and punctuation are otherwise identical and unaltered. The quote directly supports the shame/social-attractiveness facet of the content. NOTE: the broader Involuntary Defeat Strategy / social-rank-theory framing in the content/scope is synthesis drawing on Gilbert's wider work (and Price, Sloman) rather than a verbatim claim from this single abstract; full-text confirmation of IDS-specific passages was not obtained (publisher full text is paywalled, HTTP 402), so that framing remains propagation-level. Prior QUARANTINED snippet-contamination flag is cleared for the quote itself, which is now verbatim-confirmed.
scope: Grounds M5-to-M1 cascade: status loss (M5) activates threat management (M1) via the involuntary defeat strategy. In modern environments (P3), chronic status threats without resolution possibilities keep IDS activated, producing clinical depression. This is the M5 mismatch pathway to depression.

content: Shame derives from an evolved submissive defense where the organism signals awareness of lost social standing to limit damage from higher-ranking individuals. The signal function of shame is appeasement: by displaying shame (gaze aversion, postural collapse, blushing), the organism communicates acceptance of lower rank and reduces the probability of continued attack. This is adaptive in hierarchical contexts but becomes pathological when chronically activated by modern status comparison (social media, workplace evaluation, academic competition).
location: Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, 1997. PMID: 9210990. Shame mechanism section.
author_quote: The internal experiences of shame are derived from submissive strategies where one seeks to signal to others awareness of loss of social standing and limit possible damage.
caveats: Quote verified verbatim against the published abstract of Gilbert (1997), "The evolution of social attractiveness and its role in shame, humiliation, guilt and therapy," Br J Med Psychol 70(2):113-147, retrieved from PubMed (PMID 9210990) on 2026-05-29. The prior stored quote was a near-verbatim but defective rendering: it dropped the verb "are" (yielding the agrammatical "shame derived from submissive strategies" instead of the published "shame are derived from submissive strategies") and lowercased the sentence-initial "The". Corrected to the exact published wording. NOTE: the quote is sourced from the paper's ABSTRACT, not the full-text "Shame mechanism section" cited in the location field — full text was paywalled (Wiley HTTP 402), so the body-text location remains unverified. The CONTENT's extension to "chronic activation by modern status comparison (social media, workplace evaluation, academic competition)" is Cor's clinical/modern application and is NOT Gilbert's wording; the verbatim quote supports only the evolved-submissive-signal thesis. Lifts the prior "QUARANTINED — snippet-sourced, presumptively contaminated" flag: the quote is now confirmed clean from the primary abstract.
scope: Grounds DA1 for M5: shame is a defensive signal, not a pathology. It becomes harmful not because the signal is wrong but because modern environments produce chronic status threats (P3) that keep the appeasement system activated (DA5 over-activation).

content: Neocortex ratio (neocortex volume / rest-of-brain volume) predicts mean group size across 38 primate genera with r²=0.764 (t34=10.35, P<0.001). The regression equation log10(N) = 0.093 + 3.389·log10(CR) yields a predicted human group size of ~148, matching ethnographic data. Human neocortex ratio = 4.10.
location: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, Table 1 and regression analysis
author_quote: Group size is found to be a function of relative neocortical volume, but the ecological variables are not. This is interpreted as evidence in favour of the social intellect theory and against the ecological theories.
caveats: 95% CI of 100-230 reported in 1993 follow-up. Lindenfors et al 2021 Bayesian reanalysis found wider CIs (4-520). Human value of 148.1 appears as empirical data point in Table 1, not as regression prediction. See work 124 / ext 619 for the formal challenge to the human extrapolation; the primate regression itself (this row) is not disputed.
scope: 38 primate genera, cross-species comparative

content: Ecological variables fail to predict neocortex ratio. Percentage fruit in diet is unrelated. Range size and day journey length correlate in raw form but collapse to near zero when body mass is partialled out (residual r²=0.017 for range, r²<0.001 for day journey). Extractive foraging also fails once anthropoids are analyzed separately.
location: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, ecological analysis section
author_quote: even if it were true that energetic considerations constrain brain size, a proper functional explanation must still be given to explain why brains grow to the size they do.
caveats: Ecological hypotheses tested against same dataset as social hypothesis. Design cannot exclude combined ecological-social drivers.
scope: 38 primate genera

content: The number of neocortical neurons limits information-processing capacity, which constrains the number of relationships an individual can monitor simultaneously. The constraint operates on relationship structure and quality, not raw number of dyads.
author_quote: the number of neocortical neurons limits the organism's information-processing capacity and that this then limits the number of relationships that an individual can monitor simultaneously.
caveats: Mechanism connecting neocortex volume to social cognition is inferred, not directly demonstrated in this paper.
scope: Theoretical claim grounded in cross-species data

content: The regression slope of 3.389 (greater than 1) indicates large groups are created by combining smaller grooming cliques, not by uniformly expanding the social network. The cognitive limit lies in maintaining clique-internal relationship quality, not total relationship count.
location: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, discussion of slope
author_quote: large groups are created by welding together sets of smaller grooming cliques
caveats: Clique structure interpretation derived from slope analysis, not direct observation of clique formation.
scope: 38 primate genera

content: Female group size (r²=0.568) is a worse predictor of neocortex ratio than total group size (r²=0.764), indicating the cognitive constraint operates on total group membership, not just the reproductively relevant female core.
location: Journal of Human Evolution 22(6):469-493, female group size analysis
author_quote: the data suggest that the information overload occurs in terms of the structure of relationships within tightly bonded grooming cliques rather than in terms of the total number of dyads within the group as a whole.
caveats: Female group size data available for fewer genera than total group size data.
scope: 38 primate genera

content: Stepwise regression on 24 anthropoid primate species with 9 brain volume indices confirms neocortex ratio as the single most powerful predictor of group size. Independent contrasts analysis: r²=0.395, F(1,22)=15.39, P=0.001. No other brain index makes a significant contribution after neocortex ratio is included.
location: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, Table 2 and stepwise regression section. DOI: 10.1002/(SICI)1520-6505(1998)6:5<178::AID-EVAN5>3.0.CO;2-8
author_quote: Neocortex ratio is thus the single most powerful predictor of group size in these species.
caveats: Independent contrasts r² lower (0.395) than raw genus-level r² (0.764) from 1992 paper, as expected when controlling for phylogeny.
scope: 24 anthropoid primate species

content: Relative neocortex volume correlates with group size but NOT range area, while relative hippocampus size shows the reverse pattern (correlates with range but NOT group size). This double dissociation demonstrates that brain evolution is mosaic: specific brain components serve specific functions, not general intelligence.
location: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, hippocampus section, citing Barton & Purvis
author_quote: brain evolution has not been a history of simple expansion in total volume. Rather, brain evolution has been mosaic in character, with both the rate and the extent of evolution having varied between components of the system.
caveats: Double dissociation reported from Barton & Purvis analysis, not original to this paper.
scope: Cross-primate comparative

content: Human social groups cluster at characteristic values of approximately 5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000 with virtually no overlap in variance between layers. These represent stable points in the degrees of familiarity and correspond to support clique, sympathy group, band, clan/village, mega-band, and tribe respectively.
author_quote: the various human groups that can be identified in any society seem to cluster rather tightly around a series of values (5, 12, 35, 150, 500, and 2,000) with virtually no overlap in the variance around these characteristic values.
caveats: Ethnographic data drawn from small-scale societies. Layer sizes reported as descriptive clustering, not from formal statistical breakpoint analysis.
scope: Human ethnographic data across hunter-gatherer and horticultural societies

content: The social brain constraint is about ability to manipulate social information, not simply to remember individuals. Apes show grade-shifted cognitive demands per relationship compared to monkeys: apes are good psychologists (they read minds via theory of mind), while monkeys are good ethologists (they read behavior).
location: Evolutionary Anthropology 6(5):178-190, discussion of cognitive mechanisms
author_quote: there is no intrinsic reason to suppose that memory per se is the issue. The social brain hypothesis is about the ability to manipulate information, not simply to remember it.
caveats: Ape-monkey cognitive grade distinction based on tactical deception rates and theory of mind evidence, both indirect measures.
scope: Primate comparative cognition

content: Ethnographic data from hunter-gatherer and horticultural societies validates the ~150 predicted by the primate neocortex regression (95% CI 100-230). The clan/village organizational level consistently clusters at this value, supporting the social brain hypothesis prediction for human-scale groups.
author_quote: Because of the structural complexity of postagricultural societies, I considered only traditional hunter-gatherer and small-scale horticultural societies. Although census data on such societies are limited, those that are available suggest that there is indeed a consistent group size in the region of 150 individuals (Fig. 7).
caveats: Author_quote replaced under R3: the prior quote ("Conventional wisdom over the past 160 years in the cognitive and neurosciences has assumed that brains evolved to process factual information about the world.") IS genuinely verbatim — it is the opening sentence of Dunbar (1998) — but it was MISMATCHED to this row's content. The opening sentence states the paper's general thesis (brains evolved for social, not merely factual/ecological, processing) and does not support the specific claim about ethnographic validation of ~150 via Figure 7. It has been replaced with the verbatim passage that does support the claim. Note on the content: Dunbar's body text gives the predicted human group size only as "in the order of 150"; the 95% CI of 100-230 is shown graphically (the Fig. 7 caption notes "95% confidence intervals shown as dashed lines") rather than printed numerically in the body, so the explicit 100-230 figure derives from reading Fig. 7 / downstream citation. The CI is wide and the ~150 is a central tendency, not a hard limit; among hunter-gatherers the relevant unit is the clan (overnight-camp set), and among settled horticulturalists the village.
scope: Human ethnographic validation of primate neocortex regression

content: The social brain hypothesis takes two distinct forms across taxa. In primates: a quantitative relationship where group size is a monotonic function of brain size. In all other mammals and birds: a qualitative relationship where pair-bonded species have categorically larger brains than non-pair-bonded species.
location: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, abstract and introduction. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289. PMID: 19575315
author_quote: In primates, there is a quantitative relationship between brain size and social group size (group size is a monotonic function of brain size)... In other mammals and birds, the relationship is a qualitative one: Large brains are associated with categorical differences in mating system.
caveats: Abstract-limited for body text. Core claims verified from PubMed abstract and ResearchGate preview.
scope: Cross-taxa review: primates, carnivores, ungulates, bats, birds

content: Anthropoid primates generalized the bonding processes that characterize monogamous pair-bonds to non-reproductive relationships (friendships), creating a unique quantitative brain-group size relationship not seen in any other taxon. This explains why primate sociality is qualitatively different from all other mammals.
location: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, central argument. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289
author_quote: anthropoid primates may have generalized the bonding processes that characterize monogamous pairbonds to other non-reproductive relationships ('friendships'), thereby giving rise to the quantitative relationship between group size and brain size that we find in this taxon.
caveats: Theoretical claim. The mechanism by which pair-bond cognition was generalized is not directly demonstrated. Abstract-limited.
scope: Evolutionary interpretation of primate social cognition

content: The primary cognitive cost of pair-bonding is behavioral coordination and synchrony (scheduling, conflict resolution, spatial proximity maintenance), not mate choice optimization. This coordination demand requires perspective-taking capacities that may have provided the substrate for theory of mind.
location: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, Table I and discussion. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289
author_quote: the demands of behavioural coordination that are the more likely
caveats: Abstract-limited. Coordination vs mate-choice distinction based on comparative analysis, not direct experimental test.
scope: Theoretical analysis of pair-bonding cognitive demands

content: The phase shift from qualitative (pair-bonding) to quantitative (group-size) social brain processing likely occurred in the Eocene, coinciding with dietary shifts from insectivory to frugivory that may have created ecological conditions favoring larger social groups in early primates.
location: Annals of Human Biology 36(5):562-572, evolutionary timing section. DOI: 10.1080/03014460902960289
caveats: Abstract-limited. Eocene timing is inferred from phylogenetic evidence, not directly dated. Quote not available from accessible text.
scope: Evolutionary timing of primate social brain transition

content: Across five vertebrate taxa (carnivores, ungulates, bats, birds, primates), pair-bonded species consistently have larger relative brain sizes than non-pair-bonded species. Fisher combined probability test: chi-squared(10)=48.04, p<<0.001. The effect holds even excluding primates: chi-squared(8)=46.42, p<0.001.
location: Science 317(5843):1344-1347, DOI: 10.1126/science.1145463. PMID: 17823343. Companion data in Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976).
author_quote: recent analyses suggest that it may have been the particular demands of the more intense forms of pairbonding that was the critical factor that triggered this evolutionary development
caveats: Science paper abstract-limited; statistics verified from companion open-access Proceedings B paper (Shultz & Dunbar 2007).
scope: 86 carnivores, 69 artiodactyls, 45 primates, 135 birds, 54 bats

content: Primates are the sole exception to the pair-bonding rule: only in primates does group size (not pair-bonding) predict brain size. Strong positive correlation between group size and brain size in primates (lambda=0.80, F(1,40)=8.14, p<0.01). No such relationship in carnivores (p=0.80) or artiodactyls (p=0.58).
location: Science 317(5843):1344-1347 and Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976), PGLS analysis
author_quote: Primate sociality is based on bonded relationships of a kind that are found only in pairbonds in other taxa.
caveats: Primate exceptionalism claim based on phylogenetically controlled analysis (PGLS). Strepsirhine primates do NOT show the anthropoid pattern.
scope: 5 vertebrate taxa, phylogenetically controlled

content: In birds, lifelong pair-bonds (not annual re-pairing) predict larger brains. Bi-parental care does not drive the effect. The cognitive demand is specifically about maintaining long-term bonded relationships, not mate choice or parental coordination per se.
location: Science 317(5843):1344-1347 and Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B, bird analysis
caveats: Bird data provides clean test because pair-bonding and bi-parental care can be disentangled. Quote not available from abstract-limited access.
scope: 135 bird species

content: Anthropoid primates co-opted pair-bond bonding mechanisms for group-level social relationships. The everyday relationships of anthropoid primates involve a form of bondedness found only in reproductive pair-bonds in other taxa. This unique generalization created qualitatively different primate sociality.
author_quote: the everyday relationships of anthropoid primates involve a form of 'bondedness' that is only found elsewhere in reproductive pairbonds.
caveats: Theoretical interpretation of cross-taxa comparative data. The mechanism of co-option is inferred, not directly demonstrated.
scope: Evolutionary interpretation across 5 vertebrate taxa

content: Anthropoid primates differ significantly from all other taxa in proportion of species with bonded social structure (chi-squared(2)=8.49, p=0.01). Strepsirhine primates do NOT differ from ungulates and carnivores (chi-squared(2)=1.89, p=0.39). The bonding generalization is specific to anthropoids, not all primates.
location: Shultz & Dunbar 2007 Proc B (PMC2274976), bonded relationships analysis
author_quote: These results undermine conventional notions of what constitutes social complexity. Indeed, we doubt that many would have seriously suggested that pairbonded social systems are more complex (and by implication, more cognitively demanding) than large polygamous or promiscuously mating groups.
caveats: Quote from companion Proc B paper (open access), not the Science paper itself.
scope: Anthropoid vs strepsirhine vs non-primate comparison

content: Personal social networks consist of hierarchically inclusive nested layers of approximately 5/15/50/150 individuals, each layer roughly 3x the previous. Support group (~5): individuals from whom one would seek personal advice in severe distress. Sympathy group (~15): people whose sudden death would be greatly upsetting, contacted at least monthly. Affinity group (~50): casual but close friends. Active network (~150): total recognized and annually interacted with.
location: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8295.2011.02061.x. PMID: 22506741. Abstract-limited.
author_quote: Each layer increases relationship numbers by an approximate multiple of 3 (5-15-50-150) but decreasing levels of intimacy (strong, medium, and weak ties) and frequency of interaction.
caveats: Paper is behind paywall; extraction from abstract and citing sources. Layer sizes are empirical central tendencies from multiple prior studies (Hill & Dunbar 2003, Zhou et al 2005, Roberts et al 2009), synthesized here rather than newly collected.
scope: Theoretical integration of empirical social network data

content: At each social layer, the benefits of adding more relationships are asymptotic (diminishing returns), while the costs of maintenance — primarily time — are roughly linear with relationship count. The intersection of these curves creates natural breakpoints that generate the layered structure. This is a cost-benefit explanation for why Dunbar layers exist.
location: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8295.2011.02061.x. Abstract-limited.
author_quote: At each layer, the benefits are asymptotic but the costs of maintaining a relationship at that level (most obviously, the time that has to be invested in servicing it) are roughly linear with the number of relationships.
caveats: Cost-benefit model is theoretical. Time costs assumed linear without direct measurement in this paper.
scope: Theoretical framework for social network structure

content: Approximately 40% of available social time is devoted to the innermost 5 people (support clique), and another 20% to the next 10 (completing the sympathy group of 15). Two-thirds of total social time goes to just 15 people, despite having ~150 in the active network.
location: British Journal of Psychology 103(2):149-168, citing Roberts et al and other empirical sources
caveats: Time allocation data synthesized from prior empirical studies, not newly collected in this paper. Quote not available from abstract-limited access.
scope: Human time allocation across social network layers

content: Trust is the proximal psychological mechanism mediating social layer structure. Trade-offs at each layer are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and trust is itself a function of time invested. Trust operates as a cognitive heuristic that calibrates relationship investment to expected reciprocity at each layer.
author_quote: psychologically, these trade-offs are related to the level of trust in a relationship, and that this is itself a function of the time invested in the relationship.
caveats: Trust-as-mechanism claim is theoretical. Abstract-limited access.
scope: Theoretical: trust as mediator of social network structure

content: Mean Facebook friend count matches Dunbar's number prediction. Sample 1 (N=2000, nationally stratified UK): mean=155.2 friends (z=0.20, p=0.842 vs prediction of 150, 95% CI=100-200). Sample 2 (N=1375, nationally stratified UK professionals): mean=182.8 (z=1.29, p=0.198). Only 14.2% and 13.4% respectively had more than 300 friends.
location: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.150292. PMID: 26909163. PMC4736918. Full open-access text.
author_quote: The social brain hypothesis has suggested that natural social network sizes may have a characteristic size in humans. This is determined in part by cognitive constraints and in part by the time costs of servicing relationships.
caveats: First randomized stratified population sample for this question. Facebook friend count measured on categorical scales, not exact counts. Study design is cross-sectional.
scope: N=3375 UK adults, two independent stratified samples

content: Online inner social layers replicate offline sizes exactly. Support clique (crisis contacts): mean=4.1, not significantly different from offline values of 3.8+/-2.29 (z=0.13, p=0.897) or generic value of 5 (z=0.39, p=0.694). Sympathy group (close friends): mean=13.6, not different from 11.3+/-6.19 (z=0.37, p=0.711) or 15 (z=0.23, p=0.818).
location: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, inner layer analysis
author_quote: We can only interact coherently with a very small number of other people (about three, in fact) at any one time.
caveats: Inner layer data from Sample 1 only. Self-report measures for crisis contacts and close friends.
scope: N=2000 UK adults, online inner circle replication

content: Only 27.6% of Facebook friends are considered genuine (close) friends, with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%. Large online networks add only loose acquaintances, not close friends. People with unusually large networks do not increase close friendships but add weakly-defined acquaintances.
location: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, genuine friends analysis
author_quote: On average, respondents in Sample 1 considered that only 27.6% of their Facebook friends could be considered 'genuine' (i.e. close) friends, with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%.
caveats: Genuineness is self-reported. Definition of genuine/close left to respondent interpretation.
scope: N=2000 UK adults

content: Face-to-face contact is required to prevent friendships from decaying through the network layers and eventually becoming mere acquaintances. Social media may slow the natural rate of decay but cannot substitute for in-person interaction. This directly confirms that the bonding system requires physical co-presence that technology cannot replace.
author_quote: it may be that face-to-face meetings are required from time to time to prevent friendships, in particular, sliding down through the network layers and eventually slipping over the edge of the 150 layer into the category of acquaintances.
caveats: Face-to-face requirement is inferred from cross-sectional data, not from longitudinal tracking of friendship decay with/without in-person contact.
scope: Mismatch implication: technology cannot substitute for evolved bonding requirements

content: Age strongly predicts total network size (r=-0.972, p=0.006) with 18-24 year olds averaging 282 friends, but inner layers show minimal age variation (support clique: r=-0.837, p=0.077; sympathy group: r=-0.042, p=0.947). The cognitive/time constraint on intimate relationships is stable across ages even as total network size varies.
location: Royal Society Open Science 3(1):150292, age effects analysis
author_quote: social media may function mainly to prevent friendships decaying over time in the absence of opportunities for face-to-face contact.
caveats: Cross-sectional age data cannot distinguish cohort effects from developmental changes. Younger cohorts may have different social media usage patterns.
scope: Age stratification across N=3375 UK adults

content: Tomasello cites Dunbar 1998: primate brain size correlates most strongly not with physical ecology but with social group size (as proxy for social complexity). Primates' social cognition is aimed mainly at competition (Machiavellian intelligence) — tracking dominance and affiliative relationships that affect competition for food and mates. This frames Dunbar's cognitive constraint as operating specifically through competitive social tracking.
location: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 76-77 (lines 2987-2996 in text file)
author_quote: Dunbar (1998), for example, documented that primate brain size correlates most strongly not with primates' physical ecology but, rather, with their social group size (as a proxy for social complexity).
caveats: Tomasello frames the social brain finding primarily as supporting Machiavellian intelligence, not the bonding interpretation Dunbar later emphasized. The competitive framing misses the bonding/pair-bond generalization that Dunbar & Shultz (2007) identified.
scope: Cross-reference: Tomasello citing Dunbar on primate social cognition

content: Tomasello discusses the social brain hypothesis as supporting evidence for the evolution of human cooperation. Gowlett et al. (2012) traced brain-group size correlation across human evolution and found an especially big jump at ~400kya (Homo heidelbergensis), coinciding with Tomasello's hypothesized joint intentionality transition. However, Tomasello notes the hypothesis provides only a very general indication: group size is a gross indicator of social complexity and brain size a gross indicator of cognitive capacities.
location: A Natural History of Human Thinking (2014), pp. 133-134 (lines 5168-5185 in text file)
author_quote: group size is only a very gross indicator of social complexity (Dunbar focuses on the greater numbers of social relationships and reputations to be kept track of), and brain size is only a very gross indicator of cognitive capacities, so the social brain hypothesis gives us only a very general indication of the actual processes involved on either side of the correlation.
caveats: Tomasello's caveat about the social brain hypothesis being too general is methodological, not a substantive challenge. He accepts the correlation while arguing for more specific process accounts.
scope: Cross-reference: Tomasello integrating Dunbar with joint intentionality theory

content: Henrich cites Dunbar 1998 on the social brain hypothesis in the context of arguing that human intelligence is collective rather than individual. Endnote references place Dunbar alongside Byrne and Whiten (1992) and Humphrey (1976) as proponents of the Machiavellian intelligence view that Henrich then challenges: cultural evolution, not individual social cognition, is what makes humans smart. Group size matters for Henrich primarily as a driver of cumulative cultural complexity, not through Dunbar's cognitive constraint mechanism.
location: The Secret of Our Success (2016), endnotes 7 and 19 (lines 12444, 12498), main text ch. 2 and ch. 12
caveats: Dunbar references in endnotes only, not substantive main-text engagement. Henrich's argument reframes group size as cultural variable, not directly as Dunbar's cognitive constraint. No direct quote available — citation is bibliographic.
scope: Cross-reference: Henrich citing Dunbar in cultural evolution context

content: Hrdy cites Dunbar & Shultz (2007) on the correlation between large brain size and long juvenile/adolescent life phases. The neocortex discussion in Mothers and Others frames brain evolution through alloparenting: humans' large neocortex enables evaluation of allomaternal trustworthiness, while also creating the extended dependency that necessitates cooperative breeding. This connects Dunbar's social brain to Hrdy's cooperative breeding hypothesis as complementary explanations.
location: Mothers and Others (2009), endnotes ch. 8 note 4 (line 13045), main text pp. 39-40 (lines 1580-1614, 1795-1801, 2940-2943)
author_quote: Humans' large neocortex is an obvious possibility. Not only do human mothers need more help getting big-brained babies through narrow birth canals but they are better able to evaluate the costs and benefits of their own behavior.
caveats: Dunbar's social brain hypothesis is cited bibliographically rather than substantively engaged with. Hrdy's neocortex discussion focuses on maternal/alloparental functions rather than Dunbar's group-size cognitive constraint.
scope: Cross-reference: Hrdy citing Dunbar & Shultz in cooperative breeding/alloparenting context

content: Plant growth is often constrained by the scarcest essential nutrient in the soil, not by the average availability of nutrients. Adding more of an abundant nutrient does not, on its own, fully compensate for deficiency in a scarce one. Cor adopts the structural form of this claim as a heuristic for mechanism resolution: well-being is often bottlenecked by severe unresolved deficits in individual mechanisms and is not well described as a simple average across mechanism states. The agronomy content does not transfer; the bottleneck framing does. Cross-system buffering effects do exist in the human architecture (handled by DA3), so this is a heuristic about bottlenecks, not a claim of strict biochemical non-substitutability.
location: Passim (the Law of the Minimum is the central thesis of the work)
caveats: The analogy is structural, not substantive. Liebig's Law applies to plant nutrient uptake; DA9 applies to human mechanism resolution. The claim that mechanisms are non-substitutable follows from P2 (domain-sensitivity) independently of the agricultural precedent — Liebig provides the historical form, not the evidence.
scope: Structural analogy only. DA9 adopts the form of Liebig's Law (system bounded by scarcest essential input) but the domain is motivational-emotional mechanisms, not soil nutrients. The agronomy evidence is independently well-established (replicated across 180 years of agricultural science).

content: Seven distinct emotional systems identified with specific neuroanatomy and neurochemistry: SEEKING (VTA/NAcc/lateral hypothalamus, DA+), RAGE (medial amygdala→BNST→hypothalamus→PAG, substance P+), FEAR (central amygdala→hypothalamus→dorsal PAG, glutamate+/CRF+), LUST (cortico-medial amygdala/BNST/preoptic, steroids+), CARE (anterior cingulate/BNST/preoptic/VTA, oxytocin+/prolactin+), PANIC (anterior cingulate/BNST/dorsomedial thalamus/PAG, opioids−/oxytocin−/CRF+), PLAY (dorsomedial diencephalon/parafascicular/PAG, opioids+/−). Each mapped in Fig. 2 with specific neurochemical modulators.
location: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(9):1791-1804, p. 1795, Fig. 2. DOI: 10.1016/j.neubiorev.2011.08.003
author_quote: It has become increasingly clear during the past half century that primary-process affective mechanisms are concentrated in ancient subcortical midline brain regions that are anatomically and neurochemically, and hence, evolutionarily, similar in all mammalian species.
caveats: Full text accessed via open-access PDF. Seven-system taxonomy is Panksepp's mature formulation, evolved from the four systems in the 1982 paper.
scope: All mammals studied via ESB — comprehensive cross-species mapping of 7 emotional circuits

content: Electrical brain stimulation (ESB) of specific subcortical regions produces coherent emotional behaviors in all mammals tested. Animals given control over ESB self-select: they turn off stimulation evoking fear/anger responses and turn on stimulation generating playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness, and maternal care. This reward/punishment valence demonstrates genuine affective experience, not mere behavioral reflexes.
author_quote: When we artificially activate brain emotion-behavior generating circuits, animals rapidly learn to turn off ESB that evokes fear- and anger-type responses, and they turn on brain stimulation that generates playful sounds, exploration, sexual eagerness and maternal care.
caveats: Full text accessed. ESB evidence spans 40+ years of Panksepp's research program across rats, cats, guinea pigs, and other mammals.
scope: Cross-species ESB evidence for affective valence of subcortical emotional circuits

content: Lower subcortical regions, especially the periaqueductal gray (PAG), are more important for generating emotional feelings than cortical regions. Three key properties of the PAG: (1) lowest ESB energy to obtain powerful emotional changes, (2) smallest brain damage compromising consciousness, (3) most massive convergence of brain emotional systems. Lesions of higher areas do not diminish emotional responses from lower areas, while damage to lower areas dramatically compromises emotional actions generated from higher areas.
author_quote: Clearly lesions of higher areas do not diminish the emotional responses from lower areas, while damage to lower areas can dramatically compromise emotional actions generated from higher areas.
caveats: Full text accessed. PAG hierarchy claim based on lesion and stimulation studies across multiple species.
scope: Hierarchical control: subcortical primacy in emotional generation

content: All seven emotional systems survive radical neo-decortication (complete surgical removal of the cerebral cortex). Decorticate animals retain all emotional-instinctual urges intact, though their capacity to learn new instrumental behaviors is severely impaired. ESB of subcortical regions in humans produces intense affective experiences; neocortical stimulation never produces such emotional states.
author_quote: Never have such profound emotional states been provoked by stimulating neocortical regions.
caveats: Full text accessed. Decortication evidence from animal studies; human ESB evidence from Heath (1996) and Panksepp (1985) clinical studies.
scope: Critical test: emotional systems are subcortically organized and cortex-independent

content: Rats produce 50-kHz ultrasonic chirps during play that are homologous to human laughter. These joyful sounds are most abundant during rough-and-tumble play and human-administered tickling. The affective valence is confirmed by approach behavior and conditioned place preferences. This demonstrates that positive social affect is a fundamental feature of mammalian brain organization, not a human-unique construction.
author_quote: When made hungry for play, rats pounce on each other, engendering bouts of chasing and wrestling, all accompanied by joyful 50 kHz chirps signaling an intense social joy.
caveats: Full text accessed. 50-kHz = laughter homology is Panksepp's interpretation, debated by some researchers. Cross-species homology argument rests on functional and neurochemical parallels, not structural identity.
scope: Positive affect evidence: rat ultrasonic vocalizations as joy markers

content: Three convergent lines of evidence demonstrate subcortical affective states: (i) mammals are attracted to the same environmental rewards and drugs of abuse as humans; (ii) human emotional feelings depend on subcortical brain systems where evolutionarily homologous instinctual neural systems exist; (iii) artificial activations of deep brain emotional systems are liked and disliked by animals, as measured by approach and avoidance measures.
caveats: Full text accessed via University of Pennsylvania open-access PDF. The three lines of evidence are Panksepp's convergent validation framework for cross-species affective states.
scope: Convergent evidence framework for subcortical affect across mammals

content: Three empirical criteria for determining existence of emotional feelings in animals, all fulfilled: (1) neural circuits must exist that activate coherent emotional behaviors, (2) artificial arousal of such systems must generate conditioned approach/escape/avoidance, (3) key neurochemistries and brain activation patterns must correlate with predicted affective changes in humans. These criteria have been fulfilled for multiple brain systems across all mammals studied.
author_quote: These criteria have been fulfilled or approximated for a variety of brain systems that exist in all mammals studied so far.
caveats: Full text accessed. Criteria constitute Panksepp's empirical test for animal consciousness, not a consensus neuroscience position.
scope: Empirical criteria for animal emotional experience

content: Three levels of consciousness: primary-process (raw sensory/emotional feelings, subcortical), secondary (thoughts about experiences via perceptual images, learning/memory), and tertiary (thoughts about thoughts, awareness of awareness, largely human-specific, requires neocortical linguistic-symbolic processing). Affective consciousness is primary-process and subcortical; those who deny animal consciousness are thinking about tertiary cortical variants and generalizing from perceptual consciousness to affective consciousness.
author_quote: Those who are not willing to give animals any consciousness are probably thinking about the tertiary human-typical linguistic variants. They may also be generalizing too readily from human perceptual consciousness, which is clearly dependent on neocortical functions, to an affective consciousness whose locus of control is largely sub-neocortical.
caveats: Full text accessed. Three-level framework is Panksepp's theoretical contribution; the primary/tertiary distinction is central to BT1.
scope: Theoretical framework distinguishing subcortical affective from cortical cognitive consciousness

content: PANIC/separation-distress system evolved from physical pain mechanisms. Social attachments are mediated by the same neurochemistry as physical pain, particularly endogenous opioids. The PAG is the brain area from which emotional distress is most readily evoked in both humans and animals with the lowest ESB levels. Social exclusion and depression activate anterior cingulate regions known to regulate pain.
author_quote: The guiding evolutionary concept was that neural systems that elaborate social attachments have evolutionary relations with those that mediate the affective qualities of physical pain, including modulation by the same chemistries such as endogenous opioids.
caveats: Full text accessed. Pain-attachment overlap is empirically demonstrated via opioid modulation studies and brain imaging.
scope: Evolutionary link between physical pain and social separation distress

content: Phenomenal affective consciousness is not a cortical readout function. Emotional affects are critically linked to the dynamics of instinctual emotional action apparatus, which can be regulated but not created by higher cortico-cognitive activities. Play behavior survives radical decortication: animals without any neocortex play vigorously. Human children with severe higher brain damage exhibit rich affective lives when reared in loving environments.
author_quote: phenomenal affective consciousness is not simply a 'read-out' function of the neocortex. That view of emotional feelings is only a small part of the story, and hence deeply flawed as a major explanation
caveats: Full text accessed. Anti-constructivist argument directly challenges Barrett/LeDoux position. Decorticate play evidence from Panksepp et al. (1994); hydranencephalic children from Shewmon et al. (1999).
scope: Anti-constructivist evidence: subcortical emotional independence from cortex

content: Two-phase model of depression genesis: (1) sustained overactivity of the PANIC/GRIEF separation-distress system produces psychological pain, followed by (2) abnormally low SEEKING system activity during the despair phase. The initial agitated panic state transitions to shutdown when reunification attempts fail, paralleling Bowlby's protest-despair sequence.
author_quote: depression is intimately related to 1) sustained overactivity of the separation-distress PANIC system that can, if prolonged, lead to a downward cascade of psychological despair (a theoretical view originally formulated by John Bowlby); and 2) the despair phase that follows the acute PANIC response which is characterized by abnormally low activity of the SEEKING system.
caveats: Quote verified verbatim against the full-text PDF (Panksepp & Watt 2011, Psychiatry 74(1):5-13, opening summary paragraph) hosted at antoniocasella.eu/dnlaw/Panksepp_Watt_2011.pdf. The previously stored author_quote was a stitched/elided version: it silently deleted the mid-sentence parenthetical "(a theoretical view originally formulated by John Bowlby)" between "psychological despair" and "; and 2)" without an ellipsis. Restored to the exact source wording. Two-phase model integrates Bowlby's attachment theory (protest-despair) with Panksepp's affective neuroscience.
scope: Depression as PANIC overactivity + SEEKING shutdown

content: PANIC/GRIEF circuitry maps directly onto brain targets for treatment-resistant depression: starts in the PAG, ascends through dorsomedial thalamus, and terminates in subcallosal anterior cingulate — the same regions targeted by deep brain stimulation (Mayberg et al., 2005). Key neurochemistry: declining opioids and oxytocin, elevated CRF, increased glutamate. Dynorphin mediates SEEKING shutdown as a distinct form of negative affect.
author_quote: Depression may feel bad because brain separation-distress systems create psychological pain.
caveats: Full text accessed. The PANIC circuit → depression mapping is supported by DBS clinical evidence (Mayberg) but the causal chain remains theoretical.
scope: Neuroanatomical and neurochemical mapping of depression to PANIC/GRIEF circuit

content: The pain of depression arises from the evolutionary price of social bonds: PANIC/GRIEF evolved from general pain mechanisms (birds possess a homologous system). This psychic-pain system promotes social cohesion, forges bonds between infants and caretakers, and fortifies friendships and sexual relationships. Depression is the cost mammals pay for the survival advantages of social bonds.
author_quote: The pain of depression -- arising mostly from social loss and social defeat -- may be the price we mammals pay for the evolutionary advantages of social bonds that enrich our lives and promote procreation and survival.
caveats: Full text accessed. Evolutionary logic for depression as separation-distress cost. The argument that PANIC/GRIEF evolved from physical pain is supported by opioid overlap evidence but the evolutionary timing is reconstructive.
scope: Evolutionary logic: social pain as cost of social bonding architecture

content: SSRIs have modest overall efficacy (STAR*D findings); serotonin and norepinephrine regulate general arousal, not the specific affect of depression. More targeted interventions include ultra-low-dose buprenorphine (which both activates mu-opioid receptors and blocks despair-promoting dynorphin/kappa receptors), oxytocin, CRF antagonists, and glutamate modulators (ketamine). Psychotherapeutic activation of CARE and PLAY systems remains almost completely untapped.
author_quote: It is becoming harder to believe that general brain serotonergic and/or noradrenergic changes, which globally regulate aspects of forebrain arousal and dynamics, will specifically explain the morbid moods of depression.
caveats: Full text accessed. Buprenorphine evidence from Bodkin et al. (1995). SSRI critique based on STAR*D and meta-analytic evidence.
scope: Clinical implications: targeting PANIC/SEEKING circuits rather than general monoamines

content: Four primary emotional executive circuits identified via electrical brain stimulation: expectancy (later renamed SEEKING), rage, fear, and panic. Each is a transhypothalamic command circuit that concurrently activates behavioral action patterns, physiological responses, and subjective states. These circuits developed early in mammalian brain evolution and the underlying control mechanisms remain similar across species.
author_quote: Current neurobehavioral evidence indicates that there are at least four executive circuits of this type -- those which elaborate central states of expectancy, rage, fear, and panic.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote verified from abstract (Cambridge Core). BBS target article with extensive peer commentary (pp. 407-467). The 4-system framework was later expanded to 7 systems.
scope: Foundational theoretical paper proposing discrete emotional command circuits

content: Emotions arise from hard-wired neural circuits in the visceral-limbic brain, not from cortical constructions. These circuits facilitate diverse adaptive responses to major classes of environmental challenges. Theoretically guided studies of the animal brain can reveal how primitive emotions are organized in the human brain, and conversely, human introspective access can generate hypotheses for animal brain research.
author_quote: Emotions seem to arise ultimately from hard-wired neural circuits in the visceral-limbic brain that facilitate diverse and adaptive behavioral and physiological responses to major classes of environmental challenges.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote verbatim from abstract. Cross-species bidirectional inference is central to Panksepp's methodology.
scope: Theoretical foundation: subcortical hard-wired emotional circuits

content: Psychiatric disorders may arise from dysfunctional activity in the same emotional command circuits that generate normal emotions. Learning processes interact with these circuits, with emotional arousals gating sensory inputs and programming higher cognitive activities. The manner in which learning and psychiatric disorders arise from circuit activities is explored.
caveats: Abstract-limited. The psychiatry connection is stated in the abstract but details are in the paywalled full text. No author_quote per methodology Rule 3 (cannot verify beyond abstract).
scope: Psychiatric implications of emotional circuit dysfunction

content: Social play in juvenile rats constitutes a distinct emotional brain process with dedicated neural circuitry, not a byproduct of other systems. Play can be experimentally controlled via social deprivation and objectively quantified through pinning behavior (one rat pinning another during rough-and-tumble play). The underlying circuits may reveal how complex behavioral competence arises ontogenetically and yield clues to the genesis of psychopathologies.
author_quote: Existing results suggest the operation of a harmoniously operating brain process which generates a unique emotive brain process that is appropriately referred to as social play.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote verbatim from PubMed abstract. Pinning paradigm became the standard measure in subsequent play research.
scope: PLAY as distinct emotional system: operationalization and neural circuit evidence

content: Neurochemical substrates of play include the endogenous opioid system: morphine (mu-opioid agonist) increases play, naloxone (opioid antagonist) reduces play. Brain regions critical for play include the parafascicular area (PFA) of the thalamus (lesions reduced pinning by 73%) and dorsomedial thalamus (lesions reduced pinning by 33%). Play circuitry positions rigorous neural analysis as the route to empirical definition of play.
location: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 8(4):465-492, neurochemical substrates section. Follow-up data from Siviy & Panksepp 1985 (PMID: 3038140)
caveats: Abstract-limited for the 1984 paper. Neuroanatomical lesion data (PFA, DMT) from the follow-up paper Siviy & Panksepp 1985 (PMID 3038140), not from this review itself. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Neural substrates and opioid modulation of the PLAY circuit

content: Positive affect has at least two distinct neural substrates: appetitive (anticipatory) positive affect mediated by ventral striatal dopamine systems (SEEKING), and consummatory positive affect (sensory pleasure) mediated by dopamine-independent opioid and GABA receptors in ventral striatum, amygdala, and orbital frontal cortex. Various neuropeptides mediate homeostatic satisfactions as a third category.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Appetitive/consummatory distinction from the abstract. No author_quote per Rule 3. Parallels Berridge & Robinson's wanting/liking distinction but uses different theoretical framework.
scope: Dissociation between appetitive and consummatory positive affect systems

content: 50-kHz ultrasonic chirping in rats is the most robust during rough-and-tumble play and experimenter-administered tickling (which elicits more chirps than self-initiated play). Young animals prefer adults that chirp abundantly over those that chirp infrequently. Animals will run mazes and press levers to get tickled (operant reinforcement). Approach latency correlates with chirp rate (r=0.80, p<0.001). The chirping response can be selectively bred within four generations, demonstrating genetic basis.
location: Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 30(2):173-187. Supporting data from Panksepp & Burgdorf 2003 (Physiology & Behavior 79:533-547, open-access)
caveats: Abstract-limited for the 2006 paper. Quantitative data (r=0.80, selective breeding) sourced from companion open-access paper Panksepp & Burgdorf 2003. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: 50-kHz chirps as positive affect index: experimental validation across multiple paradigms

content: Contact comfort overwhelms lactation as determinant of infant attachment. Infant rhesus monkeys spent 17-18 hours/day on cloth-covered surrogate mother vs ~1 hour on wire mother, regardless of which mother provided milk. No measurable difference between cloth-fed and wire-fed groups in cloth preference. 8 newborn monkeys in dual-surrogate condition tested over 165+ consecutive days.
location: American Psychologist 13:673-685. Full text at psychclassics.yorku.ca/Harlow/love.htm
author_quote: contact comfort is a variable of overwhelming importance in the development of affectional response, whereas lactation is a variable of negligible importance.
caveats: Full text accessed via York University Classics. APA presidential address 1958. Pre-DOI era paper.
scope: 8 infant rhesus monkeys, dual surrogate mother paradigm

content: Cloth mother serves as secure base for exploration. When frightened by novel stimuli, infants consistently fled to cloth mother regardless of food source. In open-field tests with cloth mother present, emotionality scores reduced by half. Without any mother, infants froze in crouched positions. Wire mother provided zero comfort function in any fear test.
author_quote: The wire mother is biologically adequate but psychologically inept.
caveats: Full text accessed. Secure base concept later formalized by Ainsworth. Harlow's data provided the first experimental demonstration.
scope: Fear response and exploration tests with surrogate mothers

content: Late-adopted controls (surrogates introduced at day 250) reached ~9 hours daily contact within 10 days but behavioral intensity remained lower than birth-reared animals. This demonstrates a sensitive period for attachment formation — delay depresses the intensity of affectional response.
author_quote: this interval of delay depresses the intensity of the affectional response below that of the infant monkeys that were surrogate-mothered from birth onward.
caveats: Full text accessed. Sensitive period evidence from small sample (specific N not stated in accessible text).
scope: Sensitive period for attachment formation in rhesus monkeys

content: Infant monkeys raised on bare wire-mesh cage floors survived with difficulty during the first 5 days of life. Adding a wire-mesh cone improved survival. Covering the cone with terry cloth produced husky, healthy, happy babies. This demonstrates that tactile comfort is not merely a preference but a survival-critical input.
author_quote: a baby monkey raised on a bare wire-mesh cage floor survives with difficulty, if at all, during the first five days of life.
caveats: Full text accessed. Survival data establishes touch as necessary for infant viability, not just a preference.
scope: Survival dependence on tactile contact in neonatal rhesus monkeys

content: Total social isolation from birth produces devastating behavioral deficits scaling with duration. 3-month isolates slowly recovered with minimal long-term damage (one died of emotional anorexia). 6-month isolates showed severe deficits in virtually every aspect of social behavior — no contact play, only limited recovery. 12-month isolates were almost obliterated socially — zero activity play, persistent fear, no positive social behavior.
caveats: Abstract-limited (PMC has scanned images only). Content reconstructed from multiple secondary sources. Duration-severity gradient is well-established across replications. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Isolation deprivation study: 4 groups × 3-12 month durations

content: Upon release from isolation, monkeys entered a state of emotional shock characterized by autistic self-clutching and rocking, blank staring, cage circling, and self-mutilation. When placed with normal peers, isolated monkeys sat huddled in corners and were bullied. Recovery possible with younger therapist monkeys who engaged in clinging and simple play without aggression.
location: PNAS 54(1):90-97, post-isolation behavior and recovery sections
caveats: Abstract-limited. Post-isolation behaviors well-documented across secondary sources. Therapist monkey recovery finding from later Harlow & Suomi work. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Post-isolation behavioral deficits and recovery attempts

content: Dual pathway model for threat information reaching the amygdala. The low road (thalamo-amygdala, ~150-200ms) provides quick, coarse processing of simple stimulus features enabling immediate defensive responses before conscious identification. The high road (thalamo-cortico-amygdala, ~300ms) provides detailed, complex evaluation through sensory cortex and can override false alarms. Both converge on the lateral nucleus.
location: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184. DOI: 10.1146/annurev.neuro.23.1.155. PMID: 10845062
author_quote: This work has pinpointed the amygdala as an important component of the system involved in the acquisition, storage, and expression of fear memory.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from PubMed abstract. Low road/high road terminology and latency estimates from secondary sources consistent with LeDoux's published descriptions.
scope: Amygdala fear conditioning circuits: dual sensory pathway model

content: Amygdala functional architecture: lateral nucleus (LA) is the sensory interface where CS and US converge (synaptic plasticity encodes fear memories via LTP); central nucleus (CE) is the principal output for expression of conditioned fear, projecting to PAG (freezing), lateral hypothalamus (autonomic), and BNST (endocrine). Lesion studies confirm functional dissociation of these output pathways.
location: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, amygdala architecture section
caveats: Abstract-limited. Amygdala nuclei architecture well-documented across LeDoux's publications. Output pathway dissociation from lesion studies. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Amygdala internal architecture for threat processing

content: Fear conditioning involves calcium influx during CS-US pairing at lateral nucleus synapses, with subsequent gene expression and protein synthesis stabilizing long-term fear memories. LTP can be induced in the lateral nucleus by stimulating auditory thalamus. Findings from rodent fear conditioning apply to the human brain via functional neuroimaging and lesion studies.
location: Annual Review of Neuroscience 23:155-184, cellular mechanisms section
caveats: Abstract-limited. Cellular/molecular mechanisms from body text not directly accessed. Cross-species applicability stated in abstract. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Cellular mechanisms of fear memory formation in the amygdala

content: LeDoux revises his terminology: calling the threat-detection system a fear system was a mistake that led to confusion, because people assume a fear system produces conscious fear. He now distinguishes defensive survival circuits (subcortical, nonconscious, conserved across vertebrates with invertebrate analogues) from conscious fear (a cognitive construction arising from multiple neural ingredients).
author_quote: I, and others, have called the brain system that detects and responds to threats the fear system. This was a mistake that has led to much confusion.
