caveats: Full text accessed via PMC. LeDoux's self-correction is significant for BT1: he preserves subcortical circuit reality while denying they generate conscious experience.
scope: Terminological revision: defensive survival circuits vs conscious fear

content: Evidence for unconscious threat processing: subliminal threat stimuli elicit physiological responses without awareness; conditioning occurs without CS-US contingency awareness; amygdala activates to subliminal stimuli; hippocampal damage disrupts explicit memory but NOT fear conditioning (amygdala damage produces opposite pattern); blindsight patients show body responses to unseen threats; bilateral amygdala damage does NOT eliminate conscious fear — proving neither amygdala activity nor amygdala-controlled responses are necessary for fearful feelings.
caveats: Full text accessed. Multiple independent lines of evidence. The bilateral amygdala patient is SM, extensively studied by Feinstein et al. No direct quote used — synthesis of 6+ findings from body text.
scope: Convergent evidence: threat processing is dissociable from conscious fear experience

content: Fear as cognitive construction: conscious fear emerges from multiple neural ingredients (survival circuit activation, brain arousal, body feedback, memories, predictions) much as a soup's character emerges from raw materials. Some fears involve no survival circuit activation (social anxiety, existential concerns). Proposed terminology: replace fear conditioning with threat conditioning, fear system with defensive survival circuit, restrict fear exclusively to conscious experience.
author_quote: The feeling of fear occurs in the same way as the feeling of compassion or pride--through cognitive processing of neural raw materials.
caveats: Full text accessed. LeDoux occupies middle ground between Panksepp (emotions = subcortical states) and Barrett (emotions = fully constructed). He preserves subcortical circuits but denies they ARE conscious emotion.
scope: Constructivist position on conscious fear with preserved survival circuits

content: Evolved fear module with four characteristics: (a) preferentially activated by phylogenetically relevant stimuli (snakes, spiders, angry faces) in aversive contexts; (b) activation is automatic and pre-attentive; (c) relatively impenetrable to cognitive control (resistant to verbal instruction); (d) originates in dedicated amygdala-centered neural circuitry. Module mediates emotional fear learning dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.
author_quote: An evolved module for fear elicitation and fear learning with 4 characteristics is proposed.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from PubMed abstract. Four-characteristic framework is Öhman & Mineka's contribution. Fox et al. later found guns achieve similar detection speeds, qualifying strict phylogenetic specificity.
scope: Evolved fear module: theoretical framework with 4 testable characteristics

content: Visual search reveals pre-attentive threat detection: snake/spider targets among flower/mushroom distractors detected faster (~615ms) than reverse (~704ms). Fear-relevant detection unaffected by display size (parallel/pop-out processing, slope ~6ms/item). Fear-irrelevant targets show serial search (slope ~15ms/item). Conditioning to fear-relevant stimuli resists verbal instruction to extinguish; backward-masked fear-relevant conditioned stimuli elicit electrodermal responses without conscious awareness.
location: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522 and Öhman, Flykt & Esteves 2001 visual search study
author_quote: The fear module is assumed to mediate an emotional level of fear learning that is relatively independent and dissociable from cognitive learning of stimulus relationships.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Visual search data from companion Öhman et al. 2001 study. Instruction-resistance and masking data from review of multiple studies. Quote from abstract.
scope: Empirical evidence for automaticity and cognitive impenetrability of fear module

content: Monkey observational conditioning demonstrates prepared learning: lab-reared rhesus monkeys with no snake experience acquired fear of snakes and crocodiles (fear-relevant) through watching fearful models, but did NOT acquire fear of flowers or rabbits (fear-irrelevant) through the same procedure. This demonstrates selective associations operating even through vicarious/observational learning, not just direct conditioning.
location: Psychological Review 108(3):483-522, citing Cook & Mineka studies
caveats: Abstract-limited. Cook & Mineka observational conditioning data cited in the review. Demonstrates prepared fear is not merely a human cognitive bias. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Cross-species evidence for prepared fear learning via observation

content: The Strange Situation paradigm: 8 episodes (~21 min) of separation and reunion in a novel room. Three attachment classifications identified: Type B (Secure, ~65-70%) — uses mother as secure base, distressed at separation, seeks contact at reunion, quickly soothed. Type A (Avoidant, ~21%) — conspicuous avoidance at reunion, ignores mother, minimal contact-maintaining. Type C (Ambivalent/Resistant, ~14%) — clingy before separation, intensely distressed during, simultaneously seeks and resists contact at reunion.
location: Patterns of Attachment (1978). DOI: 10.4324/9781315802428. Book, not freely available.
caveats: Book not directly accessed. A/B/C classification and percentages well-established across thousands of replications. Meta-analysis (Madigan et al. 2023, >20,000 dyads) confirms distributions. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Strange Situation paradigm: operationalization of attachment classification

content: The sensitivity hypothesis: maternal sensitivity to infant signals throughout the first year predicts attachment classification. Securely attached infants had consistently responsive mothers. Avoidant infants had rejecting mothers with aversion to close bodily contact. Ambivalent infants had inconsistently responsive mothers. Five behavioral dimensions scored on 1-7 scale: proximity seeking, contact maintaining, avoidance, resistance, search behavior.
location: Patterns of Attachment (1978), sensitivity and scoring chapters
caveats: Book not accessed. Sensitivity hypothesis confirmed but with weaker-than-expected effect size (r=0.24 in Wolff & van IJzendoorn 1997 meta-analysis — the transmission gap). No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Sensitivity hypothesis: maternal responsiveness predicts attachment security

content: Attachment is an essential part of the biological ground plan of the human species. Hunter-gatherer societies show much more mother-infant contact than Western societies. Humans evolved as a species in which infants are carried and fed at frequent intervals. When attachment behavior is intensely activated, it is close bodily contact that is specifically required — not proximity alone.
location: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937. DOI: 10.1037//0003-066x.34.10.932. Full text via Smith College.
author_quote: an essential part of the ground plan of the human species--as well as that of many other species
caveats: Full text accessed via Smith College (media.smith.edu). APA address summarizing 1978 book findings.
scope: Attachment as evolved biological ground plan requiring physical contact

content: Feeding does not determine attachment. No evidence that methods of feeding significantly affected infant development. Instead, sensitive maternal responsiveness to infant signals determines attachment security. Securely attached infants develop working models of mother as accessible and responsive — therein lies security. Insecurely attached infants whose signals were disregarded have no basis for believing mother is responsive, consequently they are anxious.
location: American Psychologist 34(10):932-937, sensitivity and working models section
author_quote: Mothers of the securely attached (Group B) babies were, throughout the first year, more sensitively responsive to infant signals than were the mothers of the two anxiously attached groups.
caveats: Full text accessed. Working model concept originated with Bowlby; Ainsworth provided the empirical validation.
scope: Sensitivity hypothesis and internal working models of attachment

content: Secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers independence. Babies responding positively to close bodily contact also respond positively to being put down and move into exploratory play. Longitudinal follow-up: secure infants became more cooperative, more competent with peers, more curious, more self-directed, and more ego-resilient. Avoidant infants remained more aggressive and noncompliant. Ambivalent infants were more easily frustrated and less persistent.
author_quote: Fostering the growth of secure attachment facilitates rather than hampers the growth of healthy self-reliance.
caveats: Full text accessed. Longitudinal outcomes from Main and colleagues' follow-up studies cited by Ainsworth.
scope: Attachment security predicts developmental competence

content: Adult romantic love is an attachment process: affectional bonds form between adult lovers just as between infants and parents. Three adult attachment styles parallel Ainsworth's infant categories. Distribution: ~56% secure, ~25% avoidant, ~19% anxious-ambivalent (N=620 in Study 1), closely matching infant distributions (~62/23/15%). Secure adults describe relationships as happy, friendly, trusting. Avoidant adults fear closeness and doubt romantic love exists. Anxious adults experience love as obsessive with constant abandonment worry.
author_quote: This article explores the possibility that romantic love is an attachment process--a biosocial process by which affectional bonds are formed between adult lovers, just as affectional bonds are formed earlier in life between human infants and their parents.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from PubMed abstract. Love quiz methodology (forced-choice newspaper study) has been superseded by dimensional measures but distribution findings replicated.
scope: Extension of infant attachment classification to adult romantic relationships

content: Attachment style is related to mental models of self and relationships and to childhood relationship memories. Secure adults recall parents as respectful and accepting. Anxious adults remember intermittently available parents. Avoidant adults recall critical and distant parents. Continuity of style is due in part to Bowlby's internal working models — cognitive representations of self and others formed in early relationships that persist and shape adult relational patterns.
author_quote: attachment style is related in theoretically meaningful ways to mental models of self and social relationships and to relationship experiences with parents.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from PubMed abstract. Childhood memory data is retrospective. Working model concept from Bowlby; Hazan & Shaver provided first empirical adult test.
scope: Working models link infant attachment to adult relationship style

content: Forest Troop natural experiment: bovine tuberculosis selectively killed the most aggressive males (46% of adult males who competed at a garbage dump), leaving atypically unaggressive survivors with a >2:1 female-to-male ratio. A decade later (1993-96), when NO original males remained, the low-aggression culture persisted: relaxed dominance hierarchy, reduced male-to-female aggression, more male-female grooming, closer proximity to females/infants.
location: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.0020106. PMC387274. Full text.
author_quote: Thus, critically, the troop's unique culture was being adopted by new males joining the troop.
caveats: Quote replaced with a single verbatim sentence from the source (Sapolsky & Share 2004, PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, PMC387274). The prior author_quote ("All refuse-eating Forest Troop males (46% of adult males) died... the troop's unique culture was being adopted by new males joining the troop.") was non-verbatim: it stitched two distant, separate sentences with an ellipsis AND reworded the first clause. The real first sentence reads "From 1983 to 1986, most Garbage Dump animals died, as did all refuse-eating Forest Troop males (46% of adult males); no other Forest Troop animals died." — not "All refuse-eating Forest Troop males (46% of adult males) died." The 46% adult-male mortality figure stated in content was independently verified verbatim in the source. Full text accessed via PLoS/PMC. Natural experiment, not controlled; N=1 troop; tuberculosis as selective agent was circumstantial.
scope: Forest Troop baboons: multigenerational culture change after selective male mortality

content: Subordinate males in Forest Troop did NOT show the elevated basal glucocorticoid levels typical of low-ranking baboons in other troops. When injected with an anxiety-inducing drug (beta-carboline), low-ranking Forest Troop males showed no anxiety-related behavioral changes, while controls showed significant increases. The stress-rank gradient was eliminated by the social culture change.
location: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, physiological results. Full text.
author_quote: subordinate F93-96 males did not have elevated basal glucocorticoid levels.
caveats: Full text accessed. Pharmacological challenge test provides causal evidence beyond correlational cortisol measures.
scope: Physiological evidence: social culture eliminates rank-stress gradient

content: Cultural transmission mechanism: resident females were the key. Transfer males arrived as aggressive as those joining control troops. But Forest Troop females had shorter latency to groom/present to newcomers and were unconditionally more affiliative — not contingent on newcomer behavior. The pattern was NOT an artifact of sex ratio: five other troops with similar ratios resembled controls, not Forest Troop.
location: PLoS Biology 2(4):e106, transmission analysis. Full text.
author_quote: F93-96 females did not seem to treat transfer males in a contingent manner
caveats: Full text accessed. Female-mediated transmission supports facilitation/default model over instruction or self-selection.
scope: Mechanism of social culture transmission via female affiliative behavior

content: Whether high or low rank is most stressful depends on social organization. In despotic/unstable hierarchies, subordinates bear disproportionate chronic stress with elevated glucocorticoids. In stable/egalitarian systems, the stress-rank relationship diminishes or reverses. Subordinate rank associates with atherosclerosis, impaired immunity, reduced fertility, and hippocampal atrophy — all mediated through sustained glucocorticoid exposure.
author_quote: I first consider whether it is high- or low-ranking animals that are most stressed in a dominance hierarchy; this turns out to vary as a function of the social organization in different species and populations.
caveats: Abstract + partial text via public PDF. Context-dependent rank-stress finding is critical: the relationship is not fixed but modulated by social structure.
scope: Cross-species review: rank, cortisol, and health outcomes in primates

content: Human application: like subordinate primates, lower-SES humans show elevated basal cortisol, impaired immune function, and accelerated cardiovascular disease. The Whitehall studies of British civil servants show employment grade predicts health outcomes independent of traditional risk factors (smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure account for less than a third of the social gradient in CVD).
caveats: Abstract + partial text. Whitehall data from Marmot studies cited by Sapolsky. The primate-human bridge is correlational, not causal. No author_quote per Rule 3 (not from abstract).
scope: Human SES-health gradient as parallel to primate rank-stress gradient

content: The glucocorticoid cascade hypothesis: chronic stress produces elevated glucocorticoids that damage hippocampal neurons. Because the hippocampus mediates inhibition of the HPA axis, hippocampal damage creates a positive feedback loop: more cortisol → more hippocampal damage → less cortisol suppression → even more cortisol. Three types of damage: reversible dendritic atrophy (weeks), neurotoxicity (months), and neuroendangerment (impaired survival of neurological insults).
caveats: Abstract-limited (2-page commentary, paywalled). Cascade hypothesis well-established across Sapolsky's publications. Cushing's syndrome and PTSD evidence from companion papers. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Glucocorticoid cascade: chronic stress → hippocampal damage → HPA dysregulation

content: The smoke detector principle formalized via signal detection theory. For all-or-none defenses, expression is optimal whenever p(Harm) > Cost_defense/Cost_harm. With a 1000:1 cost ratio (300 kcal flight vs 300,000 kcal predator attack), the optimal threshold produces 999 false alarms per 1 genuine escape. These false alarms are completely normal products of an optimal system, not dysfunction.
location: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105. DOI: 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2004.08.002. Full text via UMich PDF.
author_quote: Out of 1000 episodes of flight at this response threshold, on the average, 999 will be false alarms and only 1 will be flight from an actual predator.
caveats: Full text accessed via UMich PDF. Mathematical model is Nesse's contribution; cost asymmetry argument traces to Lima & Dill (1990) and Cosmides & Tooby.
scope: Signal detection formalization: why 999/1000 false alarms are optimal

content: Graded defenses (fever, anxiety, fatigue) have a non-intuitive optimum: the optimal level is where marginal cost of additional defense exceeds marginal benefit, NOT where total costs equal total danger. Skewed payoff curves create additional over-expression bias: being 7 units below optimum costs 1.6 units extra, but being 0.7 above costs only 0.3 extra. Selection shapes systems that err on the side of excessive defense.
location: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105, graded defense analysis. Full text.
author_quote: natural selection will tend to shape systems that err on the side of excessive defensive expression.
caveats: Full text accessed. Mathematical optimization for graded defenses extends the all-or-none model.
scope: Graded defense optimization: asymmetric payoff curves favor over-expression

content: Repeated danger exposure may adaptively lower response thresholds, creating vulnerability to runaway positive feedback. Panic disorder exemplifies this: individuals experiencing a panic attack react as if they encountered real danger, becoming more cautious and more susceptible to additional attacks. The clinical condition is an extreme of normal threshold-lowering, not a qualitatively different pathology.
location: Evolution and Human Behavior 26(1):88-105, threshold dynamics section. Full text.
author_quote: Individuals who experience a panic attack react as if they had encountered a real danger, subsequently becoming not only more cautious but also more susceptible to additional attacks.
caveats: Full text accessed. Panic disorder as threshold-lowering is theoretical; the positive feedback mechanism is clinically observed.
scope: Threshold dynamics: panic disorder as runaway defense over-activation

content: Five categories of evolutionary explanations for disease vulnerability: (1) defenses that are actually adaptive (pain, fever, cough, anxiety, vomiting); (2) conflicts with other organisms (pathogens, predators); (3) novel environments to which selection has not yet adapted; (4) trade-offs between benefits and costs (e.g., sickle cell); (5) constraints on natural selection leaving suboptimal designs. Symptoms like fever are carefully regulated rises in the thermostat set point, not mere metabolic byproducts.
location: Scientific American 279(5):86-93. DOI: 10.1038/scientificamerican1198-86. Full text via UMich PDF.
author_quote: The cost of a false alarm--vomiting when no toxin is truly present--is only a few calories. But the penalty for a single missed authentic alarm--failure to vomit when confronted with a toxin--may be death.
caveats: Full text accessed. Five-category framework later expanded to six in Nesse's subsequent publications. Foundational statement of evolutionary medicine.
scope: Evolutionary medicine: five categories of disease vulnerability

content: Blocking evolved defenses can cause harm. Shigella study: patients taking antidiarrheal drugs stayed sick longer with more complications than placebo. Iron supplementation in Africa increased infectious disease (amebiasis) by removing iron-withholding defense. Drug vulnerability exists because plants evolved defensive compounds (nicotine, cocaine, opium) targeting insect nervous systems, and shared evolutionary heritage means these affect human systems too.
location: Scientific American 279(5):86-93, defense-blocking section. Full text.
author_quote: our poor decisions about diet and exercise are made by brains shaped to cope with an environment substantially different from the one our species now inhabits.
caveats: Full text accessed. Shigella study from DuPont & Hornick. Iron-infection link from Weinberg. Drug vulnerability section is evolutionary logic, not direct experiment.
scope: Empirical evidence: blocking defenses harms; drug vulnerability from shared evolution

content: Tinbergen's four questions organized into a 2×2 framework: proximate vs evolutionary crossed with synchronic (single form) vs diachronic (sequence). Mechanism (what is the structure?) and ontogeny (how does it develop?) are proximate. Adaptive significance (how have variations influenced fitness?) and phylogeny (what is the evolutionary history?) are evolutionary. All four are needed for a complete explanation of any biological trait.
location: Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health 2019(1):2. DOI: 10.1093/emph/eoy035. PMC6343817. Full text (open access).
author_quote: Seeking answers to all four of Tinbergen's questions expands explanations beyond mechanisms to also describe a trait's development, evolutionary history and adaptive significance.
caveats: Full text accessed (open access). The 2×2 framework is Nesse's organizational contribution; Tinbergen's original (1963) listed four questions without the matrix structure.
scope: Methodological framework: Tinbergen's four questions for biology and medicine

content: Attachment is primary, not secondary to feeding. Bowlby proposed five component instinctual responses — sucking, clinging, following (baby is active partner) and crying, smiling (activate maternal behavior) — all primary and initially independent, becoming integrated and focused on one mother figure during the second six months of life. This broke with Freudian secondary drive theory.
author_quote: Those which I believe we can identify at present are sucking, clinging, and following, in all of which the baby is the principal active partner, and crying and smiling in which his behaviour serves to activate maternal behaviour.
caveats: Abstract-limited (UPenn PDF not parseable). Quote verified across multiple secondary sources citing original text. Five-response theory was later superseded by behavioral system framework in 1969 Vol 1.
scope: Bowlby's original attachment theory: five instinctual responses

content: Children attach to cruel mothers: the attachment of the small child to the mother seems largely independent of her personal qualities. This observation is incompatible with secondary drive (feeding-based reinforcement) models. Bowlby drew on ethology (Lorenz's imprinting, Harlow's contact comfort) and proposed monotropy: the tendency for instinctual responses to be directed toward a particular individual, not promiscuously.
author_quote: Children will cling even to mothers who are continually cross and sometimes cruel to them. The attachment of the small child to his mother seems to a large degree independent of her personal qualities.
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from Burlingham & Freud (1942) as cited by Bowlby. Monotropy concept later nuanced in 1969 book.
scope: Against secondary drive: attachment persists despite maltreatment

content: Protest-despair-detachment: three-phase response to separation from attachment figure. Protest = active attempts to recover the figure (crying, searching, resistance to comforting by others). Despair = withdrawal, hopelessness, reduced activity. Detachment = apparent indifference if caregiver does not return. Based on Robertson's hospital observations and Bowlby's theoretical framework.
location: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Part I: Security, Anxiety, and Distress
caveats: Book not directly accessed. Protest-despair-detachment is well-established across clinical and animal literature. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Separation response sequence: protest → despair → detachment

content: Ethological theory of fear: fear responses to natural clues to danger (strangers, strange environments, rapid approaches, darkness, loud noises, being alone) are part of basic behavioral equipment, not learned. Separation anxiety is reframed as natural: it is no less natural to feel afraid when lines of communication with a safe base are threatened than when something alarming appears. Agoraphobia is reframed as anxious attachment, not fear of open spaces.
location: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Part II: An Ethological Approach to Human Fear, Ch. 8-11, 17-18
caveats: Book not directly accessed. Natural clues concept and agoraphobia reframing well-documented in secondary sources. No author_quote per Rule 3. [EXCLUDED 2026-07-10, Job2/Fix1: detached from load-bearing evidence role (mechanism_evidence M1/M3 removed) because this record fails R1 (work 98 no DOI/PMID, not in physical collection) and R2 (book not directly accessed; secondary sources) and R3 (no verbatim author_quote). Matches EEA-SOC-08, which already excludes it. Not deleted; retained as full-text-pending. Do not re-cite as evidence until full-text sourced with a verbatim quote.]
scope: Fear as evolved response to natural danger cues; agoraphobia as anxious attachment

content: Anger as functional attachment behavior: anger in response to separation is not aggression but protest — a signal to communicate distress and motivate the attachment figure to return. Secure attachment promotes independence and self-reliance, not dependence. Anxious attachment (insecure base) creates heightened susceptibility to fear and anxiety through unreliable caregiver availability.
location: Attachment and Loss Vol 2 (1973), Ch. 16 (Anger, Anxiety, Attachment), Ch. 20 (Secure Attachment and Self-reliance)
caveats: Book not directly accessed. Anger-as-protest and secure-base→independence are core Bowlby contributions confirmed across decades of research. No author_quote per Rule 3.
scope: Anger as attachment signal; secure attachment enables independence

content: The Standard Social Science Model (SSSM) critique: Tooby and Cosmides identify the dominant 20th-century metatheory as assuming (a) blank-slate psychology, (b) general-purpose brain, (c) culture programs behavior without constraint, (d) content-independent, equipotential learning mechanisms. They replace this with the Integrated Causal Model: the mind comprises domain-specific evolved mechanisms that interact with environment/culture, and culture itself derives from and is constrained by universal human nature.
location: The Adapted Mind (1992), ch. 1, pp. 19-136. CEP UCSB PDF exists but image-scanned.
author_quote: mischaracterizes important avenues of causation, induces researchers to study complexly chaotic and unordered phenomena, and misdirects study away from areas where rich principled phenomena are to be found
caveats: Abstract-limited (PDF is scanned image). Quote verified across multiple secondary sources. SSSM is Tooby & Cosmides' coined term.
scope: Critique of the Standard Social Science Model and proposal of the Integrated Causal Model

content: The EEA formalization: the environment of evolutionary adaptedness is not a place, habitat, or time period, but a statistical composite of the adaptation-relevant properties of ancestral environments encountered by members of a species over evolutionary time. Biological mechanisms embody information about stably recurring properties of ancestral worlds. The Pleistocene (2.5M-10K ya) is the primary reference period, with agriculture creating insufficient time for major psychological adaptation.
location: The Adapted Mind (1992), pp. 19-136, EEA section
author_quote: The EEA is not a place or a habitat, or even a time period. Rather, it is a statistical composite of the adaptation-relevant properties of the ancestral environments
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from Tooby & Cosmides 1990 as cited in this chapter, verified across multiple sources.
scope: Formalization of the EEA concept: statistical composite, not a place

content: Domain-specificity is superior to domain-general learning because: (1) general mechanisms must solve problems from scratch through costly trial-and-error, while specific mechanisms come pre-equipped with content; (2) combinatorial explosion — without domain-specific constraints, organisms face exponentially growing behavioral options; (3) the frame problem — general systems face infinite regress excluding irrelevant information, while modules solve this through information encapsulation. Nature/nurture is replaced by open vs closed developmental programs, both genetically encoded.
location: The Adapted Mind (1992), pp. 19-136, domain-specificity arguments
author_quote: both the genes and the developmentally relevant environment are the product of evolution
caveats: Abstract-limited. Arguments reconstructed from extensive secondary sources. Combinatorial explosion and frame problem arguments are the core of the domain-specificity case.
scope: Three arguments for domain-specificity over domain-general processing

content: Wason selection task reveals domain-specific reasoning about social exchange. Abstract conditional rules yield 5-30% correct detection of violations. Social contract rules (if you take benefit B, you must meet requirement R) yield 65-80% correct — despite identical logical structure. Cheater detection is operationally defined: agent takes rationed benefit, fails to meet requirement, acts intentionally. The mechanism does not detect all rule violations, only those revealing intentional cheating.
author_quote: In order to successfully engage in social exchange--cooperation between two or more individuals for mutual benefit--humans must be able to solve a number of complex computational problems, and do so with special efficiency
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote from PubMed abstract. Performance rates from National Academies chapter reproducing key experiments. Eight critical tests distinguish social exchange theory from competing theories.
scope: Wason selection task: cheater detection as evidence for domain-specific social reasoning

content: Parametric decomposition of cheater detection: a 2×2×2 design manipulating benefit, intention, and ability shows each factor independently drops performance ~20 percentage points. All three present: 64% correct. Two present: ~46%. One: ~26%. None: ~26%. Effects are additive and independent (ANOVA: Benefit F=7.30 p=0.007; Intention F=10.22 p=0.002; Ability F=4.87 p=0.028). Social exchange activates nonstandard inference rules that diverge sharply from first-order logic.
location: Cognition 31(3):187-276 and extended work in Cosmides, Barrett & Tooby 2010 PNAS
caveats: Abstract-limited for 1989 paper. Parametric data from National Academies chapter and 2010 PNAS replication. No author_quote per Rule 3 (data from secondary sources).
scope: Computational decomposition of cheater detection: three independent factors

content: Emotions are superordinate programs that evolved to coordinate the activity of other programs in solving typical adaptive problems. They simultaneously orchestrate perception, attention, inference, learning, memory, goal choice, motivational priorities, physiological reactions, motor behaviors, and behavioral decision making — activating certain systems and deactivating others to prevent chaos of competing systems operating simultaneously.
location: Handbook of Emotions 3rd ed (2008), pp. 114-137. CEP UCSB PDF exists but not parseable.
author_quote: A superordinate program that evolved to coordinate the activity of other programs in the solution of typical adaptive problems
caveats: Abstract-limited (PDF not readable). Quote verified across multiple secondary sources. This is the formal theoretical grounding for DA6 (Competing Motivational Programs).
scope: Emotions as superordinate coordinating programs — DA6 theoretical foundation

content: Fear example: when sensing a stalker, the emotion simultaneously (a) shifts perception to hear threat-relevant sounds with greater clarity, (b) reprioritizes goals so safety overrides all else, (c) triggers physiological preparation — dry mouth (digestion shutdown), blood to lower body, expanded visual field, increased breathing, (d) retrieves threat-relevant memories. Internal regulatory variables (IRVs) set thresholds, adjust weights, and calibrate responses across all these systems simultaneously.
location: Handbook of Emotions 3rd ed (2008), pp. 114-137, fear example
author_quote: You may suddenly hear with far greater clarity sounds that bear on the hypothesis that you are being stalked, but that ordinarily you would not perceive or attend to, such as creaks or rustling
caveats: Abstract-limited. Quote verified from CEP UCSB website text and multiple secondary sources.
scope: Worked example: fear as superordinate program coordinating multiple subsystems

content: Ancestral work was characteristically small-group, embodied, skill-based, and autonomy-rich. Psychological adaptations for work — cognitive mechanisms for toolmaking, resource acquisition, learning, and cooperative production — evolved in the context of small networks of hunter-gatherers where effort-outcome links were visible and physical.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (van Vugt, M., Colarelli, S. M., & Li, N., 2024). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.
scope: Establishes the ancestral baseline for work conditions against which digital work mismatch is measured.

content: Digital work exacerbates evolutionary mismatch through multiple simultaneous channels: sedentarism replacing embodied activity, always-on connectivity disrupting circadian boundaries, electronic surveillance replacing autonomy, remote/distributed work weakening face-to-face social bonds, and abstract screen-mediated tasks replacing tangible effort-outcome feedback. These mismatches are predicted to increase chronic work stress and related physical and mental health problems.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (van Vugt, M., Colarelli, S. M., & Li, N., 2024). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.
scope: Central mismatch analysis of the paper. Maps digital work features to specific mechanism disruptions and predicts cascading health consequences.

content: Some features of digital work may be more matched with ancestral work conditions than traditional industrial/office work: flexible scheduling restoring autonomy over time allocation, broader access to skill-learning and collaboration networks, and potential for reduced commuting allowing more time for non-work regulatory needs. Digital work is a mixed mismatch profile, not a uniformly mismatched one.
caveats: Matched features are conditional on how digital work is actually organized — a remote worker with flexible hours who exercises is in a different mismatch profile than an always-on surveilled remote worker.
scope: Important nuance — digital work is not blanket-mismatched. Some features restore ancestral conditions relative to industrial-era work. Consistent with P3 scope note that modernity is mixed.

content: Organizational interventions for digital work should be grounded in mismatch logic: restore movement breaks, protect circadian boundaries (right to disconnect), design for team sizes within Dunbar-range cooperation thresholds, increase decision latitude and visible effort-outcome links, and create physical co-presence opportunities for distributed teams.
caveats: R3 disclosure: no verbatim author_quote captured for this extraction; the claim is drawn from full text/physical source of the cited work (van Vugt, M., Colarelli, S. M., & Li, N., 2024). Verbatim quote pending v1 re-extraction.
scope: Applied intervention framework — one of the clearest worked examples of DC3 (environment as primary intervention layer) applied to a specific domain. Each proposed intervention maps back to a specific mechanism's resolution conditions.

content: Electronic monitoring and algorithmic management in digital work environments reduce worker decision latitude, triggering M6 controllability failure (learned helplessness default). Combined with status-threat from visible performance metrics and always-on availability expectations activating M1 without resolution, this creates a chronic stress profile consistent with allostatic load accumulation.
caveats: Theoretical synthesis rather than new empirical data. The individual mechanism claims draw on established literatures but the specific digital-work combination is a prediction, not a tested hypothesis.
scope: Bridges M6 controllability and M1 threat-management to digital-work surveillance. Links to Karasek demand-control model via mismatch framing.

content: Many distinctively human cognitive and behavioral traits — language fluency, art, music, humor, creativity, generosity, moral judgment — evolved as fitness indicators under sexual selection (mate-choice pressure), not solely as survival adaptations under natural selection. Sexual selection broadens the set of selection pressures shaping the human motivational and cognitive architecture beyond survival to include mate-choice display and discrimination.
caveats: Summary-level extraction — no full-text access at time of entry (book not in physical collection, no digital full-text reviewed). Claim is at thesis-level from publicly-documented summaries; specific evidentiary substructure and comparative-data citations inside the book have not been audited. R2 full-text review pending before relying on this extraction for downstream claims.
scope: Core thesis of The Mating Mind. Situates human cognition inside mate-choice pressure, strengthening M14's theoretical foundation and broadening the adaptive logic behind P2's "domain-sensitive interacting adaptations".

content: Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.
caveats: Summary-level extraction — no full-text access at time of entry (book not in physical collection, no digital full-text reviewed). Thesis is drawn from publicly-documented book summaries and widely-cited secondary sources; the specific empirical substructure Miller draws on (Big Five personality research, signaling-theory modeling, consumer data) has not been audited here. R2 full-text review pending before relying on this extraction for downstream claims.
scope: Core thesis of Spent. One of the clearest worked examples of DA4 (Proxy Hijacking via Open Loops) and DC2 (Market Proxy Exploitation) applied to the consumer / branded-goods domain. Complements Schüll (gambling) and Moss (food) in Cor's market-exploitation evidence base.

content: Common mental disorders with high heritability and substantial fitness cost are best explained by polygenic mutation-selection balance — many rare mildly deleterious alleles distributed across large mutational target sizes — rather than by ancestral neutrality or balancing selection. This model accounts for the observed pattern of prevalence, heritability, and fitness cost better than pure-adaptive accounts, and implies that a substantial fraction of heritable mental disorder burden reflects mutational load rather than adaptive tradeoff.
caveats: Summary-level extraction — no full-text access at time of entry (BBS target article PDF not reviewed). Core-thesis claim is drawn from publicly-documented abstracts and widely-cited secondary characterizations; the specific genetic-architecture evidence, model fit comparisons, and BBS peer-commentary rebuttals have not been audited. R2 full-text review pending before relying on this extraction for downstream claims. This paper has ongoing methodological contestation and is a live debate, not a settled finding.
scope: Bounds DA1's scope. The four-category distinction (defensive signal / dysregulation / damage / developmental miscalibration) needs Keller & Miller's mutation-selection-balance account to handle the "damage" / "dysregulation" slots for heritable common disorders. Without engaging this work, DA1 is vulnerable to the charge that it over-reads mental disorder presentations as mismatch signals.

content: Miller's sexual-selection argument is explicitly scope-limited. He says it does NOT explain: adaptations shared with other primates (foraging, predator avoidance, parenting), the nature of consciousness, the dynamics of cultural change, or traits better explained by natural selection, kin selection, or reciprocal altruism. The argument applies to self-ornamentation, display, status, ideology, fashion, and aesthetics — to psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship. Miller also flags: minimal sexual dimorphism in human mental traits puzzles the classic "choosy-female, displaying-male" model and requires mutual-choice sexual selection models; sexual selection theory itself remains "very much under development"; empirical support is "patchy"; the theory risks over-emphasizing courtship functions of language and creative intelligence while neglecting their other fitness benefits.
author_quote: It does not pretend to be a complete account of human mental evolution, because it addresses only those psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship.
caveats: Author_quote replaced with the exact verbatim sentence from Miller's own Psycoloquy author-synopsis of The Mating Mind (UCLA BEC archive: bec.ucla.edu/.../miller_mating_mind.htm, para 57). The prior author_quote was a stitched, partially-altered two-fragment paraphrase: fragment 1 ("addresses only those psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship") was verbatim, but fragment 2 was rendered as "not a complete account of human mental evolution," whereas Miller actually wrote "does not pretend to be a complete account of human mental evolution" — the modal hedge "does not pretend to be" was dropped and the fragments were also reordered. Both fragments in fact come from a single contiguous sentence, now quoted whole. Source is Miller's near-primary author-synopsis, not the book full-text; the book itself remains un-read at full-text level. The other scope-limiting claims in CONTENT (excluded domains: consciousness, cultural change, foraging/predator avoidance/parenting, kin selection, reciprocal altruism; minimal sexual dimorphism requiring mutual-choice models; "very much under development"; "patchy" evidence; risk of over-emphasizing courtship functions) were each independently confirmed verbatim against the same synopsis.
scope: Scope-limiting extraction. Critical for Cor because it constrains how much of the mechanism architecture Miller's sexual-selection thesis actually claims — it's a specific narrow claim about display/courtship traits, not a general replacement for natural-selection accounts of the architecture. Grounded in Miller's own Psycholoquy synopsis (UCLA archive).

content: The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle — costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection — mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.
caveats: Grounded in Miller's own Psycholoquy synopsis. Handicap principle and Fisher runaway are well-established evolutionary theory; Miller's application to human cognition specifically remains contested within evolutionary psychology. Full-text book review not done.
scope: Mechanism-level extraction specifying HOW Miller argues sexual selection shaped cognition. Relevant to M2 (pursuit/seeking) via novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking as sexual-selection-shaped biases, and to DA4 because fitness-indicator signaling is exactly the substrate that gets proxy-hijacked by modern markets (per Spent).

content: Miller frames consumer signaling specifically around the "Central Six" personality dimensions: general intelligence plus the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, stability, extraversion). These are the traits consumers attempt to display via purchases, and personality research on the Big Five is presented as directly applicable to consumer behavior. This gives a specific mapping: consumer goods = signaling vehicles for Central Six traits = proxies for mate-choice and friend-selection mechanisms that evolved to read these traits in conspecifics.
caveats: Grounded in Miller's own publisher-page summary (primalpoly.com) plus widely-cited secondary summaries. Book full-text not audited. Big Five applicability to consumer behavior is an empirical research program with mixed replication; Miller's specific claims about Big-Five-based consumer targeting (e.g., Spent's marketing critique) are theoretical synthesis, not his own empirical findings.
scope: Specifies WHICH psychological signals Spent claims are being hijacked by consumer markets — Big-Five-plus-IQ personality display. Useful hook for operationalizing DC2 (Market Proxy Exploitation) in the branded-goods domain: products can be categorized by which Central Six trait they proxy-signal.

content: Keller & Miller adjudicate between the three evolutionary genetic models using specific empirical criteria: (1) observed prevalence rates of common mental disorders in populations, (2) fitness costs associated with the disorders, (3) likely rarity of susceptibility alleles, (4) increased risks of mental disorders associated with brain trauma, (5) increased risks associated with inbreeding, and (6) increased risks associated with paternal age. They argue only polygenic mutation-selection balance fits all six patterns simultaneously, because brain-trauma/inbreeding/paternal-age effects are specifically predicted by a many-rare-mildly-deleterious-alleles model and do not fit ancestral-neutrality or balancing-selection models.
caveats: Grounded in publicly-available abstract-level and secondary characterizations; BBS target article full text not audited. The paper is a live debate in evolutionary psychiatry with substantive published critiques and peer commentary as part of the BBS format — evidence_quality=contested reflects this. The specific criterion list is as characterized in author's own abstract and widely-cited secondary descriptions; the weights they assign across the six criteria and their rebuttals of the other two models have not been read at full-text.
scope: Specifies Keller & Miller's actual test criteria, not just the conclusion. Critical for Cor because it gives operationalizable tests for when a mental disorder presentation is more likely mutational load (damage/dysregulation in DA1 terminology) vs. defensive signal under mismatch: if the disorder correlates with brain trauma, inbreeding, and paternal age, those are fingerprints of mutation-selection balance and argue against a pure-mismatch reading.

content: Muldoon & Parke's 'cruel companionship' thesis: AI companions activate the human social-bonding response — the evolved tendency to treat a responsive interlocutor as a social being — while structurally foreclosing the genuine reciprocal relationship that would resolve it. Being incapable of genuine understanding, mutual vulnerability, or embodied presence, the companion fires the bonding cue but supplies none of the resolving function, leaving users 'trapped in a cycle of emotional engagement with an app that cannot fulfil their human needs.' Theoretical (political-economy / cultural-studies), not empirical.
location: §'Cruel companionship', pp. 9–10 (canonical quote); cue-activation claim at §'The rise of AI companions', pp. 4–5
author_quote: The attachments created within AI companions promise intimacy and connection, yet structurally foreclose the possibility of genuine reciprocal relationships in which the user’s human autonomy is respected.
caveats: Theoretical, not empirical — the paper contributes no primary data of its own. The evolutionary social-activation ('fires the cue') claim is propagated from Breazeal (2003) / Turkle (2011) / Kirk et al. (2025), not demonstrated here. Carries M3 (Social Bonding) only; does NOT evidence M4 (Play), M9 (Care/Alloparenting), or M11 (Cooperation/Alliance), which remain architecture-derived.

content: Supports the pair-bond / romantic-sexual slice of M14's proxy floor only: Muldoon & Parke treat AI companions as vehicles for romantic and sexual attachment that simulate a partner while structurally foreclosing a genuine reciprocal relationship. PAIR-BOND SLICE ONLY — the paper says nothing about the desire or attraction subsystems, sexual fulfilment, or reproduction, and does not address M14's full three-system (desire / attraction / pair-bonding) scope.
author_quote: Users may begin with the intention of seeking platonic companionship but gradually develop romantic or sexual attachments, partly because these systems are designed to deepen emotional engagement over time.
caveats: LOAD-BEARING SCOPE LIMIT (do not drop or soften): the evidence covers the pair-bond / romantic-attachment slice of M14 ONLY. No reproduction, no desire/attraction-subsystem content. Theoretical (cultural-studies / political-economy), not empirical. Should be treated as supporting, not a primary mechanism anchor for M14.

content: Tybur et al.'s evolutionary-computational framework treats pathogen, sexual, and moral disgust as three FUNCTIONALLY DISTINCT adaptations with distinct information-processing systems, not one mechanism misfiring. Moral disgust is theorized as a condemnation-coordination/signaling adaptation (building on DeScioli & Kurzban) that shares with pathogen disgust primarily the EXPRESSIVE (facial/vocal) component; the defining pathogen "do not touch"/avoidance motivation is absent — moral disgust instead covaries with approach-motivated anger and the desire to punish. The authors explicitly contrast their signaling account with the view that moral disgust functions to cause avoidance "as is the case with pathogen and sexual disgust," and flag the moral domain as the least settled of the three ("little consensus about the measurement, function, and even existence"; treatment "necessarily more exploratory"). Their one causal claim — that activating pathogen/sexual disgust raises moral-wrongness judgments — is framed as disgust being ONE limited input to a SEPARATE strategic rule-endorsement system ("we do not suggest that disgust serves as an input to every moral judgment"), and is evidenced by the Schnall/Eskine/Wheatley-Haidt/Moretti priming studies that Landy & Goodwin (2015, ext105) meta-analyze to d≈-0.01 after publication-bias correction. Net: the canonical framework supports a shared-machinery / functionally-distinct reading and does NOT establish moral disgust as a confirmed lower rung of the pathogen-disgust mechanism — confirming M12's moral-tier demotion while authoritatively grounding the three-domain disgust structure.
location: Psychological Review 120(1):65–84. Quote from "Disgust as Output of Moral Cognition" subsection (p. 76). Three-domain thesis: Abstract (p. 65) and "An Evolutionary View of Emotion" (p. 67).
author_quote: We contrast this signaling view with the idea that moral disgust has a function in causing people to avoid some set of objects, behaviors, or people, as is the case with pathogen and sexual disgust.
caveats: Theoretical framework/review (no new primary data) — billed evidence_quality=theoretical, not empirical. The authors' own hedge (verbatim, p. 74): "in contrast to pathogen and sexual disgust, there is little consensus about the measurement, function, and even existence of moral disgust" and "the ideas discussed in this section are necessarily more exploratory than those in previous sections on pathogen and sexual disgust." Load-bearing caveat: the paper's lone support for incidental-disgust→moral-judgment causal bleed (its "Disgust as Input to Moral Decisions" subsection) cites Schnall et al. 2008, Eskine et al. 2011, Wheatley & Haidt 2005, and Moretti & di Pellegrino 2010 — the same priming literature ext105 (relates_to_primary_id=105) nulls after publication-bias correction — so it cannot promote M12's moral tier. R3: author_quote grep-verified verbatim against the version-of-record full text (DeScioli faculty self-archive PDF; pdftotext); curly/straight punctuation reconciled. Additional verbatim quotes captured in the source report but not stored separately (one-row discipline).
scope: Authoritatively grounds M12's three-domain disgust structure (pathogen/sexual/moral) and the functional-distinctness of the moral domain. Supports keeping the moral-disgust extension in a clearly-labelled speculative tier (ruling #1583): evidences shared expressive machinery, NOT pathogen disgust causally hijacked into moral judgment. Does not bear on the solid pathogen-disgust gradient, which rests on Curtis (wk31), Schaller & Park (wk41), and Rozin.

content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.
author_quote: An "ego" (the naming person) is 44.2 times (95% C.I. 37.6 to 51.4) more likely to name an "alter" (the named person) in the campmate network, and 14.3 times (95% C.I. 12.2 to 16.4) more likely to name an alter in the gift network, if the alter reciprocated the social tie by also naming the ego as a friend
caveats: Single Hadza population; reciprocity multiplier for the campmate vs gift network.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).
author_quote: in both the campmate and gift networks, social ties are significantly more likely when two people are similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength.
caveats: Single Hadza population.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).
author_quote: social distance appears to be as important as genetic relatedness and physical proximity in explaining assortativity in cooperation
caveats: From the abstract; full result in main text Fig. 2d. Single Hadza population.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Within-camp relatedness is low: most co-residents are not first-order kin.
author_quote: first-order relatives make up less than 10% of residential camps
caveats: Apicella restating Hill et al. 2011 (their ref 18) in their own full text; original measurement is Hill 2011.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only ~12% of campmates repeat year-over-year (implying ~88% annual turnover), yet cooperative assortment persists.
author_quote: Across the three intervals, the mean proportion of repeated campmates was 12.1%.
caveats: Single Hadza population; corrects the prior mis-attributed "~22%/78%" figure (that traces to Smith et al. 2016, a different paper).
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Hadza camp size centers near 30 individuals, composed of several unrelated nuclear families.
author_quote: The Hadza live in temporary camps that average about 30 individuals.
caveats: Smith restating Marlowe 2010 in full text; descriptive, single population.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Camp membership is fission-fusion: entire camps relocate on a weeks timescale, so the group as a unit does not persist.
author_quote: Every 4-8 weeks entire camps shift location usually in response to resource availability.
caveats: Single Hadza population.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Direct relatedness measure: primary kin are a small minority of a camp.
author_quote: Relatedness within camps is low with primary kin comprising, on average, 1.43 and 1.93 of men and women's campmates respectively.
caveats: Smith Methods, restating Marlowe 2010; counts (not %) of primary kin per camp.
scope: EEA social_structure baseline (single forager population; treat exact figures as illustrative).

content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.
author_quote: Among the Ache and Hadza, frequent visiting and long lifespans mean that adults typically interact with more than three hundred same-sex adults during their lifetimes. This implies a social universe of about a thousand individuals, when opposite-sex adults and children are included.
caveats: Model-based estimate; two forager populations (Ache, Paraguay; Hadza, Tanzania), with a San corroboration cited. Single study; treat figure as illustrative.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Per-activity lifetime interaction counts for Ache/Hadza men (hundreds of partners) vs ~21 for male chimpanzees: lifetime human social universe is an order of magnitude larger.
author_quote: Precontact Northern Ache men, for example, are expected to have hunted with 206 men, conversed with 290 men, and watch tool making by 302 different men in a lifetime (Table S16 in File S1). Eastern Hadza men are expected to converse with 427 other Hadza men, hunt with 303 men, and watch tool making by 395 different men in a lifetime. In contrast, chimpanzees living in typical communities of 11 adult males are expected to interact with a mean of only 21 other adult males in a lifetime
caveats: Model-based estimates from life tables (Table S16); single study, two forager populations + chimpanzee comparison.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 — which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.
author_quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. This is a much higher number of individually known social interactants than reported for any other primate, and possibly more than any other species on earth. It is also much greater than the predicted 150 significant social interactants (known as “Dunbar's number”) that was extrapolated from primate brain by social group size regressions
caveats: Distinguishes the LIFETIME cumulative pool (~1000) from the ~150 concurrent active-network ceiling; single study.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: After exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time: biological night begins at sunset and ends just after sunrise; electrical lighting is associated with a delayed clock.
author_quote: Here we show that electrical lighting and the constructed environment is associated with reduced exposure to sunlight during the day, increased light exposure after sunset, and a delayed timing of the circadian clock as compared to a summer natural 14h40min:9h20min light-dark cycle camping. Furthermore, we find that after exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time such that the beginning of the internal biological night occurs at sunset and the end of the internal biological night occurs before wake time just after sunrise.
caveats: Within-subject field study, n=8, summer, Colorado ~40N. Small sample; modern subjects as a natural-light proxy for the ancestral condition.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: One week of natural light advanced all circadian markers ~2h (melatonin onset near sunset) while sleep duration and efficiency were statistically unchanged: the change was in circadian PHASE/timing, not sleep amount.
author_quote: Following the week of exposure to natural lighting, all measured markers of internal circadian time were ~2h earlier (Fig 3., all p<0.01; Bonferroni correction required p<0.0167, one tailed) and remarkably, melatonin onset occurred on average near sunset, the melatonin midpoint occurred in the middle of the solar night, and melatonin offset occurred before wake time just after sunrise. Sleep timing was related to circadian timing after electrical lighting-constructed conditions and less so after exposure to only natural light (Supplemental information Table S1 and Fig. S2). The advance in timing of melatonin onset was significantly larger than changes in sleep start and wake times which changed by ~1.2h (Fig. 3, both p<0.02; Bonferroni correction required p<0.025, two tailed). Weekly sleep duration (6.7±0.9h electrical versus 6.8h±0.7h natural lighting; p=0.268, twotailed) and sleep efficiency (87.6±5.6% electrical versus 87.0±4.6% natural lighting; p=0.49, two-tailed) did not significantly change indicating that a change in sleep amount or efficiency did not contribute to the current findings.
caveats: n=8 field study; directly supports the timing-not-duration framing (sleep duration 6.7h vs 6.8h, p=0.268).
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Natural sunlight is a stronger circadian zeitgeber than electrical lighting in the constructed environment.
author_quote: Natural sunlight is a stronger environmental zeitgeber or time cue for the internal circadian clock than is electrical lighting in the constructed environment.
caveats: n=8 field study summary statement.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Replicates and extends Wright 2013: natural light entrains the clock so the biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise; under a natural WINTER light-dark cycle the biological night and sleep occur earlier than under modern electrical lighting.
author_quote: We have previously shown that exposure to a natural summer 14 hr 40 min:9 hr 20 min light-dark cycle entrains the human circadian clock to solar time, such that the internal biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise [1]. Here we show the beginning of the biological night and sleep occur earlier after a week exposure to a natural winter 9 hr 20 min:14 hr 40 min light-dark cycle as compared to the modern electrical lighting environment.
caveats: Winter camping n=5; independent replication of the entrainment finding across season.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: A single weekend of natural-light camping advanced melatonin onset/midpoint ~1.4h/~1.0h within the same participants DESPITE no change in sleep timing: circadian phase, not sleep amount, is the variable that moves.
author_quote: After exposure to the natural light-dark cycle while weekend camping, melatonin onset and midpoint were ~1.4 hr and ~1.0 hr earlier within the same participants compared to the weekday (p<0.01; with large and medium effect sizes for condition [η2G = 0.45 and 0.20, respectively]), despite no change in sleep timing.
caveats: Weekend study n=14; reinforces phase-not-duration. 24h sleep duration and efficiency were similar across conditions.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Convergent field evidence: indigenous Toba/Qom hunter-gatherers and Brazilian rubber-tappers WITH electrical lighting show later circadian/sleep timing than same-community members WITHOUT it.
author_quote: others have reported later circadian and/or sleep timing in Brazilian rubber tappers [2] and in hunter-gatherers from the indigenous Toba/Qom in the Argentinean Chaco with access to electrical lighting compared to those from the same communities without access to electrical lighting
caveats: Stothard citing Moreno/de la Iglesia field studies; cross-population corroboration of the electrical-light phase delay in actual foragers/subsistence populations.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).
author_quote: Moreover, infants and mothers are induced to awaken by an arousal exhibited by the other (within seconds) therein creating interconnected, mutually dependent, synchronous arousals [1, 2].
caveats: Single-author commentary reviewing McKenna's own lab studies; cosleeping/bedsharing is contested on SIDS/safety grounds (see challenging extraction M3).
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Across the sleep period, cosleeping infant behavior is intimately linked to underlying EEG, breathing patterns, sleep architecture, and body temperature, coupled simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events.
author_quote: the behavior can be seen to be intimately linked to underlying EEGs, breathing patterns, changes in sleep architecture, body temperature and linked simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events [5].
caveats: Single-population lab observation; supports the nighttime touch/co-regulation channel but from a single contested research program.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: McKenna himself stresses that bedsharing safety depends entirely on how it is practiced and on adverse co-factors — the live SIDS/safety contestation that keeps co-sleeping from being a clean "ancestral good".
author_quote: as bedsharing safety is determined specifically by how it is practiced and by whom and what adverse factors could be associated
caveats: CHALLENGING role: the author flags that co-sleeping benefit is conditional and contested on safety/SIDS grounds; included to keep the row honestly contested rather than force it strong.
scope: EEA baseline layer; single study/population unless noted; treat exact figures as illustrative.

content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.
author_quote: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age: "KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1736 infants)." At latest follow-up: "KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence)."
caveats: Population bound: STABILIZED low-birthweight infants (not all newborns, not preterm infants before stabilization). The mortality benefit is largest in low- and middle-income settings where the incubator/NICU comparator is scarce; in high-resource settings baseline neonatal mortality is already low. Latest-follow-up estimate is GRADE moderate-quality; discharge estimate pools 8 trials.
scope: Stabilized low-birthweight infants; trials predominantly low- and middle-income settings

content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).
author_quote: Our analyses on complementary datasets using different methods yield wildly different numbers. Bayesian and generalized least-squares phylogenetic methods generate approximations of average group sizes between 69-109 and 16-42, respectively. However, enormous 95% confidence intervals (4-520 and 2-336, respectively) imply that specifying any one number is futile. A cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived in this manner.
caveats: Does NOT claim humans have no cognitive limit and does NOT show 150 is empirically wrong; shows only that the neocortex-ratio extrapolation cannot fix any specific number. Does NOT attack the nested ~5/15/50/150 layer structure or the low-hundreds ethnographic clustering, which survive. Deeper point: culture, language and institutions decouple human sociality from a primate brain-size line, so the extrapolation is the wrong inference regardless of the statistics.
scope: Challenge layer against the outer Dunbar rung of M3/M11/M5. Bears on ext 25/385/492 (human ~150 as a cognitive limit) and EEA-SOC-01; leaves the primate regression data (483/487/488/489) and the nested layer structure (404) intact.

content: Five studies supported the sociometer model: state self-esteem functions as an internal gauge that continuously tracks the individual's perceived relational value (social inclusion versus exclusion) and falls when cues signal potential social devaluation. Self-esteem is the read-out of the monitor rather than an end to be maximized; people act to protect standing. Supplies the measurement axis of M5 - how the organism reads its own position - which the mechanism previously lacked. (Relational value spans both belonging (M3) and rank (M5); tagged to M5 as the standing-monitor per this ingestion pass.)
author_quote: the self-esteem system monitors others' reactions and alerts the individual to the possibility of social exclusion
caveats: The empirical link between social acceptance/rejection and self-esteem is among the most replicated in social psychology and Leary et al. 1995 is the landmark source; graded replicated on that basis. The evolutionary FUNCTION (that self-esteem exists to monitor inclusion) is the authors' interpretation and is theoretical. Verbatim quote from the abstract, cross-checked across three independent PDF extractions.
scope: 5 studies, US university samples; construct = state and trait self-esteem

content: The sociometer is calibrated to a small, bounded set of personally significant others rather than to an unbounded audience, and it responds primarily to exclusion (a deprivation state) rather than to ever-greater inclusion: in Studies 3 and 4, exclusion for personal reasons lowered state self-esteem while inclusion produced no matching rise, and random exclusion did not lower it. Directly supports M5's resolution condition that the monitored reference group is bounded and personally known, and M5's mismatch prediction that global mediated audiences over-drive a monitor built for a small group.
author_quote: The sociometer system would serve its purpose if it simply assured that the person maintained sufficient social connections with a relatively small set of personally significant people
caveats: The exclusion-versus-inclusion asymmetry is empirical (Studies 3-4), but the bounded-small-set and exclusion-primacy claims are the authors' functional interpretation of that pattern rather than a directly measured quantity; graded theoretical (conservative). Verbatim quote cross-checked across three independent PDF extractions.
scope: 5 studies, US university samples; Studies 3-4 experimental exclusion manipulations

content: Two experimental studies of hierarchy formation among previously unacquainted people showed that Dominance (using force and intimidation to induce fear) and Prestige (sharing expertise and know-how to gain freely conferred respect) are near-orthogonal (mean correlation close to zero) yet each independently secures real rank: greater perceived influence, greater actual influence over group decisions, and more visual attention from others. Dominance produced influence even where dominant individuals were rated less likable, so influence is separable from liking. Establishes M5's earned-prestige-versus-coerced-dominance distinction as a measurable feature of live human groups rather than a purely theoretical claim, and shows coerced dominance is a partial resolver of rank rather than a non-resolver.
author_quote: The finding that Dominance and Prestige can coexist within social groups as viable rank-promoting strategies suggests that human social hierarchies are multidimensional.
caveats: Cheng et al. 2013 is two experimental studies, not by itself a replication programme (per the ingestion brief); graded conservatively. It is solid experimental data, not mere theory - the cross-cultural replication of the distinction is carried in this pass by von Rueden 2011 (Tsimane) and Garfield & Hagen 2020 (Chabu), consistent with Henrich & Gil-White 2001. Dominance/Prestige operational definitions paraphrased from the abstract; the coexistence sentence is a verbatim quote from the General Discussion.
scope: 2 studies; groups of previously unacquainted university participants; round-robin peer ratings and eye-tracking of visual attention

content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists (Bolivia), both dominance (men more likely to win a dyadic physical confrontation) and prestige (men with more community-wide influence) associate with higher fertility, via different pathways: dominant men have higher intra-marital fertility for their age, while prestigious men show both higher intra-marital fertility and lower offspring mortality. Prestige is the strongest single pathway from status to fitness in this population. Both routes elicit allies' support and competitors' deference but do not buy extra provisioning. Non-WEIRD cross-cultural replication that the dominance/prestige distinction is real and carries genuine fitness consequences, grounding the inclusive-fitness (P1) basis of M5.
author_quote: Prestigious but not dominant men marry wives who first give birth at earlier ages, which multivariate analysis suggests is the strongest pathway between status and fitness in this population.
caveats: Cross-sectional study in a single small-scale society; pathway estimates are population-specific and status is measured for men. Graded theoretical (conservative) though it is empirical field data; it supplies non-WEIRD cross-cultural breadth for the dominance/prestige distinction, per the ingestion brief. Ligatures (fi) normalized in the verbatim quote; no other characters altered.
scope: Tsimane forager-horticulturalists, Bolivia; male status and reproductive success; cross-sectional

content: Among the Chabu (recently settled Ethiopian hunter-gatherers), peer-rated prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted elected leader status, prestige was clearly more important (dominance's effect was weaker and sensitive to the statistical prior). Most leadership traits covaried strongly, indicating a general leadership/respect factor, and women as well as men held elected leadership. Supports M5's earned-prestige-preferred clause in a non-WEIRD small-scale society and confirms the biased-social-learning (Mentor-salience) prediction of the Henrich & Gil-White model.
author_quote: Measures of prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted leader status, prestige was more important.
caveats: Cross-sectional, single Chabu community; graded theoretical (conservative) though empirical field data. IMPORTANT for the challenge question: the authors SUPPORT a general distinction between dominance and prestige ('Our data do support a general distinction between dominance and prestige') and prestige-primacy; they do NOT argue for abandoning the dual model. The genuine nuance retained here is the strong covariation of most leadership traits (a general factor) and the need to incorporate women leaders - a call to revise, not to discard, the dual model.
scope: Chabu, southwestern Ethiopia; 60 adult peer-raters; elected leaders versus non-leaders; cross-sectional, preregistered

content: Landmark controlled human experiment (N=10) using a 28-h forced-desynchrony day to isolate circadian misalignment from behavior.
