With subjects eating and sleeping about 12 h out of phase, leptin fell 17 percent, glucose rose 6 percent despite a 22 percent rise in insulin, the daily cortisol rhythm fully reversed, mean arterial pressure rose 3 percent, and sleep efficiency dropped 20 percent; 3 of 8 subjects reached postprandial glucose in the prediabetic range. Direct causal human evidence that circadian misalignment, as in shift work and jet lag, produces adverse cardiometabolic change independent of the amount of sleep or food.
author_quote: Circadian misalignment, when subjects ate and slept ≈12 h out of phase from their habitual times, systematically decreased leptin (−17%, P < 0.001), increased glucose (+6%, P < 0.001) despite increased insulin (+22%, P = 0.006), completely reversed the daily cortisol rhythm ( P < 0.001), increased mean arterial pressure (+3%, P = 0.001), and reduced sleep efficiency (−20%, P < 0.002). Notably, circadian misalignment caused 3 of 8 subjects (with sufficient available data) to exhibit postprandial glucose responses in the range typical of a prediabetic state.
caveats: Small sample (N=10) and acute laboratory misalignment, not chronic field shift work. Same laboratory (Scheer) as work 134 (Morris 2016); treat the pair as related rather than independent replication. Full text obtained: PMC2657421.
scope: N=10 healthy adults; 10-day forced-desynchrony (28-h day) misalignment protocol

content: Controlled human study (two 8-day protocols with a rapid 12-h inversion simulating night-shift misalignment) showing circadian misalignment raised 24-h systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 3.0 and 1.5 mmHg, driven mainly by higher blood pressure during sleep opportunities (systolic +5.6 mmHg), and lowered wake cardiac vagal modulation by 8 to 15 percent. Direct causal human evidence that misalignment itself raises cardiovascular risk factors, helping explain shift-work hypertension.
author_quote: Here we show—by using two 8-d laboratory protocols—that short-term circadian misalignment (12-h inverted behavioral and environmental cycles for three days) adversely affects cardiovascular risk factors in healthy adults. Circadian misalignment increased 24-h systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) by 3.0 mmHg and 1.5 mmHg, respectively.
caveats: Controlled laboratory misalignment, not field shift work. Same laboratory (Scheer senior author) as work 133 (Scheer 2009); related rather than independent. Full text obtained: PMC4790999.
scope: Two 8-day laboratory protocols; rapid 12-h behavioral inversion simulating night-shift misalignment

content: In the same misalignment protocol, circadian misalignment raised 24-h inflammatory markers (interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, resistin, and tumour necrosis factor-alpha) by 3 to 29 percent. Human evidence that circadian misalignment drives systemic inflammation, coupling the circadian system (M7) to immune regulation (M8) and giving a mechanism for shift-work cardiovascular and immune risk.
author_quote: Circadian misalignment increased 24-h serum interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, resistin, and tumor necrosis factor-α levels by 3–29%.
caveats: Controlled laboratory misalignment. Same laboratory as work 133 (Scheer 2009). Full text obtained: PMC4790999.
scope: Same misalignment protocol; 24-h serum inflammatory markers

content: Dose-response study of the human circadian pacemaker to evening light. Half of the maximal phase delay and half of the maximal melatonin suppression produced by bright evening light (about 9000 lux) were obtained with just over 1 percent of that intensity, about 100 lux of dim room light, both following a logistic dose-response curve. Ordinary indoor evening light is therefore enough to suppress melatonin and shift circadian phase, putting M7's indoor (ATTENUATED) and evening-screen (DEFEATED) rungs on direct dose-response evidence.
author_quote: Contrary to expectations, we found that half of the maximal phase-delaying response achieved in response to a single episode of evening bright light (∼9000 lux (lx)) can be obtained with just over 1 % of this light (dim room light of ∼100 lx). The same held true for the acute suppressive effects of light on plasma melatonin concentrations. This indicates that even small changes in ordinary light exposure during the late evening hours can significantly affect both plasma melatonin concentrations and the entrained phase of the human circadian pacemaker.
caveats: Single controlled study; the specific 100-lux half-max is this study's quantification of a field-established phenomenon (evening light resets the human clock). Czeisler laboratory, as with work 136 (Khalsa 2003). Full text obtained: PMC2270041.
scope: N=23; single 6.5-h nocturnal light exposure across a range of illuminances (3 to 9100 lux)

content: Definitive characterization of the human phase-response curve (PRC) to single bright-light pulses. Light before the core-body-temperature minimum delays the clock, light after it advances the clock, and there is no phase shift exactly at the critical phase; the melatonin-midpoint PRC has a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h with no prolonged photic dead zone during the subjective day. Grounds the core M7 claim that light is the entraining signal and that its effect is timing-dependent, so mistimed evening light actively mis-sets the clock.
author_quote: The resultant PRC of the midpoint of the melatonin rhythm revealed a characteristic type 1 PRC with a significant peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h. Phase delays occurred when the light stimulus was centred prior to the critical phase at the core body temperature minimum, phase advances occurred when the light stimulus was centred after the critical phase, and no phase shift occurred at the critical phase.
caveats: Single comprehensive study; the PRC shape is field-replicated across laboratories, the amplitude value is this study's. Czeisler laboratory. Full text obtained: PMC2342968.
scope: N=21; single bright-light pulses scheduled across the circadian cycle; melatonin-based phase in constant routine

content: Systematic review and meta-analysis of shift work and vascular events (34 studies, 2,011,935 people). Shift work was associated with myocardial infarction (risk ratio 1.23, 95 percent CI 1.15 to 1.31), ischaemic stroke (1.05, 1.01 to 1.09), and any coronary event (1.24, 1.10 to 1.39); population attributable risks at Canadian shift-work prevalence were about 7.0 percent for MI and 7.3 percent for coronary events. First shift-work epidemiology in M7's base, directly evidencing the shift-work (MINIMAL) rung. It also cuts on the flagged PARTIAL-versus-MINIMAL ordering: shift work is tied to hard cardiovascular endpoints, more severe than social jetlag's BMI-only association, supporting shift work as the more severe rung.
author_quote: Shift work is associated with vascular events, which may have implications for public policy and occupational medicine.
caveats: Observational studies (association, with Scheer and Morris supplying the causal mechanism). Honest limits: shift work was NOT associated with increased mortality (vascular or all-cause), and the coronary-event pooled estimate had high heterogeneity (I-squared 85 percent). Full text obtained: PMC3406223.
scope: 34 observational studies, 2,011,935 people; primary outcomes myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, any coronary event

content: First nationally representative estimate of the US chronotype distribution, from 12 years of American Time Use Survey diaries (n=53,689, chronotype = weekend mid-sleep). Chronotype is near-normally distributed and spans almost 10 hours; the mean shifts later through adolescence to a peak in lateness at about 19 years and earlier thereafter, and men are later chronotypes than women before 40 but earlier after. Adolescents are on average the latest chronotypes, which the authors note supports later school start times. Grounds M7's social-jetlag (PARTIAL) rung: fixed social and school schedules collide with a wide, developmentally shifting range of internal circadian phase, and the resolution condition is aligning schedule to internal time.
author_quote: The distribution’s mean value is systematically different with age, shifting later during adolescence, showing a peak in ‘lateness’ at ~19 years, and shifting earlier thereafter. Men are typically later chronotypes than women before 40, but earlier types after 40.
caveats: Cross-sectional survey; chronotype inferred from weekend mid-sleep, a validated proxy for dim-light melatonin onset. The age and sex chronotype pattern is field-replicated across German, Italian, Finnish, New Zealand, and Brazilian samples cited in the paper. Till Roenneberg (MCTQ) is senior author. Full text obtained: PMC5479630.
scope: n=53,689; American Time Use Survey diaries pooled 2003-2014; chronotype = weekend mid-sleep (MSFWe)

content: Longitudinal study of 624 Filipino men followed 4.5 years (Cebu cohort). Single nonfathers with high waking testosterone at baseline were more likely to become partnered fathers by follow-up. Men who became partnered fathers then showed large declines in waking (median -26%) and evening (median -34%) testosterone, significantly exceeding the declines of men who stayed single nonfathers. Fathers reporting 3 or more hours of daily childcare had lower testosterone at follow-up than fathers not involved in care. Testosterone and reproductive strategy are bidirectional in human males: high testosterone predicts mating success, then testosterone drops when men take up direct care of offspring.
location: PNAS 108(39):16194-16199. Abstract + Results, full text via PMC3182719.
author_quote: Our findings suggest that T mediates tradeoffs between mating and parenting in humans, as seen in other species in which fathers care for young.
caveats: Single population (Cebu, Philippines), though large and representative. The childcare dose effect (3+ h/day) is observational within the cohort. Any mismatch interpretation (reduced direct father care in isolated nuclear settings) is layered on top of the finding and stays theoretical.
scope: Human males, prospective longitudinal cohort

content: fMRI study of 89 first-time parents in three groups: primary-caregiving mothers, secondary-caregiving fathers, and primary-caregiving fathers raising infants without maternal involvement. All parents activated a shared global parental caregiving network integrating emotional processing and mentalizing circuits. Primary-caregiving fathers showed amygdala activation comparable to primary-caregiving mothers alongside father-typical superior temporal sulcus activation, and amygdala-STS connectivity scaled with time spent in direct childcare across all fathers. The care network is shared across sexes and its recruitment tracks caregiving experience.
location: PNAS 111(27):9792-9797. Abstract + Results, full text via PMC4103311.
author_quote: Among all fathers, time spent in direct childcare was linked with the degree of amygdala-STS connectivity.
caveats: Single study (n=89); graded thin until the wider paternal-brain literature is ingested. Group assignment was not random: primary-caregiving fathers were recruited from two-father families. Cross-sectional design, so caregiving time and connectivity are correlated rather than causally ordered.
scope: First-time parents, fMRI

content: Systematic review of father-absence studies restricted to causal-inference designs: lagged dependent variable models, growth curve models, individual and sibling fixed effects, natural experiments, and propensity score matching. Rigorous designs continue to find negative effects of father absence on offspring wellbeing, with smaller magnitudes than traditional cross-sectional estimates. Evidence is strongest and most consistent for high school graduation, social-emotional adjustment in childhood, and adult mental health.
location: Annual Review of Sociology 39:399-427. Abstract + Conclusion, full text via PMC3904543.
author_quote: Our assessment is that studies using more rigorous designs continue to find negative effects of father absence on offspring well-being, although the magnitude of these effects is smaller than what is found using traditional cross-sectional designs.
caveats: Effects are averages across heterogeneous causes of absence (divorce, nonmarital birth). Father absence bundles loss of direct paternal care with loss of income and household stability; the review cannot fully separate these channels. Mostly US and comparable industrialized samples.
scope: US and comparable industrialized populations

content: Polderman and colleagues aggregate virtually the entire twin literature: twin correlations and reported variance components for 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications, covering 14,558,903 partly dependent twin pairs. Across all traits the reported heritability is 49%, and heritability estimates cluster strongly within functional domains. This is the twin-design leg of the C15 triangulation: individual variation in every measured behavioral and psychological trait domain is substantially heritable.
author_quote: We report a meta-analysis of twin correlations and reported variance components for 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications including 14,558,903 partly dependent twin pairs, virtually all published twin studies of complex traits. Estimates of heritability cluster strongly within functional domains, and across all traits the reported heritability is 49%.
caveats: Reported heritability is the average across all published estimates, weighting traits as reported rather than as an unbiased trait sample; twin pairs across publications are partly dependent (the same cohorts contribute to multiple trait reports).

content: The pooled twin correlations across all traits: monozygotic 0.636 versus dizygotic 0.339, the classic roughly-double MZ resemblance that signals additive genetic influence. Reported heritability across all traits is 0.488 and the reported shared-environment component is 0.174. For a majority (69%) of traits the observed correlations are consistent with a parsimonious model in which twin resemblance is due solely to additive genetic variation. Quantifies DA10's heritable-ranges claim at the scale of the whole literature, and simultaneously shows half the variance is not additive-genetic.
author_quote: The meta-analyses of all traits yielded an average rMZ of 0.636 (s.e.m. = 0.002) and an average rDZ of 0.339 (s.e.m. = 0.003). The reported heritability (h2) across all traits was 0.488 (s.e.m. = 0.004), and the reported estimate of shared environmental effects (c2) was 0.174 (s.e.m. = 0.004)
caveats: Quote is the opening of the all-traits results paragraph; h2 and c2 are as reported by the source publications, not re-estimated from raw data. Superscript 2 in h2/c2 rendered as plain digit.

content: The founding GCTA result: estimating genetic variance directly from 294,831 common SNPs genotyped in 3,925 unrelated individuals recovers 45% of the variance in height, with no twin or family structure anywhere in the design. Heritability estimated by twin and family designs is real and hiding in many variants of individually small effect rather than missing. This is the molecular leg of C15, a method family fully independent of the other two; the SNP-heritability approach has since been replicated across traits and cohorts throughout complex-trait genetics.
author_quote: We estimated the proportion of variance for human height explained by 294,831 SNPs genotyped on 3,925 unrelated individuals using a linear model analysis, and validated the estimation method by simulations based upon the observed genotype data. We show that 45% of variance can be explained by considering all SNPs simultaneously. Thus, most of the heritability is not missing but has not previously been detected because the individual effects are too small to pass stringent significance tests.
caveats: Height, not a behavioral trait; the extraction carries the method-family point (heritability from unrelated individuals) rather than a behavioral estimate. SNP heritability bounds below twin estimates because it captures only common-variant effects. Quote from the PMC author manuscript of the paper.

content: Turkheimer's canonical compression of five decades of behavior-genetic findings into three laws. For DA10 the first law states the heritable-variation claim across all human behavioral traits; the second and third laws carry the guard rail: shared family environment accounts for less variance than genes, and a substantial residual is accounted for by neither, so heritability describes population variance partitioning, not individual determinism. Later quantitatively confirmed at scale by Polderman et al. 2015.
author_quote: First Law. All human behavioral traits are heritable. Second Law. The effect of being raised in the same family is smaller than the effect of genes. Third Law. A substantial portion of the variation in complex human behavioral traits is not accounted for by the effects of genes or families.
caveats: Bullet markers before each law dropped; the three laws are printed as a bulleted list in the original. Turkheimer himself argues in the same paper that these laws should reshape, not end, the nature-nurture debate.

content: Plomin, DeFries, Knopik and Neiderhiser's top-ten list opens with the first-law finding: all psychological traits show significant and substantial genetic influence, across cognitive abilities, psychopathology and personality, corroborated across twin, family, and adoption designs with cross-national replication. The adoption/family-design leg of C15: genetic influence on parameter variation appears whether resemblance is measured in twins, in adoptees and their birth parents, or in extended families. The same review notes that four of the ten findings are about environmental influence, which is DA10's guard rail from inside behavior genetics itself.
author_quote: Finally, we note that four of the top-10 findings (2, 7, 8 and 9) are about environmental influences rather than genetic influences. By using genetically sensitive designs such as twin studies, behavioral genetics has revealed almost as much about the environment as about genetics.
caveats: Finding 1's own summary sentence ("We are unable to find any reliably measured behavioral trait for which genetic influence is not significantly different from zero in more than one adequately powered study") is the adoption-corroborated claim; the quoted passage is the review's framing of the environment findings. Quote from the PMC author manuscript.

content: The Panksepp-school statement of what M2 is: the mesolimbic dopamine system activates an instinctual appetitive SEEKING state that induces organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli. SEEKING is the general-purpose engagement disposition of the awake animal rather than a response to a specific deficit signal, which is why its activation profile is not homeostatic in the M13 sense: no single tissue variable builds pressure and terminates it.
author_quote: The affective neuroethological perspective presented here, views the ML-DA system in terms of its ability to activate an instinctual emotional appetitive state (SEEKING) evolved to induce organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli and to avoid harms.
caveats: The SEEKING construct is Panksepp-school theory over replicated dopamine physiology; graded theoretical for the affective interpretation, not for the underlying ML-DA findings. Comma after "here" is in the original. Quote from the PMC rendering of the author manuscript.

content: The physiological basis for M2's mixed activation profile: dopamine transmission runs in two modes. Phasic release is short-lasting, impulse-dependent, cue and reward-prediction locked; tonic extracellular dopamine sits at low concentration and changes slowly, carrying a background level of appetitive engagement that varies with state (sleep-wake, arousal). For activation_class this grounds tonic_baseline as M2's primary class with event_triggered phasic spikes as secondary; the phasic incentive-salience side is already carried in C6 by Berridge.
location: Section 2.5, Electric activity of DA cells
author_quote: Phasic DA transmission is the short-lasting and impulse-dependent release that appears as a consequence of neural burst firing (Gonon, 1988; Suaud-Chagny et al., 1992). Following such bursts, high levels of DA molecules are released into the synaptic cleft at up to mM concentration (Garris et al., 1994), and then rapidly removed via a re-uptake system (Floresco et al. 2003). To the contrary, tonic DA levels are diffused in the extracellular space outside the synaptic clefts, but exist in very small concentrations (in the nM range), and change relatively slowly (Grace, 2000).
caveats: Spacing inside parenthetical citations normalized from the PMC HTML rendering; wording otherwise verbatim, inline citations retained. Tonic/phasic DA transmission is replicated electrophysiology; the mapping onto SEEKING's affective profile is the Panksepp-school interpretation.

content: The incentive-motivation account of M14: sexual motivation is activated by external sexual incentive stimuli interacting with a central motive state; it is not a homeostatic reservoir in which unexpended sexual energy accumulates as an internal need. The review endorses Beach's rejection of an internal origin ("sexual motivation is active only in the presence of an external stimulus") and builds the modern model on Bindra and Toates incentive theory. No tissue deficit accumulates during abstinence; desire follows cue-triggered arousal rather than spontaneous internal pressure. For activation_class: event_triggered (incentive), not homeostatic.
author_quote: Sexual incentive stimuli activate sexual motivation and heighten the level of general arousal. The sexual motive may induce the individual to approach the incentive, and eventually to initiate sexual acts.
caveats: The Lorenz/Freud psychohydraulic reservoir is rejected across the modern literature the review synthesizes; the quoted abstract states the positive model. The Beach endorsement quoted in the content field is at section 3.3. Sexual motivation still interacts with state variables (general arousal, hormonal status), which is gain modulation rather than deficit accumulation.

content: Hormones set the gain, not the pressure: in rats and humans, testicular hormones control the long-term activity level of the sexual central motive state (in men via androgen receptors directly; in rats partly via aromatization to estrogens), while short-term variation in sexual motivation is driven by incentive stimuli, not by hormone fluctuation. The same structure is proposed for women (androgens needed for basic long-term activity of the central motive state). This is the hormonal gain-modulation half of M14's activation profile: testosterone tunes cue-sensitivity; cues do the triggering.
location: Section on endocrine control of the central motive state
author_quote: Thus, in rats and humans there is no doubt that testicular hormones, either directly or via aromatization, are in charge of the control of the long-term activity of the sexual central motive state.
caveats: The review notes the molecular mechanisms of these hormone actions remain obscure, and that it is unknown whether sexually relevant stimuli cause testosterone release in women; the long-term/short-term division (hormones set baseline gain, incentives drive momentary motivation) is the load-bearing claim.

content: The Minnesota Starvation Experiment (Keys, 1944-45, 36 conscientious objectors under controlled semi-starvation) documents reproductive-axis shutdown under sustained energy deficit: sexual interest collapsed almost immediately once semi-starvation began, while food became the dominant preoccupation and social engagement narrowed. Evidence that an unresolved M13 deficit suppresses M14, supporting state-dependent drive priority: DA8 priority relations behave as slope functions of current state rather than a fixed order.
location: Section on the psychological effects of semistarvation, participant interviews
author_quote: Several of the men, like Max Kampelman, agreed that nearly immediately after semistarvation began, all interest in women and dating was lost: "I can tell you, the sex drive disappeared. There was none."
caveats: Historical review reporting Keys's experiment and participant recollections, not the primary monograph (Keys et al. 1950, The Biology of Human Starvation); single landmark controlled experiment, N=36, all male volunteers; the quoted line is a participant recollection collected decades later.
